papers.abstract: Jinhe Bi, Yujun Wang, Haokun Chen, Xun Xiao, Artur Hecker, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Causal Abstraction: A Theoretical Foundation for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Under what conditions does a transparent algorithm constitute a faithful interpretation of the known, but opaque, low-level details of a black box model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper generalizes the theory of causal abstraction from mechanism replacement to arbitrary mechanism transformation, and uses this framework to provide a flexible, precise formalization for core mechanistic interpretability concepts (polysemantic neurons, linear representation hypothesis, modular features, graded faithfulness) and to unify a wide range of existing interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: Causal abstraction provides a solid theoretical foundation for mechanistic interpretability, enabling precise definitions of core concepts and a unified perspective on existing methods, which facilitates rigorous falsification through experimentation.
papers.key_findings:
Causal abstraction theory is generalized to allow for arbitrary mechanism transformations (interventionals), which enables the isolation of quantities distributed across overlapping sets of microvariables.
The core concepts of polysemantic neurons, the linear representation hypothesis, modular features, and graded faithfulness are given flexible, mathematically precise definitions within the causal abstraction framework.
A wide range of mechanistic interpretability methods (e.g., activation patching, causal scrubbing, sparse autoencoders, steering) and behavioral interpretability methods (e.g., LIME, integrated gradients) are unified under the common language of causal abstraction.
papers.abstract: Causal abstraction provides a theoretical foundation for mechanistic interpretability, the field concerned with providing intelligible algorithms that are faithful simplifications of the known, but opaque low-level details of black box AI models. Our contributions are (1) generalizing the theory of causal abstraction from mechanism replacement (i.e., hard and soft interventions) to arbitrary mechanism transformation (i.e., functionals from old mechanisms to new mechanisms), (2) providing a flexible, yet precise formalization for the core concepts of polysemantic neurons, the linear representation hypothesis, modular features, and graded faithfulness, and (3) unifying a variety of mechanistic interpretability methods in the common language of causal abstraction, namely, activation and path patching, causal mediation analysis, causal scrubbing, causal tracing, circuit analysis, concept erasure, sparse autoencoders, differential binary masking, distributed alignment search, and steering.

papers.title: Layer of Truth: Probing Belief Shifts under Continual Pre-Training Poisoning
papers.research_question: How does repeated exposure to plausible falsehoods during continual pre-training alter the internal factual representations (beliefs) in large language models? Specifically, does poisoning cause systematic belief replacement, where in the network is corruption localized and recoverable, and how do these shifts generalize across prompts, tasks, and languages?
papers.core_contribution: Continual pre-training on plausible misinformation can systematically overwrite specific factual knowledge in LLMs without degrading overall performance, with belief shifts concentrated in late transformer layers and generalizing across prompts and tasks.
papers.conclusion: Continual pre-training poisoning can overwrite internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating the need for representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.
papers.key_findings:
Poisoning shifts probability mass from correct to counterfactual answers without increasing ambiguity, indicating systematic belief replacement rather than diffuse uncertainty.
Belief flips occur abruptly across checkpoints and are concentrated in late transformer layers (e.g., Layers 29–36 in 3B models).
Activation patching in late layers can partially reverse the corruption, rescuing up to 56.8% of poisoned beliefs.
Poisoned beliefs generalize beyond training prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag) while leaving alignment benchmarks (TruthfulQA, HH-RLHF) largely stable.
Cross-lingual transfer of poisoned beliefs is imperfect, with weaker expression and higher ambiguity in languages not used during poisoning (e.g., Russian vs. English).
papers.abstract: We show that continual pretraining on plausible misinformation can overwrite specific factual knowledge in large language models without degrading overall performance. Unlike prior poisoning work under static pretraining, we study repeated exposure to counterfactual claims during continual updates. Using paired fact-counterfact items with graded poisoning ratios, we track how internal preferences between competing facts evolve across checkpoints, layers, and model scales. Even moderate poisoning (50-100%) flips over 55% of responses from correct to counterfactual while leaving ambiguity nearly unchanged. These belief flips emerge abruptly, concentrate in late layers (e.g., Layers 29-36 in 3B models), and are partially reversible via patching (up to 56.8%). The corrupted beliefs generalize beyond poisoned prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning while leaving alignment benchmarks largely intact and transferring imperfectly across languages. These results expose a failure mode of continual pre-training in which targeted misinformation replaces internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.

papers.title: CausalFormer-HMC: a hybrid memory-driven transformer with causal reasoning and counterfactual explainability for leukemia diagnosis
papers.research_question: How can a hybrid AI model combining CNNs, vision transformers, and causal reasoning improve the accuracy and interpretability of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) diagnosis from peripheral blood smear images?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Causal-Former-HMC, a novel hybrid AI architecture that integrates CNNs, vision transformers, and a causal graph learner with counterfactual reasoning to achieve high accuracy and interpretability in diagnosing Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia from peripheral blood smear images.
papers.conclusion: Causal-Former-HMC represents a significant step forward in AI-driven leukemia detection, combining superior accuracy with transparency, and paves the way for its application in real-world clinical care.
papers.key_findings:
The model achieved perfect classification accuracy (100%) and macro-averaged F1-scores on the ALL dataset.
On the C-NMC dataset, the model achieved up to 98.5% accuracy with a 0.9975 ROC-AUC.
Explainable AI techniques (Grad-CAM, LIME, Integrated Gradients, SHAP) consistently highlighted clinically relevant features such as nuclear contour irregularities and chromatin condensation.
The model demonstrated robust generalization across two independent datasets using stratified 5-fold cross-validation.
The hybrid architecture effectively combines local feature extraction (CNNs), global contextual understanding (ViTs), and causal reasoning for improved diagnostic precision.
papers.limitation:
The datasets employed are relatively modest in size and originate from limited sources, which may restrict generalizability.
The reported 100% accuracy on the ALL dataset raises concerns about potential overfitting in homogeneous data settings.
The datasets represent controlled environments that may not fully capture variability in real-world clinical workflows (e.g., differences in staining protocols, imaging devices).
future_direction: Large-scale, multi-center validation across diverse populations and real-world laboratory conditions.
Integration of multimodal data, such as PBS images with health records or genomic profiles.
Real-world deployment and testing in live clinical settings to assess integration into existing workflows.
papers.abstract: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is a prevalent malignancy particularly among children. It poses diagnostic challenges due to its morphological similarities with normal cells and the limitations of conventional methods like bone marrow biopsies, which are invasive and resource-intensive. This study introduces Causal-Former-HMC, a novel hybrid AI architecture integrating convolutional neural networks, vision transformers, and a causal graph learner with counterfactual reasoning to enhance diagnostic precision and interpretability from peripheral blood smear (PBS) images. We utilized two robust datasets: the ALL Image collection, comprising 89 patients and 3,256 PBS images (504 benign, 2,752 malignant across Pro B, Pre B, and Early Pre B subtypes), and C-NMC dataset, containing 15,135 segmented cell images from 118 patients (7,272 leukemic, 3,389 normal). To address class imbalance, we implemented class-aware data augmentation, standardizing image counts across classes and resizing to 128 × 128 pixels for compatibility with our model. The proposed model is evaluated via stratified 5-fold cross-validation with Nadam, SGD, and Radam (fractional) optimizers, Causal-Former-HMC achieved perfect classification accuracy (100%) and macro-averaged F1-scores on the ALL dataset, and up to 98.5% accuracy with 0.9975 ROC-AUC on the C-NMC dataset hence demonstrating superior generalization. Interpretability was ensured through advanced explainable AI techniques, including Grad-CAM, LIME, Integrated Gradients, and SHAP, which consistently highlighted attention to clinically relevant features such as nuclear contour irregularities and chromatin condensation. These results underscore the potential of the model to deliver non-invasive, accurate and transparent diagnostics that pave the way for its integration into clinical hematology workflows and advancing AI-driven leukemia screening paradigms. Index Terms-Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL); Causal-Former-HMC; Hybrid Deep Learning; Peripheral Blood Smear Classification; Explainable AI in Medical Imaging.

papers.title: Exploring the LLM Journey from Cognition to Expression with Linear Representations
papers.research_question: How do cognitive and expressive capabilities develop and interact in large language models across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback stages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cognitive capabilities in LLMs are established during pretraining, while expressive capabilities develop during SFT and RLHF, with cognitive capability setting an upper bound for expressive capability.
papers.conclusion: This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of LLM training processes.
papers.key_findings:
Cognitive capability is primarily established during the pretraining stage, whereas expressive capability develops during SFT and RLHF.
There is a strong statistical correlation between cognitive and expressive capabilities, with cognitive capability acting as an upper bound.
The gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities can be bridged by optimization-free methods such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling.
The vocabulary linear layer plays a crucial role in expressive capability, and its training during SFT/RLHF helps reduce the gap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals a plateau in cognitive capability in deeper layers, indicating redundancy in the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring additional linear analysis techniques for model analysis and control.
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the evolution and interplay of cognitive and expressive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a specific focus on Baichuan-7B and Baichuan-33B, an advanced bilingual (Chinese and English) LLM series. We define and explore the model's cognitive and expressive capabilities through linear representations across three critical phases: Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Cognitive capability is defined as the quantity and quality of information conveyed by the neuron output vectors within the network, similar to the neural signal processing in human cognition. Expressive capability is defined as the model's capability to produce word-level output. Our findings unveil a sequential development pattern, where cognitive abilities are largely established during Pretraining, whereas expressive abilities predominantly advance during SFT and RLHF. Statistical analyses confirm a significant correlation between the two capabilities, suggesting that cognitive capacity may limit expressive potential. The paper also explores the theoretical underpinnings of these divergent developmental trajectories and their connection to the LLMs' architectural design. Moreover, we evaluate various optimization-independent strategies, such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling, which bridge the gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities. This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of their training processes.

papers.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: What are the primary mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in large language models during continual fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies three primary mechanisms of catastrophic forgetting in LLMs during sequential fine-tuning: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening around prior task minima.
papers.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting in LLMs is driven by three interacting mechanisms (attention disruption, representational drift, loss landscape flattening), providing a mechanistic foundation for developing targeted continual learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 15-23% of attention heads, particularly in lower layers, undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, driving early forgetting.
Representational drift in intermediate layers, measured by CKA similarity, decreases by 0.32 to 0.47, indicating significant geometric changes.
Gradient interference, especially in query and key projection matrices, strongly predicts forgetting severity (correlation r=0.87).
The loss landscape around previous task minima flattens substantially (maximum Hessian eigenvalue drops from 147.3 to 34.2), making recovery difficult.
These three mechanisms interact and operate at different timescales, with attention disruption early, representational drift accumulating, and landscape flattening emerging later.
papers.limitation:
Experimental design focused on task sequences with clear boundaries, not continuous adaptation to gradually shifting distributions.
Examined forgetting over relatively short task sequences (4 to 6 tasks), while practical systems may encounter hundreds of sequential tasks.
Mechanistic analysis primarily characterized average behaviors across many model instances; understanding individual variability and rare failure modes remains important.
future_direction: Developing architecture modifications that inherently resist the identified forgetting mechanisms, such as attention heads with built-in stability constraints or intermediate layers with protected representational subspaces.
Designing optimization algorithms that explicitly manage gradient interference, representational drift, and landscape geometry during fine-tuning.
Creating diagnostic tools that monitor mechanistic signatures in real-time to prevent catastrophic forgetting before it occurs.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit remarkable performance across diverse tasks through pre-training and fine-tuning paradigms. However, continual fine-tuning on sequential tasks induces catastrophic forgetting, where newly acquired knowledge interferes with previously learned capabilities. Despite widespread observations of this phenomenon, the mechanistic understanding remains limited. Here, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of catastrophic forgetting in transformer-based LLMs during sequential fine-tuning. Through systematic experiments across multiple model scales (109B to 400B total parameters) and task sequences, we identify three primary mechanisms driving forgetting: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening. We demonstrate that forgetting severity correlates strongly with task similarity (Pearson r = 0.87) and gradient alignment metrics. Our analysis reveals that approximately 15 to 23 percent of attention heads undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, with lower layers showing greater susceptibility. These findings establish mechanistic foundations for developing targeted mitigation strategies in continual learning systems.

papers.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in Medical Imaging: Techniques, Applications, Challenges, and Future Directions
papers.research_question: How can Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques be applied in medical imaging to enhance interpretability, transparency, and clinical trust?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive review of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques in medical imaging, discussing their applications, challenges, and future directions to enhance interpretability and clinical trust.
papers.conclusion: XAI is crucial for bridging the gap between high-performing deep learning models and the need for interpretability in clinical environments, with future work needed to address challenges and improve usability.
papers.key_findings:
Feature visualization techniques like Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients are widely used to highlight important image regions in medical diagnostics.
Attention mechanisms improve model interpretability by focusing on relevant regions, but lack standardized metrics for clinical validation.
Rule-based and symbolic XAI approaches offer high interpretability and align well with clinical guidelines, as demonstrated in vertebral fracture detection.
Example-based methods, such as case-based reasoning, provide intuitive explanations by referencing similar past cases, enhancing clinical trust.
Major challenges include the trade-off between accuracy and interpretability, ethical concerns, and integration barriers in clinical workflows.
future_direction: Refining example-based techniques for better interpretability.
Developing ethical frameworks to address bias and privacy concerns.
Improving generalizability and performance of explainable models.
papers.abstract: The integration of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) into medical imaging is pivotal in addressing the “black-box” limitations of deep learning models, which often hinder clinical trust and regulatory approval. This review provides a comprehensive examination of XAI techniques that enhance interpretability and transparency in diagnostic imaging applications. Key approaches such as feature visualization (Grad-CAM, Integrated Gradients), attention mechanisms, symbolic reasoning, and example-based methods—are explored alongside their practical implementations. Specific cases in cardiac imaging, cancer diagnostics, and brain lesion segmentation illustrate the value of XAI in improving clinical decision-making and patient care. Moreover, the review highlights major challenges, including the trade-off between accuracy and interpretability, ethical and legal constraints, integration barriers within clinical workflows, and the complexity of medical data. To address these issues, future research directions are proposed, including the development of more robust example-based models, ethical frameworks, generalizable architectures, advanced visualization techniques, and interdisciplinary collaboration. With continued refinement and responsible deployment, XAI systems can enable AI models to become not only accurate but also interpretable and clinically relevant. This paper underscores the transformative potential of XAI in building trustworthy, transparent, and effective AI-driven diagnostic tools aligned with the practical demands of modern healthcare systems.

papers.title: time2time: Causal Intervention in Hidden States to Simulate Rare Events in Time Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do time series foundation models internalize semantic concepts like market regimes, and can their internal representations be leveraged to simulate rare events such as market crashes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces activation transplantation, a causal intervention method that provides evidence that time series foundation models learn high-level semantic concepts of real-world events, enabling steerable simulations for stress-testing.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides causal evidence that time series foundation models encode abstract, steerable market regime concepts, enabling deterministic control of forecasts and revealing a continuous severity axis in their latent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Activation transplantation can deterministically steer forecasts by implanting the statistical signature of one event into another.
Models encode event severity as a continuous latent variable, with the activation vector norm correlating with shock magnitude.
The steerable representations are robust across different model architectures (decoder-only Toto and encoder-decoder Chronos).
A unified 'crash' concept emerges across layers, with early layers showing anti-correlation and later layers converging to a shared subspace.
The model's internal representation of a crash is not binary but continuous, allowing for graded interventions.
papers.limitation: The work is a foundational proof-of-concept and it remains to be investigated whether steerable semantic subspaces are universal beyond Transformers to other architectures like State Space Models or LSTMs.
future_direction: Investigate whether steerable semantic subspaces are universal across sequence models beyond Transformers, such as State Space Models and LSTMs.
Discover a broader semantic vocabulary within TSFMs, probing for concepts like earnings surprises in finance or seizure onsets in EEG data.
papers.abstract: While transformer-based foundation models excel at forecasting routine patterns, two questions remain: do they internalize semantic concepts such as market regimes, or merely fit curves? And can their internal representations be leveraged to simulate rare, high-stakes events such as market crashes? To investigate this, we introduce activation transplantation, a causal intervention that manipulates hidden states by imposing the statistical moments of one event (e.g., a historical crash) onto another (e.g., a calm period) during the forward pass. This procedure deterministically steers forecasts: injecting crash semantics induces downturn predictions, while injecting calm semantics suppresses crashes and restores stability. Beyond binary control, we find that models encode a graded notion of event severity, with the latent vector norm directly correlating with the magnitude of systemic shocks. Validated across two architecturally distinct TSFMs, Toto (decoder only) and Chronos (encoder-decoder), our results demonstrate that steerable, semantically grounded representations are a robust property of large time series transformers. Our findings provide evidence for a latent concept space that governs model predictions, shifting interpretability from post-hoc attribution to direct causal intervention, and enabling semantic "what-if" analysis for strategic stress-testing.

papers.title: Multimodal Task Vectors Enable Many-Shot Multimodal In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How to enable Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) to perform many-shot in-context learning without being limited by context length, by compressing examples into implicit representations (task vectors) in the model's attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Multimodal Task Vectors (MTV), compact implicit representations of in-context examples stored in attention heads, enabling many-shot multimodal in-context learning without fine-tuning and overcoming context length limitations.
papers.conclusion: MTV enables many-shot multimodal in-context learning, scales with examples, and generalizes to similar tasks without requiring fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
MTV outperforms zero-shot and few-shot ICL on various vision-language tasks.
MTV performance scales with the number of compressed examples (shots and iterations).
MTV can be used alongside explicit few-shot examples, freeing up context length.
MTV attention heads extracted on one task can generalize to similar out-of-domain tasks.
papers.limitation:
MTV requires interleaved LMMs and may not work as well on non-interleaved models.
Computing mean activations requires multiple forward passes, which can be computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: The recent success of interleaved Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) in few-shot learning suggests that in-context learning (ICL) with many examples can be promising for learning new tasks. However, this many-shot multimodal ICL setting has one crucial problem: it is fundamentally limited by the model's context length set at pretraining. The problem is especially prominent in the multimodal domain, which processes both text and images, requiring additional tokens. This motivates the need for a multimodal method to compress many shots into fewer tokens without finetuning. In this work, we enable LMMs to perform multimodal, many-shot in-context learning by leveraging Multimodal Task Vectors (MTV) -- compact implicit representations of in-context examples compressed in the model's attention heads. Specifically, we first demonstrate the existence of such MTV in LMMs and then leverage these extracted MTV to enable many-shot in-context learning for various vision-and-language tasks. Our experiments suggest that MTV can scale in performance with the number of compressed shots and generalize to similar out-of-domain tasks without additional context length for inference. Code: https://github.com/Brandon3964/MultiModal-Task-Vector

papers.title: Counterfactual reasoning: an analysis of in-context emergence
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning, i.e., predicting consequences of hypothetical scenarios by inferring unobserved latent concepts and copying contextual noise from factual observations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models are capable of in-context counterfactual reasoning, and through analysis of Transformers, finds that self-attention, model depth, and pre-training data diversity drive performance, with mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and that designated noise abduction heads emerge.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can perform counterfactual reasoning by leveraging self-attention and depth, and this ability extends to sequential data, suggesting potential for counterfactual story generation.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning on synthetic linear regression tasks.
Self-attention is crucial for counterfactual reasoning; MLP-only models fail.
Model depth improves counterfactual reasoning performance.
Pre-training data diversity improves performance and out-of-distribution generalization.
The latent parameter is linearly encoded in the residual stream, and designated noise abduction heads emerge in attention layers.
papers.limitation: The synthetic setup may not fully capture the complexity of natural language counterfactual reasoning.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to natural language tasks and more complex functions.
Further exploration of the role of attention heads in counterfactual reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit remarkable performance in in-context learning: the ability to learn and reason about the input context on the fly. This work studies in-context counterfactual reasoning in language models, that is, the ability to predict consequences of a hypothetical scenario. We focus on a well-defined, synthetic linear regression task that requires noise abduction. Accurate prediction is based on (1) inferring an unobserved latent concept and (2) copying contextual noise from factual observations. We show that language models are capable of counterfactual reasoning. Further, we enhance existing identifiability results and reduce counterfactual reasoning for a broad class of functions to a transformation on in-context observations. In Transformers, we find that self-attention, model depth and pre-training data diversity drive performance. Moreover, we provide mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and we introduce designated \textit{noise abduction heads} central to performing counterfactual reasoning. Lastly, our findings extend to counterfactual reasoning under SDE dynamics and reflect that Transformers can perform noise abduction on sequential data, providing preliminary evidence on the potential for counterfactual story generation. Our code is available under https://github.com/mrtzmllr/iccr.

papers.title: Desiderata for Representation Learning: A Causal Perspective
papers.research_question: How can representation learning desiderata (non-spuriousness, efficiency, disentanglement) be formalized using causal notions, and how can metrics and algorithms be developed to learn such representations from single observational datasets?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a causal framework for representation learning that formalizes desiderata like non-spuriousness, efficiency, and disentanglement using counterfactual notions (probabilities of causation) and provides metrics and algorithms (CAUSAL-REP and IOSS) to learn such representations from single observational datasets.
papers.conclusion: Causality provides a fruitful perspective for representation learning, allowing intuitive desiderata to be formalized and leading to metrics and algorithms that can learn non-spurious and disentangled representations from single observational datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Non-spuriousness and efficiency in supervised representation learning can be formalized using probabilities of sufficiency (PS) and necessity (PN), leading to the CAUSAL-REP algorithm.
Disentanglement in unsupervised representation learning can be formalized via causal disentanglement, leading to the Independence-of-Support Score (IOSS) metric.
CAUSAL-REP learns non-spurious representations that improve out-of-distribution prediction on image and text datasets compared to baseline methods.
IOSS can distinguish disentangled from entangled representations better than existing unsupervised metrics on synthetic and real datasets.
The causal perspective enables the development of calculable metrics and algorithms for representation learning desiderata without requiring multiple environments or labeled features.
papers.limitation:
CAUSAL-REP requires the pinpointability condition (i.e., the unobserved common cause C can be pinpointed from X) for identification.
IOSS assumes compact support of the representation and may not apply to representations with unbounded support.
papers.abstract: Representation learning constructs low-dimensional representations to summarize essential features of high-dimensional data. This learning problem is often approached by describing various desiderata associated with learned representations; e.g., that they be non-spurious, efficient, or disentangled. It can be challenging, however, to turn these intuitive desiderata into formal criteria that can be measured and enhanced based on observed data. In this paper, we take a causal perspective on representation learning, formalizing non-spuriousness and efficiency (in supervised representation learning) and disentanglement (in unsupervised representation learning) using counterfactual quantities and observable consequences of causal assertions. This yields computable metrics that can be used to assess the degree to which representations satisfy the desiderata of interest and learn non-spurious and disentangled representations from single observational datasets.

papers.title: FocusLearn: Fully-Interpretable, High-Performance Modular Neural Networks for Time Series
papers.research_question: How to build a fully-interpretable modular neural network for time series that matches or surpasses the predictive performance of non-interpretable deep networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FocusLearn, a fully-interpretable modular neural network for time series that uses attention for feature selection and node bootstrapping to achieve predictive performance comparable to non-interpretable deep networks.
papers.conclusion: FocusLearn achieves interpretability without sacrificing predictive performance, matching or outperforming state-of-the-art non-interpretable models on time series tasks.
papers.key_findings:
FocusLearn outperforms interpretable models (NAM and SPAM) on both regression and classification tasks across multiple metrics.
FocusLearn matches or surpasses the performance of non-interpretable models (LSTM and XGBoost) on the tested datasets.
The Attention-based Node Bootstrapping (ANB) and Attention-based Feature Selection (AFS) components are effective in improving predictive performance.
FocusLearn provides NAM-style interpretability with feature contribution plots.
Selecting a subset of features via AFS improves accuracy compared to using all features.
future_direction: Evaluate trade-offs such as the number of modules and feature interactions in practice.
Investigate the possibility of using attention to create higher-order feature interactions for implementation into a single network module.
Investigate the practical value of the explanations provided and how they may inform model intervention.
papers.abstract: Multivariate time series have had many applications in areas from healthcare and finance to meteorology and life sciences. Although deep neural networks have shown excellent predictive performance for time series, they have been criticised for being non-interpretable. Neural Additive Models, however, are known to be fully-interpretable by construction, but may achieve far lower predictive performance than deep networks when applied to time series. This paper introduces FocusLearn, a fully-interpretable modular neural network capable of matching or surpassing the predictive performance of deep networks trained on multivariate time series. In FocusLearn, a recurrent neural network learns the temporal dependencies in the data, while a multi-headed attention layer learns to weight selected features while also suppressing redundant features. Modular neural networks are then trained in parallel and independently, one for each selected feature. This modular approach allows the user to inspect how features influence outcomes in the exact same way as with additive models. Experimental results show that this new approach outperforms additive models in both regression and classification of time series tasks, achieving predictive performance that is comparable to state-of-the-art, non-interpretable deep networks applied to time series.

papers.title: Explaining Latent Representations with a Corpus of Examples
papers.research_question: How can we explain the latent representations of machine learning models? Specifically, which corpus examples explain a test example's prediction, and what features of these corpus examples are relevant?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SimplEx, a method that explains latent representations by decomposing them as a mixture of corpus examples, and introduces Integrated Jacobians to attribute feature importance in the decomposition.
papers.conclusion: SimplEx offers a flexible and effective approach for explaining latent representations, enhancing model transparency and user trust.
papers.key_findings:
SimplEx provides more accurate and robust approximations in latent and output space compared to KNN baselines and the representer theorem.
Jacobian projections effectively identify important features in corpus examples for the decomposition.
SimplEx can detect out-of-distribution examples by measuring corpus residuals.
The method allows users to choose any corpus, enabling personalized explanations.
papers.limitation: The method requires the model to have a linear output layer (Assumption 2.1).
papers.abstract: Modern machine learning models are complicated. Most of them rely on convoluted latent representations of their input to issue a prediction. To achieve greater transparency than a black-box that connects inputs to predictions, it is necessary to gain a deeper understanding of these latent representations. To that aim, we propose SimplEx: a user-centred method that provides example-based explanations with reference to a freely selected set of examples, called the corpus. SimplEx uses the corpus to improve the user's understanding of the latent space with post-hoc explanations answering two questions: (1) Which corpus examples explain the prediction issued for a given test example? (2) What features of these corpus examples are relevant for the model to relate them to the test example? SimplEx provides an answer by reconstructing the test latent representation as a mixture of corpus latent representations. Further, we propose a novel approach, the Integrated Jacobian, that allows SimplEx to make explicit the contribution of each corpus feature in the mixture. Through experiments on tasks ranging from mortality prediction to image classification, we demonstrate that these decompositions are robust and accurate. With illustrative use cases in medicine, we show that SimplEx empowers the user by highlighting relevant patterns in the corpus that explain model representations. Moreover, we demonstrate how the freedom in choosing the corpus allows the user to have personalized explanations in terms of examples that are meaningful for them.

papers.title: Improving Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks in Medical Diagnosis by Investigating the Individual Units
papers.research_question: How can attribution techniques like LRP and RAP improve the interpretability of DNNs in medical diagnosis by visualizing significant factors and revealing inconsistencies between human and DNN intentions?
papers.core_contribution: Attribution methods like LRP and RAP can effectively localize lesions in chest X-rays without bounding box supervision and reveal that DNNs may learn based on normal lung features rather than disease lesions, highlighting the need for interpretability in medical diagnosis.
papers.conclusion: Attribution techniques such as LRP and RAP offer efficient ways to interpret DNN decisions in medical diagnosis by localizing lesions and uncovering potential inconsistencies, underscoring the necessity of explainability for reliable adoption.
papers.key_findings:
LRP and RAP achieve higher IOU scores than CAM for localizing lesions in chest X-ray images, indicating better visualization accuracy.
Attribution methods provide detailed pixel-wise explanations compared to CAM's broad visualizations from resized feature maps.
DNNs trained for pneumonia classification may focus on normal lung features rather than pneumonia lesions, showing inconsistency with human intentions.
CheXNet, pretrained for multiple diseases, provides clear visual explanations aligned with lesion areas, unlike models trained only on pneumonia data.
The study emphasizes the importance of explainability to ensure DNNs' decision criteria align with clinical expectations.
papers.abstract: As interpretability has been pointed out as the obstacle to the adoption of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), there is an increasing interest in solving a transparency issue to guarantee the impressive performance. In this paper, we demonstrate the efficiency of recent attribution techniques to explain the diagnostic decision by visualizing the significant factors in the input image. By utilizing the characteristics of objectness that DNNs have learned, fully decomposing the network prediction visualizes clear localization of target lesion. To verify our work, we conduct our experiments on Chest X-ray diagnosis with publicly accessible datasets. As an intuitive assessment metric for explanations, we report the performance of intersection of Union between visual explanation and bounding box of lesions. Experiment results show that recently proposed attribution methods visualize the more accurate localization for the diagnostic decision compared to the traditionally used CAM. Furthermore, we analyze the inconsistency of intentions between humans and DNNs, which is easily obscured by high performance. By visualizing the relevant factors, it is possible to confirm that the criterion for decision is in line with the learning strategy. Our analysis of unmasking machine intelligence represents the necessity of explainability in the medical diagnostic decision.

papers.title: Video Prediction of Dynamic Physical Simulations With Pixel-Space Spatiotemporal Transformers
papers.research_question: This study investigates a transformer adaptation for video prediction with a simple end-to-end approach, comparing various spatiotemporal self-attention layouts, focusing on causal modelling of physical simulations over time.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a simple, interpretable pure transformer model (PSViT) for end-to-end autoregressive video prediction in pixel-space, which extends the time horizon for physically accurate predictions by up to 50% compared to existing latent-space approaches.
papers.conclusion: The presented simple, interpretable pure transformer for end-to-end autoregressive video prediction extends the horizon for physically accurate predictions while maintaining competitive performance on standard video quality metrics, highlighting the benefits of a straightforward end-to-end approach.
papers.key_findings:
The PSViT model achieves increased temporal accuracy in predicting PDE-driven video sequences compared to existing approaches, as measured by an object tracking metric.
The model maintains competitive performance on standard video quality metrics (SSIM, PSNR).
Interpretability experiments identify network regions that encode information useful for estimating PDE simulation parameters via probing.
The learned encoding of underlying physics generalizes to the estimation of out-of-distribution simulation parameters.
The model's performance is evaluated on several physics simulation datasets and common video prediction benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
For three of the simulation datasets increasing PSViT model size has minimal impact on performance over time.
For stochastic video-generation results on BAIR, the approach falls short compared to latent space models.
Object shapes, although positioned accurately, can distort over time, particularly when rotation is involved.
By performing end-to-end training, the model doesn't benefit from the large-scale pretrained image encoders/decoders often employed by latent space models.
future_direction: Developing more sophisticated metrics for evaluating physical accuracy, moving beyond current object-based pixel distance methods.
Training larger models on higher-resolution datasets featuring increased visual fidelity and physical complexity.
papers.abstract: Inspired by the performance and scalability of autoregressive large language models (LLMs), transformer-based models have seen recent success in the visual domain. This study investigates a transformer adaptation for video prediction with a simple end-to-end approach, comparing various spatiotemporal self-attention layouts. Focusing on causal modeling of physical simulations over time; a common shortcoming of existing video-generative approaches, we attempt to isolate spatiotemporal reasoning via physical object tracking metrics and unsupervised training on physical simulation datasets. We introduce a simple yet effective pure transformer model for autoregressive video prediction, utilizing continuous pixel-space representations for video prediction. Without the need for complex training strategies or latent feature-learning components, our approach significantly extends the time horizon for physically accurate predictions by up to 50% when compared with existing latent-space approaches, while maintaining comparable performance on common video quality metrics. In addition, we conduct interpretability experiments to identify network regions that encode information useful to perform accurate estimations of PDE simulation parameters via probing models, and find that this generalizes to the estimation of out-of-distribution simulation parameters. This work serves as a platform for further attention-based spatiotemporal modeling of videos via a simple, parameter efficient, and interpretable approach.

papers.title: A Model of Causal Explanation on Neural Networks for Tabular Data
papers.research_question: How to provide causal explanations for neural network predictions on tabular data, addressing pseudo-correlation and combinatorial reasons?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CENNET, a causal explanation method for neural network predictors on tabular data, which uses structural causal models and an entropy-based index to provide explanations that eliminate pseudo-correlations and handle combinatorial reasons.
papers.conclusion: CENNET provides causal explanations for neural network predictions on tabular data, eliminating pseudo-correlations and indirect factors, and effectively handles combinatorial reasons.
papers.key_findings:
CENNET outperforms existing XAI methods (LIME, S-LIME, SHAP, ACV) in non-linear non-additive and categorical synthetic datasets.
In quasi-real datasets, CENNET ranks direct causal variables higher in 7 out of 10 settings.
CENNET's use of characteristic correlated variables (CCVs) achieves a lower entropy bound, providing a compact explanation.
CENNET can explain predictions that require combinatorial reasons, unlike additive methods.
The method avoids distortions from linear and additive approximations common in other XAI methods.

papers.title: Combining Causal Models for More Accurate Abstractions of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we improve the faithfulness of causal abstractions of neural networks by combining multiple high-level causal models to allow for different computational states depending on the input?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for combining causal models to create more faithful abstractions of neural networks, enabling different computational states for different inputs and demonstrating a trade-off between hypothesis strength and faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: Combining causal models enables more nuanced interpretations of neural computation, providing stronger interpretability hypotheses while maintaining high faithfulness, as demonstrated on arithmetic and boolean logic tasks with GPT 2-small.
papers.key_findings:
Combined causal models provide stronger interpretability hypotheses at high faithfulness levels (0.9-1.0 IIA) compared to individual models.
There is a trade-off between faithfulness (measured by Interchange Intervention Accuracy) and hypothesis strength (proportion of inputs assigned to non-trivial models).
In GPT 2-small fine-tuned on arithmetic and boolean tasks, the model does not transition discretely between computational states; combined models can capture this nuance.
The method allows modulation between strength and faithfulness, providing the most accurate combination of models given a faithfulness level.
Early layers of GPT 2-small represent input variables separately, while later layers represent summed quantities, with a gradual transition in intermediate layers.
papers.limitation: Experiments are conducted on toy tasks (arithmetic and boolean logic) for clear analysis and validation.
future_direction: Extend the framework to more complex tasks.
Integrate with other mechanistic interpretability methods.
Enhance with more sophisticated optimization objectives for constructing input space partitions.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse engineer neural networks by uncovering which high-level algorithms they implement. Causal abstraction provides a precise notion of when a network implements an algorithm, i.e., a causal model of the network contains low-level features that realize the high-level variables in a causal model of the algorithm. A typical problem in practical settings is that the algorithm is not an entirely faithful abstraction of the network, meaning it only partially captures the true reasoning process of a model. We propose a solution where we combine different simple high-level models to produce a more faithful representation of the network. Through learning this combination, we can model neural networks as being in different computational states depending on the input provided, which we show is more accurate to GPT 2-small fine-tuned on two toy tasks. We observe a trade-off between the strength of an interpretability hypothesis, which we define in terms of the number of inputs explained by the high-level models, and its faithfulness, which we define as the interchange intervention accuracy. Our method allows us to modulate between the two, providing the most accurate combination of models that describe the behavior of a neural network given a faithfulness level.

papers.title: Visual Interpretable and Explainable Deep Learning Models for Brain Tumor MRI and COVID-19 Chest X-ray Images
papers.research_question: What do deep learning models learn in medical images? The paper evaluates attribution methods for illuminating how deep neural networks analyze medical images.
papers.core_contribution: The paper evaluates adaptive path-based gradient integration attribution methods (Guided Integrated Gradients and XRAI) on CNN models for medical image analysis, demonstrating their ability to highlight salient features and improve model transparency for domain experts.
papers.conclusion: Different input attribution methods have varying degrees of explainability. A robust representation learner and the right attribution approach are crucial for obtaining interpretable saliency maps from deep CNNs in medical image analysis, which can help build trust for clinical adoption.
papers.key_findings:
DenseNet121 achieved the best test performance (98.10% accuracy) on the brain tumor MRI dataset, while InceptionResNetV2 performed best on the COVID-19 chest X-ray dataset (89.0% accuracy).
The XRAI attribution method provided the most interpretable saliency maps, highlighting regions of interest that corresponded well with expert tumor segmentations in the MRI dataset.
Vanilla Gradient and Guided Integrated Gradient methods produced noisier and less stable saliency maps compared to XRAI.
The choice of baseline (e.g., zero pixels) significantly affects the resulting saliency maps from gradient-based attribution methods.
Combining multiple attribution methods (e.g., XRAI and Blur IG) can improve model interpretability for domain experts by highlighting important features.
papers.limitation:
The COVID-19 chest X-ray dataset lacks ground truth segmentation masks, making it difficult to evaluate attribution maps against expert annotations.
CNNs have frequency, texture, and shape biases that differ from human visual processing, which may affect the interpretability of saliency maps.
future_direction: Research into volumetric medical imaging data
Quantification of explainability of visual attribution methods
Developing benchmarks for visual attribution methods
papers.abstract: Deep learning shows promise for medical image analysis but lacks interpretability, hindering adoption in healthcare. Attribution techniques that explain model reasoning may increase trust in deep learning among clinical stakeholders. This paper aimed to evaluate attribution methods for illuminating how deep neural networks analyze medical images. Using adaptive path-based gradient integration, we attributed predictions from brain tumor MRI and COVID-19 chest X-ray datasets made by recent deep convolutional neural network models. The technique highlighted possible biomarkers, exposed model biases, and offered insights into the links between input and prediction. Our analysis demonstrates the method's ability to elucidate model reasoning on these datasets. The resulting attributions show promise for improving deep learning transparency for domain experts by revealing the rationale behind predictions. This study advances model interpretability to increase trust in deep learning among healthcare stakeholders.

papers.title: Best of both worlds: local and global explanations with human-understandable concepts
papers.research_question: How to bridge the gap between local and global explanation techniques by combining Integrated Gradients and TCAV to provide consistent local and global concept-based explanations.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Integrated Conceptual Sensitivity (ICS), a method that combines Integrated Gradients and TCAV to provide consistent local and global concept-based explanations for model decisions.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the potential of combining local and global explanation techniques and encourages further research in this direction.
papers.key_findings:
ICS provides more faithful global explanations compared to vanilla TCAV, as measured by Model Contrast Score (MCS).
ICS offers local concept-based attributions that correctly reflect concept importance per example.
The method works across various baselines, model architectures, and concepts.
Data augmentation improves CAV quality and ICS scores, especially for deeper layers.
A user study shows that providing both local and global explanations improves human ability to predict model behavior.
papers.limitation:
The method requires human-defined concepts, which may be incomplete or biased.
The curse of dimensionality can affect CAV quality, especially in wide layers.
ICS is computationally more expensive than TCAV due to the integral approximation.
The set of concepts selected may not cover all relevant features, leading to incomplete explanations.
future_direction: Combine concept-based explanations with feature-based attributions to provide a more complete picture.
papers.abstract: Interpretability techniques aim to provide the rationale behind a model's decision, typically by explaining either an individual prediction (local explanation, e.g. 'why is this patient diagnosed with this condition') or a class of predictions (global explanation, e.g. 'why is this set of patients diagnosed with this condition in general'). While there are many methods focused on either one, few frameworks can provide both local and global explanations in a consistent manner. In this work, we combine two powerful existing techniques, one local (Integrated Gradients, IG) and one global (Testing with Concept Activation Vectors), to provide local and global concept-based explanations. We first sanity check our idea using two synthetic datasets with a known ground truth, and further demonstrate with a benchmark natural image dataset. We test our method with various concepts, target classes, model architectures and IG parameters (e.g. baselines). We show that our method improves global explanations over vanilla TCAV when compared to ground truth, and provides useful local insights. Finally, a user study demonstrates the usefulness of the method compared to no or global explanations only. We hope our work provides a step towards building bridges between many existing local and global methods to get the best of both worlds.

papers.title: Causal Learning and Explanation of Deep Neural Networks via Autoencoded Activations
papers.research_question: How can we explain deep neural networks by constructing causal models on salient concepts extracted from network activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a causal approach to explain DNN predictions by extracting human-understandable concepts from network activations using autoencoders and building a Bayesian causal model to quantify the causal effect of these concepts on the output.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents an approach to explaining DNN predictions using causal semantics and interpretable concepts, and suggests future work on improving the variable construction and extending to non-image domains.
papers.key_findings:
The method can extract interpretable concepts from DNN activations using autoencoders trained with a novel deep reconstruction loss.
A causal Bayesian network can be learned from interventions on the extracted concepts to model the causal relationships within the DNN.
The causal model can identify and rank concepts by their expected causal effect on the network's classification output.
The approach provides visual explanations by showing the concept features and their nearest neighbors in the dataset.
The method is demonstrated on image classification networks (VGG16, VGG19, JN6) applied to pedestrian and bird datasets.
papers.limitation:
The use of mean-pooling and binning for constructing variable observations for the Bayes net is a simplification that may be improved.
The method is currently applied only to image classification domains.
Additional specific results are omitted due to space constraints.
future_direction: Using variational autoencoders to encode away irrelevant image structure for better variable construction.
Exploring structure learning for reducing the size of the Bayes net skeleton.
Extending the approach to non-image domains.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are complex and opaque. As they enter application in a variety of important and safety critical domains, users seek methods to explain their output predictions. We develop an approach to explaining deep neural networks by constructing causal models on salient concepts contained in a CNN. We develop methods to extract salient concepts throughout a target network by using autoencoders trained to extract human-understandable representations of network activations. We then build a bayesian causal model using these extracted concepts as variables in order to explain image classification. Finally, we use this causal model to identify and visualize features with significant causal influence on final classification.

papers.title: Intrinsic User-Centric Interpretability through Global Mixture of Experts
papers.research_question: How to design intrinsically interpretable neural networks that are user-centric, faithful, and sparse, while maintaining comparable performance to non-interpretable models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces InterpretCC, a family of intrinsically interpretable neural networks that use conditional computation to provide faithful, sparse, and human-centric explanations while maintaining performance comparable to non-interpretable models.
papers.conclusion: InterpretCC provides a unique design for interpretable models that balances human-centric actionability, faithfulness, and performance, as validated by experiments and a user study.
papers.key_findings:
InterpretCC models perform comparably to non-interpretable baselines (matching or exceeding 95% CIs in 15 of 16 comparisons).
InterpretCC models outperform intrinsically interpretable baselines (e.g., ICC Feature Gating is 9.05% better on average than SENN Features and 3.27% better on average than NAM).
In a user study, teachers preferred ICC explanations over baselines in terms of actionability, usefulness, conciseness, and trustworthiness.
InterpretCC provides faithful explanations (high Feature Agreement and Rank Agreement on synthetic data).
The models are sparse, activating only a subset of features or groups per instance.
papers.limitation:
The authors cannot guarantee that InterpretCC will always perform on par with or better than baseline models across all data types and domains.
The models are not safe for direct use in production tasks (e.g., detecting breast cancer) without further validation and adaptation by domain professionals.
future_direction: Extending InterpretCC to other modalities (e.g., vision, audio).
Exploring automated grouping methods.
papers.abstract: In human-centric settings like education or healthcare, model accuracy and model explainability are key factors for user adoption. Towards these two goals, intrinsically interpretable deep learning models have gained popularity, focusing on accurate predictions alongside faithful explanations. However, there exists a gap in the human-centeredness of these approaches, which often produce nuanced and complex explanations that are not easily actionable for downstream users. We present InterpretCC (interpretable conditional computation), a family of intrinsically interpretable neural networks at a unique point in the design space that optimizes for ease of human understanding and explanation faithfulness, while maintaining comparable performance to state-of-the-art models. InterpretCC achieves this through adaptive sparse activation of features before prediction, allowing the model to use a different, minimal set of features for each instance. We extend this idea into an interpretable, global mixture-of-experts (MoE) model that allows users to specify topics of interest, discretely separates the feature space for each data point into topical subnetworks, and adaptively and sparsely activates these topical subnetworks for prediction. We apply InterpretCC for text, time series and tabular data across several real-world datasets, demonstrating comparable performance with non-interpretable baselines and outperforming intrinsically interpretable baselines. Through a user study involving 56 teachers, InterpretCC explanations are found to have higher actionability and usefulness over other intrinsically interpretable approaches.

papers.title: Finding the DeepDream for Time Series: Activation Maximization for Univariate Time Series
papers.research_question: How can activation maximization be adapted to time series data to improve model interpretability and generate realistic, informative sequences?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sequence Dreaming, an adaptation of Activation Maximization for univariate time series, enhanced with regularization techniques to generate realistic and interpretable sequences that reveal salient temporal features learned by neural networks.
papers.conclusion: Sequence Dreaming, with enhanced regularization, effectively generates activation-maximizing time series for interpretability, allowing precise targeting of activation regions and providing insights into the model's internal processes.
papers.key_findings:
Sequence Dreaming can generate time series that target specific activation regions (e.g., class centers or borders) in the model's activation space.
The method produces smoother and more realistic time series compared to other activation maximization approaches, as validated by visual and quantitative (Mahalanobis distance) evaluation.
The generated time series are often out-of-distribution compared to the training data, indicating the model learns abstract patterns for classification.
Activation maximization with regularization terms is highly parameter-sensitive but can produce convincing results comparable to frequency-domain approaches.
Sequence Dreaming can reveal different learned representations by the model, including non-periodic patterns, which are not captured by frequency-domain methods.
papers.limitation:
Activation maximization with regularization terms is highly parameter-sensitive.
The generated time series are often out-of-distribution compared to the original training data.
future_direction: Exploring advanced regularization techniques, such as perturbations directed by attributions.
Adopting genetic or evolutionary algorithms for optimizing activation maximization.
Incorporating wavelet transforms for a richer representation of time series features.
papers.abstract: Understanding how models process and interpret time series data remains a significant challenge in deep learning to enable applicability in safety-critical areas such as healthcare. In this paper, we introduce Sequence Dreaming, a technique that adapts Activation Maximization to analyze sequential information, aiming to enhance the interpretability of neural networks operating on univariate time series. By leveraging this method, we visualize the temporal dynamics and patterns most influential in model decision-making processes. To counteract the generation of unrealistic or excessively noisy sequences, we enhance Sequence Dreaming with a range of regularization techniques, including exponential smoothing. This approach ensures the production of sequences that more accurately reflect the critical features identified by the neural network. Our approach is tested on a time series classification dataset encompassing applications in predictive maintenance. The results show that our proposed Sequence Dreaming approach demonstrates targeted activation maximization for different use cases so that either centered class or border activation maximization can be generated. The results underscore the versatility of Sequence Dreaming in uncovering salient temporal features learned by neural networks, thereby advancing model transparency and trustworthiness in decision-critical domains.

papers.title: Efficiently Disentangle Causal Representations
papers.research_question: How to efficiently disentangle causal representations by measuring generalization ability instead of adaptation speed?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an efficient approach to learning disentangled representations with causal mechanisms by measuring generalization ability instead of adaptation speed.
papers.conclusion: The proposed approach is significantly more efficient than the adaptation-speed-based method for causal representation learning.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method is 1.9–11.0× more sample efficient and 9.4–32.4× quicker than the baseline method.
The method is robust to some noise but fails when noise is too large.
The method can identify causal direction correctly in various tasks.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work when the noise is too large.
In edge cases where intervention reduces the entropy of the cause variable, the estimator may be negative and fail.
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an efficient approach to learning disentangled representations with causal mechanisms based on the difference of conditional probabilities in original and new distributions. We approximate the difference with models' generalization abilities so that it fits in the standard machine learning framework and can be efficiently computed. In contrast to the state-of-the-art approach, which relies on the learner's adaptation speed to new distribution, the proposed approach only requires evaluating the model's generalization ability. We provide a theoretical explanation for the advantage of the proposed method, and our experiments show that the proposed technique is 1.9--11.0$\times$ more sample efficient and 9.4--32.4 times quicker than the previous method on various tasks. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/yuanpeng16/EDCR}.

papers.title: Explaining deep learning for ECG using time-localized clusters
papers.research_question: How can we interpret deep learning models for ECG analysis by extracting time-localized clusters from internal representations to understand how different waveform regions contribute to predictions and assess decision certainty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel interpretability method for CNN-based ECG analysis that extracts time-localized clusters from internal representations, segmenting the ECG according to learned characteristics and quantifying representation uncertainty, thereby enhancing trust and facilitating discovery of clinically relevant patterns.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method provides intuitive visualizations and quantifiable uncertainty measures for CNN-based ECG analysis, enhancing model transparency and trustworthiness for clinical diagnostics and biomedical discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Clusters extracted from internal representations correlate with diagnostic labels and specific phases of the ECG waveform, providing physiologically meaningful segmentation.
The uncertainty of cluster assignments differs from gradient-based saliency maps (e.g., Grad-CAM), offering a distinct view of model confidence in its internal representations.
A random forest classifier trained on cluster proportions achieves performance comparable to the original 1D-ResNet, indicating the clusters capture discriminative information.
The method is robust to the amount of data used for clustering and the number of clusters, with performance stabilizing beyond 20 clusters.
Applied to age prediction, the method reveals age-specific clustering patterns, with younger patients' ECGs represented by fewer, more certain clusters and older patients' by more dispersed, uncertain representations.
papers.limitation:
The unsupervised nature of the method and the exclusion of the classifier require the addition of expert knowledge to interpret clusters, which may introduce biases.
Assigning a single global label to an entire 10-second ECG strip can be problematic in the presence of transient morphologies, such as occasional ectopic beats.
papers.abstract: Deep learning has significantly advanced electrocardiogram (ECG) analysis, enabling automatic annotation, disease screening, and prognosis beyond traditional clinical capabilities. However, understanding these models remains a challenge, limiting interpretation and gaining knowledge from these developments. In this work, we propose a novel interpretability method for convolutional neural networks applied to ECG analysis. Our approach extracts time-localized clusters from the model's internal representations, segmenting the ECG according to the learned characteristics while quantifying the uncertainty of these representations. This allows us to visualize how different waveform regions contribute to the model's predictions and assess the certainty of its decisions. By providing a structured and interpretable view of deep learning models for ECG, our method enhances trust in AI-driven diagnostics and facilitates the discovery of clinically relevant electrophysiological patterns.

papers.title: A Methodology for Explainable Large Language Models with Integrated Gradients and Linguistic Analysis in Text Classification
papers.research_question: How to provide explainability for Large Language Models in text classification tasks, specifically for identifying and explaining lexical features relevant to Alzheimer's Disease detection?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces SLIME, an explainable LLM method that combines Integrated Gradients, LIWC, and statistical analysis to identify and explain which lexical components are most important for a model's classification decision in the context of Alzheimer's Disease detection.
papers.conclusion: The SLIME method provides a framework for explaining neural language models in computational linguistics, particularly for Alzheimer's Disease classification, and offers a freely available, reproducible tool to promote transparency and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The SLIME method identified 64 linguistic features relevant for classification (28 for control group, 36 for AD group).
Five categories (e.g., social referents, female references) improved accuracy for the control group, while five others (e.g., all-or-none thinking, male references) improved accuracy for the AD group.
SLIME attributes provide identity separation capabilities that cannot be captured solely by feature counts, offering greater explanatory potential than a count-based model.
The method provides faithful and plausible explanations, with identified linguistic features aligning with known clinical patterns in Alzheimer's Disease.
The framework does not indiscriminately enhance explainability but selectively improves the discriminability of features that genuinely impact classification.
papers.abstract: Neurological disorders that affect speech production, such as Alzheimer's Disease (AD), significantly impact the lives of both patients and caregivers, whether through social, psycho-emotional effects or other aspects not yet fully understood. Recent advancements in Large Language Model (LLM) architectures have developed many tools to identify representative features of neurological disorders through spontaneous speech. However, LLMs typically lack interpretability, meaning they do not provide clear and specific reasons for their decisions. Therefore, there is a need for methods capable of identifying the representative features of neurological disorders in speech and explaining clearly why these features are relevant. This paper presents an explainable LLM method, named SLIME (Statistical and Linguistic Insights for Model Explanation), capable of identifying lexical components representative of AD and indicating which components are most important for the LLM's decision. In developing this method, we used an English-language dataset consisting of transcriptions from the Cookie Theft picture description task. The LLM Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) classified the textual descriptions as either AD or control groups. To identify representative lexical features and determine which are most relevant to the model's decision, we used a pipeline involving Integrated Gradients (IG), Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC), and statistical analysis. Our method demonstrates that BERT leverages lexical components that reflect a reduction in social references in AD and identifies which further improve the LLM's accuracy. Thus, we provide an explainability tool that enhances confidence in applying LLMs to neurological clinical contexts, particularly in the study of neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Dissecting Role Cognition in Medical LLMs via Neuronal Ablation
papers.research_question: Whether role prompts induce distinct, role-specific cognitive processes in LLMs or merely modify linguistic style.
papers.core_contribution: Role-playing prompts in LLMs do not induce role-specific reasoning pathways; they only affect surface-level linguistic style without altering the core decision-making mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Role-playing prompts primarily alter language style rather than enabling models to replicate the cognitive processes of real doctors, highlighting the limitations of current methods for building reliable cognitive agents in medical AI.
papers.key_findings:
Role-playing prompts do not significantly improve the medical reasoning accuracy of LLMs across multiple datasets and model scales.
Neuron ablation experiments show similar performance degradation across different roles, indicating a lack of role-specific cognitive pathways.
Representation analysis (CKA, PCA) reveals high similarity and overlapping clusters in hidden states across different roles, showing no hierarchical cognitive differentiation.
Jensen-Shannon Divergence analysis shows role effects are concentrated in early to middle layers and attenuate with depth, not affecting deeper reasoning structures.
Current Prompt-Based Role Playing (PBRP) methods fail to replicate the cognitive complexity and differentiated reasoning strategies of real-world medical professionals.
future_direction: Developing models that go beyond language imitation and incorporate cognitive modeling techniques.
Integrating domain-specific knowledge into the training process and designing systems that can simulate the reasoning strategies of different medical professionals.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have gained significant traction in medical decision support systems, particularly in the context of medical question answering and role-playing simulations. A common practice, Prompt-Based Role Playing (PBRP), instructs models to adopt different clinical roles (e.g., medical students, residents, attending physicians) to simulate varied professional behaviors. However, the impact of such role prompts on model reasoning capabilities remains unclear. This study introduces the RP-Neuron-Activated Evaluation Framework(RPNA) to evaluate whether role prompts induce distinct, role-specific cognitive processes in LLMs or merely modify linguistic style. We test this framework on three medical QA datasets, employing neuron ablation and representation analysis techniques to assess changes in reasoning pathways. Our results demonstrate that role prompts do not significantly enhance the medical reasoning abilities of LLMs. Instead, they primarily affect surface-level linguistic features, with no evidence of distinct reasoning pathways or cognitive differentiation across clinical roles. Despite superficial stylistic changes, the core decision-making mechanisms of LLMs remain uniform across roles, indicating that current PBRP methods fail to replicate the cognitive complexity found in real-world medical practice. This highlights the limitations of role-playing in medical AI and emphasizes the need for models that simulate genuine cognitive processes rather than linguistic imitation.We have released the related code in the following repository:https: //github.com/IAAR-Shanghai/RolePlay_LLMDoctor

papers.title: Shapley Flow: A Graph-based Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions
papers.research_question: How can we interpret model predictions by accounting for dependencies among features using causal graphs?
papers.core_contribution: Shapley Flow is a novel edge attribution method that generalizes Shapley values to causal graphs, providing a complete view of feature importance by accounting for both direct and indirect effects.
papers.conclusion: Shapley Flow extends Shapley value axioms to causal graphs, resulting in a unique edge attribution method that unifies previous approaches and enables joint understanding of direct and indirect feature impacts.
papers.key_findings:
Shapley Flow uniquely satisfies a generalization of Shapley value axioms for directed acyclic graphs.
It unifies previous feature attribution methods including SHAP, Asymmetric Shapley Values (ASV), and Owen values.
Shapley Flow enables understanding of both direct and indirect impacts of features on model predictions.
The method is model-agnostic and can be applied to arbitrary machine learning pipelines.
Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that Shapley Flow provides more comprehensive explanations compared to existing approaches.
