In parallel, Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown great potential in identifying patterns and generating insights from text data. In this paper we investigate applying LLMs to the problem of determining the directionality of edges in causal discovery. Specifically, we test our approach on a deidentified set of Non Small Cell Lung Cancer(NSCLC) patients that have both electronic health record and genomic panel data. Graphs are validated using Bayesian Dirichlet estimators using tabular data. Our result shows that LLMs can accurately predict the directionality of edges in causal graphs, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods. These findings suggests that LLMs can play a significant role in advancing causal discovery and help us better understand complex systems.

papers.title: CLIN-SUMM: Temporal Summarization of Longitudinal Clinical Notes
papers.abstract: Abstract Electronic health records (EHRs) contain years of longitudinal clinical notes that capture evolving patient health, treatments, and outcomes. However, their value is difficult to realize in practice: notes are fragmented across encounters, highly redundant, and inconsistent, leaving temporal patterns underutilized for downstream modeling. We present CLIN-SUMM (Clinical Longitudinal Insight from Notes using Summarization), a framework that uses a large language model (LLM) to consolidate multi-visit EHR narratives into a concise, date-partitioned patient summary. CLIN-SUMM uses a two-prompt architecture to summarize both the first clinical note and subsequent incremental updates, a redundancy filter to skip near-identical notes, and a sliding-window approach to manage long patient histories. In a dementia prediction case study (N=1,500, 120,213 visit notes), CLIN-SUMM achieved up to 85% token reduction while preserving clinical fidelity in an initial clinician review (correctness: 4.84/5, completeness: 4.79/5). Fine-tuning Clinical-ModernBERT on these summaries yielded an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (AUROC) of 0.79 for classification up to 30 days before diagnosis and 0.75 for prediction three years prior to diagnosis. Analyses of prediction trajectories and saliency patterns revealed clinically meaningful temporal trends and risk markers. CLIN-SUMM can help bridge the gap between unstructured multi-visit narratives and predictive modeling by improving efficiency while surfacing rich temporal patterns and early risk signals, enhancing disease modeling, risk prediction, and other longitudinal reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Sequential pattern transformer (SPT): a generative and interpretable framework for predicting disease trajectories
papers.research_question: How can we develop a model that goes beyond simple prediction to generate explainable disease trajectories, addressing noise in electronic health records and lack of interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Sequential Pattern Transformer (SPT), a framework that integrates sequential pattern mining with a generative transformer to predict and generate explainable disease trajectories, addressing noise and interpretability in clinical data.
papers.conclusion: SPT provides a transparent, robust, and scalable framework for mapping the complex temporal dynamics of disease, bridging the gap between high-performance AI and interpretable clinical application.
papers.key_findings:
SPT achieved 85.78% Top-5 accuracy, significantly outperforming an LSTM baseline (71.47%).
The model generates clinically coherent disease trajectories, with stable BLEU-1 and ROUGE-L scores over generation horizons.
Interpretability analysis reveals learned disease relationships that align with clinical knowledge, such as clustering of cardiorenal metabolic conditions.
Model performance improves with longer patient histories, indicating effective use of contextual information for prediction.
The framework is domain-agnostic and capable of efficient fine-tuning for adaptation to diverse clinical conditions.
papers.limitation:
Dataset is inpatient-only, providing deep insight into acute exacerbations but lacking the long-term outpatient history of chronic illness.
Methodology concentrates on common disease trajectories and is not intended for rare diseases or highly atypical patient journeys.
future_direction: Incorporate outpatient data to create a more holistic model of disease progression.
Enhance the framework with time-aware attention mechanisms to explicitly model intervals between clinical events.
Assess the framework's real-world value through prospective clinical trials to determine impact on patient outcomes.
papers.abstract: Abstract The effective integration of artificial intelligence into clinical workflows requires models that go beyond simple prediction to generate comprehensive, explainable, and actionable disease trajectories. Addressing the limitations of opaque deep learning architectures and the noise inherent in electronic health records, we introduce the sequential pattern transformer (SPT), a novel framework that synergizes sequential pattern mining with generative transformer modeling. Using four years of inpatient data from 258,460 type 2 diabetes patients, we applied the PrefixSpan algorithm to distill noisy diagnostic histories into a curated vocabulary of 95,630 statistically validated disease progression patterns. A decoder-only transformer was trained exclusively on these evidence-based sequences to learn the temporal dynamics of disease evolution. This pattern-guided approach shifts the modeling paradigm from classification to probabilistic trajectory generation. The model achieved a robust 85.78% Top-5 accuracy, significantly outperforming a standard LSTM baseline (71.47%). Beyond predictive accuracy, the framework constructs a dynamic Disease Atlas, a branching tree structure that visualizes likely future pathways, augmented by multi-level explainable AI (XAI) including learned clinical clusters, SHAP-based feature attribution, and counterfactual simulations. Crucially, this methodology is domain-agnostic and capable of efficient fine-tuning, making it a transferable solution for adapting to diverse clinical conditions and local hospital settings. SPT thus offers a transparent, robust, and scalable framework for mapping the complex temporal dynamics of disease, bridging the gap between high-performance AI and interpretable clinical application.

papers.title: No Black Box Anymore: Demystifying Clinical Predictive Modeling with Temporal-Feature Cross Attention Mechanism
papers.research_question: How can predictive accuracy and interpretability be enhanced in clinical predictive modeling for Chronic Kidney Disease progression to End-Stage Renal Disease?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Temporal-Feature Cross Attention Mechanism (TFCAM), a novel deep learning framework that captures dynamic interactions among clinical features across time to improve predictive accuracy and provide multi-level interpretability for clinical decision-making.
papers.conclusion: TFCAM advances interpretable machine learning for CKD progression prediction by combining superior predictive performance with multi-level explainability, offering insights into disease dynamics and supporting clinical decision-making.
papers.key_findings:
TFCAM outperformed LSTM and RETAIN baselines in predicting CKD progression to ESRD, achieving an AUROC of 0.95 and F1-score of 0.69.
TFCAM provides temporal-level explainability by identifying critical periods, such as a crossing point around time step t4 that separates ESRD progressors from non-progressors.
Feature-level explainability ranks key clinical features, with diabetes status, CKD stages S4 and S5, and laboratory values like eGFR being highly important.
Cross-temporal feature explainability quantifies how features influence each other over time, revealing potential causal pathways and dynamic interactions.
The model demonstrates improved handling of class imbalance and captures complex temporal dependencies that baseline models miss.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation focuses solely on CKD progression; validation on other chronic diseases is needed for broader utility.
The MICE-based imputation may not fully capture temporal dependencies in missing data.
future_direction: Validating TFCAM on other chronic diseases with complex progression patterns.
Improving time-series imputation methods to better handle missing data.
Integrating TFCAM's predictions with generative AI and large language models to advance healthcare informatics.
papers.abstract: Despite the outstanding performance of deep learning models in clinical prediction tasks, explainability remains a significant challenge. Inspired by transformer architectures, we introduce the Temporal-Feature Cross Attention Mechanism (TFCAM), a novel deep learning framework designed to capture dynamic interactions among clinical features across time, enhancing both predictive accuracy and interpretability. In an experiment with 1,422 patients with Chronic Kidney Disease, predicting progression to End-Stage Renal Disease, TFCAM outperformed LSTM and RETAIN baselines, achieving an AUROC of 0.95 and an F1-score of 0.69. Beyond performance gains, TFCAM provides multi-level explainability by identifying critical temporal periods, ranking feature importance, and quantifying how features influence each other across time before affecting predictions. Our approach addresses the "black box" limitations of deep learning in healthcare, offering clinicians transparent insights into disease progression mechanisms while maintaining state-of-the-art predictive performance.

papers.title: Toward Causal Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How can causality contribute to modern machine learning research, particularly in addressing transfer learning, generalization, and robustness? What is the problem of causal representation learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reviews and synthesizes fundamental concepts of causal inference and relates them to open problems in machine learning, arguing that causality can help address limitations in transfer learning, generalization, and robustness, and introduces the problem of causal representation learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that causality can significantly contribute to machine learning by providing a framework for robust and generalizable models, and that causal representation learning is a key research area at the intersection of both fields.
papers.key_findings:
Causality provides a framework for modeling interventions and distribution shifts, which can improve robustness and generalization in machine learning.
Causal representation learning, the discovery of high-level causal variables from low-level observations, is a central problem for AI and causality.
The independent causal mechanism (ICM) principle and the sparse mechanism shift (SMS) hypothesis are key for learning causal models.
Causal models can answer interventional and counterfactual questions, going beyond statistical associations.
Combining causality with machine learning can lead to more versatile AI systems.
future_direction: Causal representation learning: discovering high-level causal variables from low-level observations.
Combining the strengths of causality and machine learning to build more versatile AI.
Developing methods for causal discovery and learning from data with weak assumptions.
papers.abstract: The two fields of machine learning and graphical causality arose and are developed separately. However, there is, now, cross-pollination and increasing interest in both fields to benefit from the advances of the other. In this article, we review fundamental concepts of causal inference and relate them to crucial open problems of machine learning, including transfer and generalization, thereby assaying how causality can contribute to modern machine learning research. This also applies in the opposite direction: we note that most work in causality starts from the premise that the causal variables are given. A central problem for AI and causality is, thus, causal representation learning, that is, the discovery of high-level causal variables from low-level observations. Finally, we delineate some implications of causality for machine learning and propose key research areas at the intersection of both communities.

papers.title: Medical Interpretability and Knowledge Maps of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) represent and process medical knowledge, and where is knowledge about patient demographics, symptoms, diseases, drugs, and dosages stored in the models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a systematic interpretability analysis of five LLMs for medical knowledge, integrating four techniques to build knowledge maps that show where medical knowledge is stored, and discovers phenomena such as non-linear age encoding, circular disease progression, and activation collapse in certain models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability methods can identify layers where medical knowledge is stored, and the findings can guide future fine-tuning, unlearning, or de-biasing of LLMs for medical tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Age is encoded in a non-linear manner with discontinuities (e.g., at age 18) in intermediate layers.
Disease progression representations are circular and non-monotonic, with late stages sometimes closer to early stages.
In Llama3.3-70B, drugs cluster better by medical specialty than by mechanism of action.
Gemma3-27B and MedGemma-27B exhibit activation collapse at intermediate layers, which recover by the final layers.
Most medical knowledge in Llama3.3-70B is processed in the first half of the model's layers.
papers.limitation:
Lack of ground-truth data makes validation difficult.
For drug dosage, results are inconclusive and not well understood.
future_direction: Using knowledge maps to guide fine-tuning, unlearning, or de-biasing of LLMs for medical tasks.
Developing regularizers to enforce monotonic disease progression in models.
Further research into drug dosage representations.
papers.abstract: We present a systematic study of medical-domain interpretability in Large Language Models (LLMs). We study how the LLMs both represent and process medical knowledge through four different interpretability techniques: (1) UMAP projections of intermediate activations, (2) gradient-based saliency with respect to the model weights, (3) layer lesioning/removal and (4) activation patching. We present knowledge maps of five LLMs which show, at a coarse-resolution, where knowledge about patient's ages, medical symptoms, diseases and drugs is stored in the models. In particular for Llama3.3-70B, we find that most medical knowledge is processed in the first half of the model's layers. In addition, we find several interesting phenomena: (i) age is often encoded in a non-linear and sometimes discontinuous manner at intermediate layers in the models, (ii) the disease progression representation is non-monotonic and circular at certain layers of the model, (iii) in Llama3.3-70B, drugs cluster better by medical specialty rather than mechanism of action, especially for Llama3.3-70B and (iv) Gemma3-27B and MedGemma-27B have activations that collapse at intermediate layers but recover by the final layers. These results can guide future research on fine-tuning, un-learning or de-biasing LLMs for medical tasks by suggesting at which layers in the model these techniques should be applied.

papers.title: Quantifying Symptom Causality in Clinical Decision Making: An Exploration Using CausaLM
papers.research_question: What is the causal influence of key symptoms (specifically 'chest pain') on diagnostic predictions made by clinical NLP models?
papers.core_contribution: This work presents a method to assess the causal effect of symptoms on disease prediction models by leveraging the CausaLM framework to generate counterfactual text representations and using the TReATE metric to quantify the causal influence.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the potential of causal inference tools to provide a richer, more principled understanding of model behavior in clinical decision support, moving beyond correlation to capture causal effects.
papers.key_findings:
The presence of the symptom 'chest pain' significantly shifts the model's predicted probability distribution for diseases like Bronchitis and Anemia.
The TReATE metric provides a more robust causal interpretation of symptom influence compared to correlation-based metrics like CONEXP.
The adversarial training approach successfully creates text representations that are agnostic to the presence of the target symptom, enabling counterfactual analysis.
papers.limitation:
The causal interpretation hinges on the fidelity of the adversarial training process; imperfect 'forgetting' of the target concept may affect the strength of causal claims.
Disentangling the effect of one symptom may oversimplify the true medical decision-making process, as patients often present with multiple co-occurring symptoms.
future_direction: Exploring multiple treatment concepts simultaneously and controlling for sets of confounding variables.
Integrating structured medical knowledge to ground the analyses more firmly.
Testing the approach on diverse clinical corpora to validate robustness and generalizability.
papers.abstract: Current machine learning approaches to medical diagnosis often rely on correlational patterns between symptoms and diseases, risking misdiagnoses when symptoms are ambiguous or common across multiple conditions. In this work, we move beyond correlation to investigate the causal influence of key symptoms-specifically "chest pain" on diagnostic predictions. Leveraging the CausaLM framework, we generate counterfactual text representations in which target concepts are effectively "forgotten" enabling a principled estimation of the causal effect of that concept on a model's predicted disease distribution. By employing Textual Representation-based Average Treatment Effect (TReATE), we quantify how the presence or absence of a symptom shapes the model's diagnostic outcomes, and contrast these findings against correlation-based baselines such as CONEXP. Our results offer deeper insight into the decision-making behavior of clinical NLP models and have the potential to inform more trustworthy, interpretable, and causally-grounded decision support tools in medical practice.

papers.title: Does TabPFN Understand Causal Structures?
papers.research_question: Does TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model, encode causal knowledge in its internal representations beyond statistical correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and introduces an adapter framework that can extract this information for causal discovery, outperforming traditional statistical methods.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and the proposed adapter framework can extract this information for causal discovery, establishing a new direction for interpretable and adaptable tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Causal information is concentrated in the middle layers (4-6) of TabPFN's encoder.
The proposed framework extracts causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and outperforms statistical baselines (GIES, IGSP, DCDI) on ROC AUC, performing closely to the specialized neural causal discovery model A VICI.
The decoder architecture is crucial for performance; using a learnable decoder significantly improves results compared to using no decoder.
Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, particularly for dense graph structures like Erdős-Rényi and Stochastic Block Model graphs.
Using embeddings from the pre-trained TabPFN encoder (optimal weights) yields better causal discovery performance than using randomly initialized or degraded encoder weights.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, and the approach is sensitive to the type of graph structure.
future_direction: Leveraging pre-trained tabular models for extracting causal structures and improving their interpretability.
Understanding how tabular foundation models reason about different datasets.
Repurposing tabular foundation models for different downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Causal discovery is fundamental for multiple scientific domains, yet extracting causal information from real world data remains a significant challenge. Given the recent success on real data, we investigate whether TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model pre-trained on synthetic datasets generated from structural causal models, encodes causal information in its internal representations. We develop an adapter framework using a learnable decoder and causal tokens that extract causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and decode them into adjacency matrices for causal discovery. Our evaluations demonstrate that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, outperforming several traditional causal discovery algorithms, with such causal information being concentrated in mid-range layers. These findings establish a new direction for interpretable and adaptable foundation models and demonstrate the potential for leveraging pre-trained tabular models for causal discovery.

papers.title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How can causality contribute to modern machine learning research, particularly in addressing transfer and generalization? Additionally, how can we discover high-level causal variables from low-level observations (causal representation learning)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reviews and synthesizes key contributions at the intersection of causality and machine learning, arguing that causality can help address limitations in machine learning such as robustness and generalization, and identifies causal representation learning as a central problem for AI.
papers.conclusion: Causality offers a promising framework to address key challenges in machine learning, such as robustness and generalization, and causal representation learning is a crucial step towards more versatile AI.
papers.key_findings:
Causality provides a framework for robust prediction under distribution shifts and interventions, going beyond statistical associations.
The Independent Causal Mechanisms (ICM) principle and the Sparse Mechanism Shift hypothesis are key for learning causal models from data.
Causal representation learning, the discovery of high-level causal variables from low-level observations, is a central challenge for AI and causality.
Current machine learning methods often fail under distribution shifts because they rely on i.i.d. data and statistical associations rather than causal mechanisms.
Combining causality with machine learning can lead to more versatile AI capable of reasoning, planning, and robust generalization.
future_direction: Causal representation learning: discovering high-level causal variables from low-level observations.
Combining causality with self-supervision, data augmentation, and pre-training to improve robustness and generalization.
Applying causal learning to reinforcement learning and planning for more intelligent agents.
papers.abstract: The two fields of machine learning and graphical causality arose and developed separately. However, there is now cross-pollination and increasing interest in both fields to benefit from the advances of the other. In the present paper, we review fundamental concepts of causal inference and relate them to crucial open problems of machine learning, including transfer and generalization, thereby assaying how causality can contribute to modern machine learning research. This also applies in the opposite direction: we note that most work in causality starts from the premise that the causal variables are given. A central problem for AI and causality is, thus, causal representation learning, the discovery of high-level causal variables from low-level observations. Finally, we delineate some implications of causality for machine learning and propose key research areas at the intersection of both communities.

papers.title: Learning Interpretable Concepts: Unifying Causal Representation Learning and Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How can we learn human-interpretable concepts from data by unifying causal representation learning and foundation models, and under what conditions are such concepts identifiable?
papers.core_contribution: This paper unifies causal representation learning and foundation models by formally defining concepts as affine subspaces in latent representation spaces, proving near-optimal identifiability guarantees for concept learning with only n+2 environments, and applying this framework to explain and improve inference-time intervention for aligning LLMs towards truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a unified framework for learning interpretable concepts that bridges causal representation learning and foundation models, providing identifiability guarantees and demonstrating practical utility in improving LLM alignment via enhanced inference-time steering.
papers.key_findings:
Concepts defined as affine subspaces are identifiable up to linear transformations with only n+2 environments, a significant reduction compared to traditional CRL which requires dimension-dependent environments.
A contrastive learning algorithm validates the identifiability theory on synthetic data with concept conditional distributions.
The framework explains why inference-time intervention (ITI) steering vectors work for truthfulness in LLMs and proposes using steering matrices for better alignment, showing improved performance on TruthfulQA with LLaMA.
papers.abstract: To build intelligent machine learning systems, there are two broad approaches. One approach is to build inherently interpretable models, as endeavored by the growing field of causal representation learning. The other approach is to build highly-performant foundation models and then invest efforts into understanding how they work. In this work, we relate these two approaches and study how to learn human-interpretable concepts from data. Weaving together ideas from both fields, we formally define a notion of concepts and show that they can be provably recovered from diverse data. Experiments on synthetic data and large language models show the utility of our unified approach.

papers.title: Interpretable Additive Recurrent Neural Networks For Multivariate Clinical Time Series
papers.research_question: How to build accurate time series models that are interpretable, specifically for clinical time series data, allowing users to understand the contribution of individual input features.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Interpretable-RNN (I-RNN), an additive recurrent neural network model for clinical time series that provides interpretable feature contributions (global and local feature importances) while achieving accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art black-box models.
papers.conclusion: The I-RNN model provides an interpretable and accurate approach for clinical time series prediction, enabling trust and validation in healthcare applications without sacrificing performance.
papers.key_findings:
I-RNN achieves accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art RNN models (GRU-D, RITS) on hemodynamic intervention prediction (AUC ~0.86) and similar performance on in-hospital mortality prediction.
I-RNN provides interpretable risk curves and feature importances directly from its hidden state activations, which correlate with input features and the prediction target.
The model refutes the common tradeoff between accuracy and interpretability in time series modeling for clinical data.
I-RNN does not use missingness information as input, which may improve generalization across different clinical practice patterns compared to models that exploit informative missingness.
The additive structure of I-RNN allows for easy validation and correction of feature-outcome associations by domain experts.
papers.limitation: The model may not generalize well to institutions with different care patterns because it does not use missingness information, which can be informative but also institution-specific.
papers.abstract: Time series models with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can have high accuracy but are unfortunately difficult to interpret as a result of feature-interactions, temporal-interactions, and non-linear transformations. Interpretability is important in domains like healthcare where constructing models that provide insight into the relationships they have learned are required to validate and trust model predictions. We want accurate time series models where users can understand the contribution of individual input features. We present the Interpretable-RNN (I-RNN) that balances model complexity and accuracy by forcing the relationship between variables in the model to be additive. Interactions are restricted between hidden states of the RNN and additively combined at the final step. I-RNN specifically captures the unique characteristics of clinical time series, which are unevenly sampled in time, asynchronously acquired, and have missing data. Importantly, the hidden state activations represent feature coefficients that correlate with the prediction target and can be visualized as risk curves that capture the global relationship between individual input features and the outcome. We evaluate the I-RNN model on the Physionet 2012 Challenge dataset to predict in-hospital mortality, and on a real-world clinical decision support task: predicting hemodynamic interventions in the intensive care unit. I-RNN provides explanations in the form of global and local feature importances comparable to highly intelligible models like decision trees trained on hand-engineered features while significantly outperforming them. I-RNN remains intelligible while providing accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art decay-based and interpolation-based recurrent time series models. The experimental results on real-world clinical datasets refute the myth that there is a tradeoff between accuracy and interpretability.

papers.title: Integrating clinical reasoning into large language model-based diagnosis through etiology-aware attention steering
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the diagnostic accuracy and clinical reasoning ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in complex clinical scenarios?
papers.core_contribution: This study proposes an Etiology-Aware Attention Steering Framework that integrates structured clinical reasoning into LLM-based diagnosis by identifying and steering attention heads crucial for etiology reasoning, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy and reasoning focus.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework integrates etiology-aware attention guidance with authoritative clinical guidelines, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy, attention stability, and reasoning interpretability, holding strong potential for real-world clinical deployment in complex diagnostic environments.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework improves average diagnostic accuracy by 15.65% and boosts the average Reasoning Focus Score by 31.6% over baselines on the Consistent Diagnosis Cohort.
External validation on the Discrepant Diagnosis Cohort confirms the framework's effectiveness in enhancing diagnostic accuracy in real-world complex scenarios.
The Etiology-Aware Head Identification algorithm successfully pinpoints attention heads that exhibit strong alignment with etiological reasoning.
Ablation studies demonstrate the importance of each component (CRS annotation, Etiology-Aware Head Identification, Reasoning-Guided Loss) for overall performance.
The framework enhances the model's attention stability and reasoning interpretability across diverse diagnostic tasks.
future_direction: Extending the framework to a broader range of diseases and clinical scenarios.
Integrating multimodal data (e.g., medical images, lab waveforms) to enhance diagnostic reasoning.
Incorporating contrastive or self-supervised objectives to further enhance model robustness in low-resource or noisy environments.
papers.abstract: Objective: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate significant capabilities in medical text understanding and generation. However, their diagnostic reliability in complex clinical scenarios remains limited. This study aims to enhance LLMs' diagnostic accuracy and clinical reasoning ability. Method: We propose an Etiology-Aware Attention Steering Framework to integrate structured clinical reasoning into LLM-based diagnosis. Specifically, we first construct Clinical Reasoning Scaffolding (CRS) based on authoritative clinical guidelines for three representative acute abdominal emergencies: acute appendicitis, acute pancreatitis, and acute cholecystitis. Next, we develop the Etiology-Aware Head Identification algorithm to pinpoint attention heads crucial for the model's etiology reasoning. To ensure reliable clinical reasoning alignment, we introduce the Reasoning-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning that embeds etiological reasoning cues into input representations and steers the selected Etiology-Aware Heads toward critical information through a Reasoning-Guided Loss function. Result: On the Consistent Diagnosis Cohort, our framework improves average diagnostic accuracy by 15.65% and boosts the average Reasoning Focus Score by 31.6% over baselines. External validation on the Discrepant Diagnosis Cohort further confirms its effectiveness in enhancing diagnostic accuracy. Further assessments via Reasoning Attention Frequency indicate that our models exhibit enhanced reliability when faced with real-world complex scenarios. Conclusion: This study presents a practical and effective approach to enhance clinical reasoning in LLM-based diagnosis. By aligning model attention with structured CRS, the proposed framework offers a promising paradigm for building more interpretable and reliable AI diagnostic systems in complex clinical settings.

papers.title: Explainable deep learning for disease activity prediction in chronic inflammatory joint diseases
papers.research_question: How can we predict future disease activity scores in chronic inflammatory joint diseases using an explainable deep learning model that also facilitates patient similarity assessment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes DAS-Net, an explainable multi-task deep learning model that transforms longitudinal patient data into comparable representations to predict future disease activity scores and identify patients with similar disease progression.
papers.conclusion: DAS-Net provides an effective and explainable approach for predicting disease activity and assessing patient similarity in chronic inflammatory joint diseases, offering a step towards clinical decision support systems.
papers.key_findings:
DAS-Net outperforms temporal and non-temporal baseline models (LSTM, XGBoost, MLP, naive) in predicting future disease activity scores (DAS28 and ASDAS).
The model's latent representations enable effective patient similarity matching, with k-NN regression on these representations outperforming baselines using raw data.
Explainability analyses (SHAP, attention attribution, case-based similarity) highlight past disease activity scores as the strongest predictors, aligning with clinical knowledge.
Model performance improves with longer patient histories, indicating the importance of temporal context.
The attention mechanism shows that recent events are weighted more heavily, but older events still contribute to predictions.
papers.limitation: The study uses data from a single national registry (Switzerland), which may limit generalizability to other populations.
future_direction: Incorporating a clustering loss in the training objective to further improve the patient similarity framework.
papers.abstract: Analysing complex diseases such as chronic inflammatory joint diseases (CIJDs), where many factors influence the disease evolution over time, is a challenging task. CIJDs are rheumatic diseases that cause the immune system to attack healthy organs, mainly the joints. Different environmental, genetic and demographic factors affect disease development and progression. The Swiss Clinical Quality Management in Rheumatic Diseases (SCQM) Foundation maintains a national database of CIJDs documenting the disease management over time for 19'267 patients. We propose the Disease Activity Score Network (DAS-Net), an explainable multi-task learning model trained on patients' data with different arthritis subtypes, transforming longitudinal patient journeys into comparable representations and predicting multiple disease activity scores. First, we built a modular model composed of feed-forward neural networks, long short-term memory networks and attention layers to process the heterogeneous patient histories and predict future disease activity. Second, we investigated the utility of the model's computed patient representations (latent embeddings) to identify patients with similar disease progression. Third, we enhanced the explainability of our model by analysing the impact of different patient characteristics on disease progression and contrasted our model outcomes with medical expert knowledge. To this end, we explored multiple feature attribution methods including SHAP, attention attribution and feature weighting using case-based similarity. Our model outperforms temporal and non-temporal neural network, tree-based, and naive static baselines in predicting future disease activity scores. To identify similar patients, a k-nearest neighbours regression algorithm applied to the model's computed latent representations outperforms baseline strategies that use raw input features representation.

papers.title: LLM Interpretability with Identifiable Temporal-Instantaneous Representation
papers.research_question: How can we learn interpretable temporal and instantaneous causal representations from LLM activations with theoretical guarantees?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a temporal causal representation learning framework for LLM interpretability that captures time-delayed and instantaneous causal relations with theoretical guarantees.
papers.conclusion: The proposed temporal causal representation learning framework provides a principled way to uncover temporal and instantaneous causal structures in LLM activations, offering a step toward more interpretable and controllable language models.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully discovers meaningful concept relationships in LLM activations by extending sparse autoencoder techniques.
Modeling both temporal and instantaneous conceptual relationships advances the interpretability of LLMs.
The method provides theoretical guarantees for identifiability under linear assumptions and sparsity constraints.
It demonstrates efficacy on synthetic datasets scaled to real-world complexity and on activations from real LLMs.
The approach offers a principled way to uncover causal structures in LLM activations.
papers.limitation: The linearity assumption may not hold in practice, and the scalability to very high-dimensional spaces is limited by the need to estimate large matrices.
future_direction: Extending the framework to nonlinear models.
Scaling the approach to larger models and higher-dimensional spaces.
Incorporating domain knowledge to guide the discovery of causal structures.
papers.abstract: Despite Large Language Models' remarkable capabilities, understanding their internal representations remains challenging. Mechanistic interpretability tools such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs) were developed to extract interpretable features from LLMs but lack temporal dependency modeling, instantaneous relation representation, and more importantly theoretical guarantees, undermining both the theoretical foundations and the practical confidence necessary for subsequent analyses. While causal representation learning (CRL) offers theoretically grounded approaches for uncovering latent concepts, existing methods cannot scale to LLMs' rich conceptual space due to inefficient computation. To bridge the gap, we introduce an identifiable temporal causal representation learning framework specifically designed for LLMs' high-dimensional concept space, capturing both time-delayed and instantaneous causal relations. Our approach provides theoretical guarantees and demonstrates efficacy on synthetic datasets scaled to match real-world complexity. By extending SAE techniques with our temporal causal framework, we successfully discover meaningful concept relationships in LLM activations. Our findings show that modeling both temporal and instantaneous conceptual relationships advances the interpretability of LLMs.

papers.title: Can Attention Be Used to Explain EHR-Based Mortality Prediction Tasks: A Case Study on Hemorrhagic Stroke
papers.research_question: Can attention be used to explain EHR-based mortality prediction tasks, specifically for hemorrhagic stroke?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an interpretable attention-based transformer model for early mortality prediction in hemorrhagic stroke, demonstrating superior performance and fidelity compared to traditional methods.
papers.conclusion: The proposed attention-based transformer model has shown promise in early mortality prediction in hemorrhagic stroke patients, providing improved performance and interpretability over traditional logistic regression models.
papers.key_findings:
The attention-based transformer model outperforms logistic regression and LSTM-Fusion models in AUROC and AUPRC for mortality prediction.
Attention scores as intrinsic explanations achieve higher fidelity (Fidelity+ and Fidelity-) compared to SHAP-based explanations.
Important attributes for prediction include physiological indicators like Glasgow Coma Scale and vital signs at later time points.
The model's explanations align with clinical relevance, showing deterioration in vital signs for patients with positive mortality predictions.
future_direction: Validating the model in other settings and disease states
Enhancing the model's predictive power and explainability
papers.abstract: Stroke is a significant cause of mortality and morbidity, necessitating early predictive strategies to minimize risks. Traditional methods for evaluating patients, such as Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE II, IV) and Simplified Acute Physiology Score III (SAPS III), have limited accuracy and interpretability. This paper proposes a novel approach: an interpretable, attention-based transformer model for early stroke mortality prediction. This model seeks to address the limitations of previous predictive models, providing both interpretability (providing clear, understandable explanations of the model) and fidelity (giving a truthful explanation of the model's dynamics from input to output). Furthermore, the study explores and compares fidelity and interpretability scores using Shapley values and attention-based scores to improve model explainability. The research objectives include designing an interpretable attention-based transformer model, evaluating its performance compared to existing models, and providing feature importance derived from the model.

papers.title: Causality is Key for Interpretability Claims to Generalise
papers.research_question: How can interpretability claims be made more rigorous and generalizable? The paper argues that causal inference specifies what constitutes a valid mapping from model activations to invariant high-level structures and the evidence needed to support such claims.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a causal framework for interpretability, arguing that claims should be stated in the language of causal inference and identifiability to ensure they generalize. It uses Pearl's causal hierarchy to diagnose claim-evidence mismatches and causal representation learning to specify assumptions.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability claims should be grounded in causal inference to ensure they generalize, and practitioners should use a causal framework to align methods, evidence, and claims.
papers.key_findings:
There is a frequent gap between the evidence provided by interpretability methods (e.g., associational) and the strength of the claims made (e.g., interventional or counterfactual).
A pilot study of 50 papers found roughly half of interpretability claims can admit a stronger interpretation than the evidence supports, indicating a field-wide terminological challenge.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research on large language models (LLMs) has yielded important insights into model behaviour, yet recurring pitfalls persist: findings that do not generalise, and causal interpretations that outrun the evidence. Our position is that causal inference specifies what constitutes a valid mapping from model activations to invariant high-level structures, the data or assumptions needed to achieve it, and the inferences it can support. Specifically, Pearl's causal hierarchy clarifies what an interpretability study can justify. Observations establish associations between model behaviour and internal components. Interventions (e.g., ablations or activation patching) support claims how these edits affect a behavioural metric (\eg, average change in token probabilities) over a set of prompts. However, counterfactual claims -- i.e., asking what the model output would have been for the same prompt under an unobserved intervention -- remain largely unverifiable without controlled supervision. We show how causal representation learning (CRL) operationalises this hierarchy, specifying which variables are recoverable from activations and under what assumptions. Together, these motivate a diagnostic framework that helps practitioners select methods and evaluations matching claims to evidence such that findings generalise.

papers.title: Sequential Interpretability: Methods, Applications, and Future Direction for Understanding Deep Learning Models in the Context of Sequential Data
papers.research_question: What are the current techniques for interpreting deep learning models that process sequential data, and what are the limitations and future directions for this research area?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive review and taxonomy of interpretability techniques specifically for deep learning models that process sequential data, categorizing methods into network analysis, sequential saliency, and multivariate attribution, and identifies gaps and future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The paper summarizes the current state of interpretability techniques for deep sequential models, presents a goal-oriented taxonomy, and highlights specific limitations and opportunities for future research in data modalities, application domains, and interpretable techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The majority of interpretability research has focused on image processing, with less attention on sequential data despite its importance in domains like NLP and healthcare.
Interpretability techniques for sequential data can be categorized into three primary trends: network analysis (e.g., weight inspection, maximum activation), sequential saliency (e.g., attention, gradient-based saliency), and multivariate attribution (e.g., dual attention mechanisms, backwards neuron attribution).
Attention mechanisms have become a widespread form of sequential interpretability but have drawbacks, such as being easily manipulated and not always reliably indicating the most predictive input features.
There is a notable lack of interpretable frameworks for video data and for modeling sequences as arbitrary-length subsequences rather than contiguous single time steps.
Several domain- and model-agnostic interpretability approaches (e.g., LIME, meta-learning, adversarial techniques) have not yet been explored or demonstrated for sequential data and applications.
papers.limitation:
The most common data type in the reviewed literature is text, followed by time series, discrete sequences, and video, with a surprising lack of interpretable frameworks for video processing.
Nearly all reviewed works identify salient subsequences as contiguous, single salient time steps rather than by directly modeling a sequence as a series of arbitrary length subsequences.
Several domain- and model-agnostic interpretability approaches (e.g., LIME, meta learning, deep nearest neighbors, adversarial techniques) have not been explored or demonstrated for sequential data.
future_direction: Extending interpretability research to video data modalities.
Developing methods to model sequences as series of arbitrary-length subsequences rather than just contiguous time steps.
Exploring and demonstrating general interpretability methods (like LIME, meta-learning, adversarial techniques) for sequential data and applications.
papers.abstract: Deep learning continues to revolutionize an ever-growing number of critical application areas including healthcare, transportation, finance, and basic sciences. Despite their increased predictive power, model transparency and human explainability remain a significant challenge due to the "black box" nature of modern deep learning models. In many cases the desired balance between interpretability and performance is predominately task specific. Human-centric domains such as healthcare necessitate a renewed focus on understanding how and why these frameworks are arriving at critical and potentially life-or-death decisions. Given the quantity of research and empirical successes of deep learning for computer vision, most of the existing interpretability research has focused on image processing techniques. Comparatively, less attention has been paid to interpreting deep learning frameworks using sequential data. Given recent deep learning advancements in highly sequential domains such as natural language processing and physiological signal processing, the need for deep sequential explanations is at an all-time high. In this paper, we review current techniques for interpreting deep learning techniques involving sequential data, identify similarities to non-sequential methods, and discuss current limitations and future avenues of sequential interpretability research.

papers.title: On the Mechanistic Interpretability of Neural Networks for Causality in Bio-statistics
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability techniques be transposed to bio-statistics, and how effective are they?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability tools can be leveraged to probe and validate internal representations learned by neural networks for causal inference, discover and visualize computational pathways for confounders and treatments, and compare learned mechanisms across model types.
papers.abstract: Interpretable insights from predictive models remain critical in bio-statistics, particularly when assessing causality, where classical statistical and machine learning methods often provide inherent clarity. While Neural Networks (NNs) offer powerful capabilities for modeling complex biological data, their traditional "black-box" nature presents challenges for validation and trust in high-stakes health applications. Recent advances in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) aim to decipher the internal computations learned by these networks. This work investigates the application of MI techniques to NNs within the context of causal inference for bio-statistics. We demonstrate that MI tools can be leveraged to: (1) probe and validate the internal representations learned by NNs, such as those estimating nuisance functions in frameworks like Targeted Minimum Loss-based Estimation (TMLE); (2) discover and visualize the distinct computational pathways employed by the network to process different types of inputs, potentially revealing how confounders and treatments are handled; and (3) provide methodologies for comparing the learned mechanisms and extracted insights across statistical, machine learning, and NN models, fostering a deeper understanding of their respective strengths and weaknesses for causal bio-statistical analysis.

papers.title: A Monosemantic Attribution Framework for Stable Interpretability in Clinical Neuroscience Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we produce stable, clinically meaningful explanations from large language models by integrating attributional and mechanistic interpretability to address polysemanticity and inter-method variability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified interpretability framework that integrates attributional and mechanistic perspectives through monosemantic feature extraction, using sparse autoencoders to transform polysemantic activations and an explanation optimizer (TEO) to produce stable and clinically meaningful explanations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed monosemantic attribution framework advances the safe and trustworthy application of LLMs in cognitive health and neurodegenerative disease by providing stable and clinically meaningful explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The SAE layer improves attribution stability (lower RIS/ROS) and clinical meaningfulness.
TEO with SAE (TEO-SAE) achieves the most stable attributions across in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets.
The UMAP linear constraint helps linearize the attribution space and yields robust scores.
The framework provides clinically interpretable attribution maps highlighting relevant biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis.
SAE-guided attribution yields more reliable explanations than traditional attribution methods.
papers.abstract: Interpretability remains a key challenge for deploying large language models (LLMs) in clinical settings such as Alzheimer's disease progression diagnosis, where early and trustworthy predictions are essential. Existing attribution methods exhibit high inter-method variability and unstable explanations due to the polysemantic nature of LLM representations, while mechanistic interpretability approaches lack direct alignment with model inputs and outputs and do not provide explicit importance scores. We introduce a unified interpretability framework that integrates attributional and mechanistic perspectives through monosemantic feature extraction. By constructing a monosemantic embedding space at the level of an LLM layer and optimizing the framework to explicitly reduce inter-method variability, our approach produces stable input-level importance scores and highlights salient features via a decompressed representation of the layer of interest, advancing the safe and trustworthy application of LLMs in cognitive health and neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: Embeddings to Diagnosis: Latent Fragility under Agentic Perturbations in Clinical LLMs
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how clinical LLMs exhibit latent fragility under small, clinically meaningful input perturbations, and proposes a geometry-aware evaluation framework to probe this robustness.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LAPD, a geometry-aware evaluation framework, and LDFR, a metric that captures latent representational instability in clinical LLMs under structured perturbations, revealing a gap between surface robustness and semantic stability.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a framework to uncover latent diagnostic instability in clinical LLMs, with LDFR providing a geometry-aware signal for auditing robustness, underscoring the need for evaluation beyond surface metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Latent fragility is exposed under perturbations like masking and negation, even when surface metrics remain high.
LDFR shows instability that traditional metrics miss, with masking causing the largest drop in accuracy and LDFR.
Patterns of fragility generalize from synthetic notes to real clinical notes from DiReCT.
Different models exhibit varying levels of fragility, with smaller models like Mistral-7B being more vulnerable.
Entity masking induces sharp latent shifts and diagnostic flips, highlighting over-reliance on surface cues.
papers.limitation:
Synthetic notes may not reflect real-world clinical variability.
Using a fixed BERT embedding space may misalign with model-specific representations.
No expert adjudication of whether diagnostic flips induced by perturbations are clinically warranted.
future_direction: Explore non-linear boundaries via manifold learning.
Expand perturbation analysis to include more types.
Align latent shifts with expert judgments for validation.
papers.abstract: LLMs for clinical decision support often fail under small but clinically meaningful input shifts such as masking a symptom or negating a finding, despite high performance on static benchmarks. These reasoning failures frequently go undetected by standard NLP metrics, which are insensitive to latent representation shifts that drive diagnosis instability. We propose a geometry-aware evaluation framework, LAPD (Latent Agentic Perturbation Diagnostics), which systematically probes the latent robustness of clinical LLMs under structured adversarial edits. Within this framework, we introduce Latent Diagnosis Flip Rate (LDFR), a model-agnostic diagnostic signal that captures representational instability when embeddings cross decision boundaries in PCA-reduced latent space. Clinical notes are generated using a structured prompting pipeline grounded in diagnostic reasoning, then perturbed along four axes: masking, negation, synonym replacement, and numeric variation to simulate common ambiguities and omissions. We compute LDFR across both foundation and clinical LLMs, finding that latent fragility emerges even under minimal surface-level changes. Finally, we validate our findings on 90 real clinical notes from the DiReCT benchmark (MIMIC-IV), confirming the generalizability of LDFR beyond synthetic settings. Our results reveal a persistent gap between surface robustness and semantic stability, underscoring the importance of geometry-aware auditing in safety-critical clinical AI.

papers.title: Integrating Deep Learning and Interpretable Regression Models for Transparent Decision Support in Healthcare Diagnostics
papers.research_question: How can deep learning and interpretable regression models be integrated to achieve transparent decision support in healthcare diagnostics while maintaining predictive performance?
papers.core_contribution: This study demonstrates that a hybrid framework integrating deep learning embeddings with interpretable regression models can achieve competitive predictive performance while providing transparent, clinically interpretable explanations for healthcare diagnostics.
papers.conclusion: The hybrid approach bridges the gap between predictive accuracy and explainability, offering a viable pathway for transparent AI in healthcare diagnostics, though limitations include static data and approximate explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The hybrid model (Logistic Regression on embeddings) achieved AUC=0.9829 and high sensitivity, balancing performance and interpretability.
SHAP analysis revealed that clinical variables like age, creatinine, and blood pressure were top contributors to predictions, aligning with medical knowledge.
The deep model's embeddings captured complex physiological patterns, enabling effective use in interpretable regression.
Baseline logistic regression on raw features showed perfect scores on test data, indicating potential overfitting or data leakage.
The framework provides both global and local explanations through coefficients and SHAP values.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was constrained to static, tabular representations of patient data, excluding temporal dynamics.
Interpretability is limited to feature-level attributions and linear coefficients, which are descriptive rather than causal.
SHAP approximations can be sensitive to background distribution and assume feature independence, potentially leading to misleading attributions.
Mapping from embeddings to raw features is inherently approximate and may not provide stable interpretations.
Generalizability concerns due to dataset from a single medical center and potential data leakage.
future_direction: Incorporate temporal modeling using LSTMs or Transformers to capture sequential patient data.
Extend the framework to multi-class and multi-label diagnostic outcomes.
Integrate causal interpretability and counterfactual reasoning for actionable insights.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have demonstrated exceptional predictive capabilities in healthcare diagnostics, yet their black-box nature limits clinical adoption due to a lack of interpretability and trust. This study addresses this limitation by developing a hybrid decision-support framework that integrates deep representation learning with interpretable regression modeling. Using the MIMIC-IV dataset, sourced from U.S. intensive care units, and comprising patient demographics, vital signs, and laboratory data, we train a deep neural network to learn 128-dimensional patient embeddings that capture underlying physiological patterns. These embeddings are then used as inputs to interpretable regression models, Logistic Regression, and Generalized Additive Models, to predict hospital mortality while maintaining transparency. SHAP-based interpretability analysis is employed to quantify and visualize the contribution of each embedding dimension and clinical feature to model predictions. Experimental results show that the hybrid model achieves competitive performance relative to standalone deep models, while providing clear feature-level explanations through regression coefficients and SHAP importance rankings. The findings demonstrate that deep–deep-interpretable hybrid architectures can bridge the performance–explainability divide, offering a viable pathway for deploying transparent, trustworthy AI systems in clinical diagnostics. This integration not only enhances predictive reliability but also strengthens clinician confidence through evidence-based, interpretable decision support.

papers.title: The Non-Linear Representation Dilemma: Is Causal Abstraction Enough for Mechanistic Interpretability?
papers.research_question: Is causal abstraction sufficient for mechanistic interpretability when alignment maps are not constrained to be linear?
papers.core_contribution: Causal abstraction becomes vacuous when alignment maps are allowed to be arbitrarily complex, leading to the non-linear representation dilemma where there is no principled way to balance map complexity and accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Causal abstraction is not enough for mechanistic interpretability without assumptions about how models encode information.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretically, any algorithm can be perfectly mapped to any neural network under reasonable assumptions if alignment maps are arbitrarily complex.
Empirically, non-linear alignment maps can achieve near-perfect interchange intervention accuracy even on randomly initialized models that do not solve the task.
The complexity of alignment maps needed to achieve perfect IIA decreases as the model trains.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical result relies on assumptions such as input-injectivity and output-surjectivity of the neural network.
Empirical alignment map training can suffer from grokking and requires careful hyperparameter tuning.
future_direction: Studying the connection between information-encoding assumptions and causal abstraction.
papers.abstract: The concept of causal abstraction got recently popularised to demystify the opaque decision-making processes of machine learning models; in short, a neural network can be abstracted as a higher-level algorithm if there exists a function which allows us to map between them. Notably, most interpretability papers implement these maps as linear functions, motivated by the linear representation hypothesis: the idea that features are encoded linearly in a model's representations. However, this linearity constraint is not required by the definition of causal abstraction. In this work, we critically examine the concept of causal abstraction by considering arbitrarily powerful alignment maps. In particular, we prove that under reasonable assumptions, any neural network can be mapped to any algorithm, rendering this unrestricted notion of causal abstraction trivial and uninformative. We complement these theoretical findings with empirical evidence, demonstrating that it is possible to perfectly map models to algorithms even when these models are incapable of solving the actual task; e.g., on an experiment using randomly initialised language models, our alignment maps reach 100\% interchange-intervention accuracy on the indirect object identification task. This raises the non-linear representation dilemma: if we lift the linearity constraint imposed to alignment maps in causal abstraction analyses, we are left with no principled way to balance the inherent trade-off between these maps' complexity and accuracy. Together, these results suggest an answer to our title's question: causal abstraction is not enough for mechanistic interpretability, as it becomes vacuous without assumptions about how models encode information. Studying the connection between this information-encoding assumption and causal abstraction should lead to exciting future work.

papers.title: Foundations of Causal ML
papers.core_contribution: This chapter provides a tutorial on causal machine learning, covering causal structure discovery and causal inference, with a focus on applications in healthcare and biomedical sciences.
papers.conclusion: Causal ML is essential for healthcare applications to move beyond prediction to intervention, and requires careful protocol and validation.
papers.abstract: Abstract The present chapter covers the important dimension of causality in ML both in terms of causal structure discovery and causal inference. The vast majority of biomedical ML focuses on predictive modeling and does not address causal methods, their requirements and properties. Yet these are essential for determining and assisting patient-level or healthcare-level interventions toward improving a set of outcomes of interest. Moreover causal ML techniques can be instrumental for health science discovery.

papers.title: CausalFormer: An Interpretable Transformer for Temporal Causal Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we uncover causal relations in time series data by interpreting the whole structure of a deep learning model, rather than just local parameters?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes CausalFormer, an interpretable transformer-based model for temporal causal discovery that uses a causality-aware transformer with multi-kernel causal convolution and a decomposition-based causality detector with regression relevance propagation to achieve global interpretability and state-of-the-art performance.
papers.conclusion: CausalFormer achieves state-of-the-art performance in discovering the causal relations of time series and demonstrates high applicability on real-world datasets.
papers.key_findings:
CausalFormer outperforms existing deep learning-based methods on synthetic, simulated, and real datasets.
The decomposition-based causality detector (with regression relevance propagation) is critical for performance.
The multi-kernel causal convolution helps establish independent series-to-series data flow for meticulous causality representation.
The bias item in regression relevance propagation helps avoid incorrect attribution of contributions.
CausalFormer can identify causal relationships consistent with known physical processes, as shown in the sea surface temperature case study.
papers.limitation: The precision of delay (PoD) of CausalFormer is inferior to some baselines because it fairly employs the observations of the whole time window, whereas other methods impose penalties on more distant observations.
future_direction: Exploring constraint or penalty on the causal convolution process to improve the precision of delay while maintaining the performance of temporal causal discovery.
papers.abstract: Temporal causal discovery is a crucial task aimed at uncovering the causal relations within time series data. The latest temporal causal discovery methods usually train deep learning models on prediction tasks to uncover the causality between time series. They capture causal relations by analyzing the parameters of some components of the trained models, e.g., attention weights and convolution weights. However, this is an incomplete mapping process from the model parameters to the causality and fails to investigate the other components, e.g., fully connected layers and activation functions, that are also significant for causal discovery. To facilitate the utilization of the whole deep learning models in temporal causal discovery, we proposed an interpretable transformer-based causal discovery model termed CausalFormer, which consists of the causality-aware transformer and the decomposition-based causality detector. The causality-aware transformer learns the causal representation of time series data using a prediction task with the designed multi-kernel causal convolution which aggregates each input time series along the temporal dimension under the temporal priority constraint. Then, the decomposition-based causality detector interprets the global structure of the trained causality-aware transformer with the proposed regression relevance propagation to identify potential causal relations and finally construct the causal graph. Experiments on synthetic, simulated, and real datasets demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of CausalFormer on discovering temporal causality. Our code is available at https://github.com/lingbai-kong/CausalFormer.

papers.title: Causal SHAP: Feature Attribution with Dependency Awareness through Causal Discovery
papers.research_question: How to integrate causal relationships into SHAP feature attribution to address its limitation of not differentiating between causality and correlation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Causal SHAP, a framework that integrates causal discovery (PC algorithm) and causal strength quantification (IDA) into SHAP to provide feature attributions that respect causal relationships, while preserving SHAP's desirable properties.
papers.conclusion: Causal SHAP is a comprehensive feature attribution method that integrates causality using PC and IDA algorithms, demonstrating effectiveness in experiments and preserving SHAP properties.
papers.key_findings:
Causal SHAP effectively respects causal relationships, even in the presence of highly correlated features, as shown in synthetic datasets.
It achieves superior insertion scores (e.g., AUROC) on real-world datasets compared to other SHAP variants.
It preserves key theoretical properties of SHAP: local accuracy, missingness, and consistency.
On synthetic datasets, Causal SHAP achieves the lowest RMSE against ground truth, accurately capturing true causal effects.
Causal SHAP correctly attributes zero importance to non-causal features (e.g., drink coffee in lung cancer dataset) where other methods misattribute.
papers.limitation:
Assumes no hidden variables in the dataset, which may not hold in real-world scenarios.
PC algorithm can become computationally expensive as the number of features scales.
future_direction: Address cases with hidden variables using the FCI algorithm.
Explore Greedy Equivalence Search (GES) when the PC algorithm becomes computationally expensive.
Enhance the framework to handle causal structure uncertainty by aggregating multiple possible causal graphs.
papers.abstract: Explaining machine learning (ML) predictions has become crucial as ML models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains such as healthcare. While SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) is widely used for model interpretability, it fails to differentiate between causality and correlation, often misattributing feature importance when features are highly correlated. We propose Causal SHAP, a novel framework that integrates causal relationships into feature attribution while preserving many desirable properties of SHAP. By combining the Peter-Clark (PC) algorithm for causal discovery and the Intervention Calculus when the DAG is Absent (IDA) algorithm for causal strength quantification, our approach addresses the weakness of SHAP. Specifically, Causal SHAP reduces attribution scores for features that are merely correlated with the target, as validated through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. This study contributes to the field of Explainable AI (XAI) by providing a practical framework for causal-aware model explanations. Our approach is particularly valuable in domains such as healthcare, where understanding true causal relationships is critical for informed decision-making.

papers.title: Discovering Hierarchical Latent Capabilities of Language Models via Causal Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How can we causally evaluate language model capabilities and discover hierarchical latent capabilities from benchmark performance data while accounting for base model heterogeneity?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a causal representation learning framework (Hierarchical Component Analysis) that identifies a hierarchical linear causal structure among latent language model capabilities from benchmark performance data, revealing a causal direction from general problem-solving to instruction-following to mathematical reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Controlling for base model variation is critical for uncovering causal relationships among latent capabilities, and the discovered hierarchical capability structure provides substantial scientific insights beyond simple numerical rankings.
papers.key_findings:
Performance data exhibit heterogeneity across base models, necessitating control for base model variation in evaluations.
A subset of base models (Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B) share similar latent performance patterns.
A three-node linear causal structure (general problem-solving → instruction-following → mathematical reasoning) reliably explains observed benchmark performance variations.
The causal effect from instruction-following to mathematical reasoning is stable across domains and is stronger for Qwen models compared to Llama models.
The method can impute missing benchmark performance more accurately by accounting for base model heterogeneity compared to global matrix completion.
papers.limitation: The causal model recovery can be sensitive to the choice of base models and may be affected by finite-sample errors and violations of causal assumptions.
future_direction: Further investigation of the effect of finite-sample error and violations of causal assumptions on causal graph recovery.
papers.abstract: Faithful evaluation of language model capabilities is crucial for deriving actionable insights that can inform model development. However, rigorous causal evaluations in this domain face significant methodological challenges, including complex confounding effects and prohibitive computational costs associated with extensive retraining. To tackle these challenges, we propose a causal representation learning framework wherein observed benchmark performance is modeled as a linear transformation of a few latent capability factors. Crucially, these latent factors are identified as causally interrelated after appropriately controlling for the base model as a common confounder. Applying this approach to a comprehensive dataset encompassing over 1500 models evaluated across six benchmarks from the Open LLM Leaderboard, we identify a concise three-node linear causal structure that reliably explains the observed performance variations. Further interpretation of this causal structure provides substantial scientific insights beyond simple numerical rankings: specifically, we reveal a clear causal direction starting from general problem-solving capabilities, advancing through instruction-following proficiency, and culminating in mathematical reasoning ability. Our results underscore the essential role of carefully controlling base model variations during evaluation, a step critical to accurately uncovering the underlying causal relationships among latent model capabilities.

papers.title: Linear Causal Representation Learning by Topological Ordering, Pruning, and Disentanglement
papers.research_question: How can we recover latent causal features and the underlying causal DAG from observed data under weaker assumptions about environment heterogeneity and data-generating distributions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces CREATOR, a novel linear causal representation learning algorithm that operates under weaker assumptions about environment heterogeneity and data distributions than existing methods, recovering latent causal features and the causal DAG up to an equivalence class.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents CREATOR, a new linear CRL algorithm that works under weaker assumptions and demonstrates competitive performance in synthetic experiments and a proof-of-concept application to LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CREATOR recovers latent causal features and the causal DAG up to an equivalence class under weaker assumptions than existing methods.
In synthetic experiments, CREATOR outperforms the competing method LiNGCReL in terms of LocR2 and structural Hamming distance.
CREATOR can be applied to large language models to uncover latent causal mechanisms in their hidden states, demonstrating its potential for AI interpretability.
papers.limitation: The method is limited to linear models and extension to nonlinear structural causal models is difficult.
future_direction: Extend the algorithm to nonlinear settings.
Investigate recovering latent concepts with fewer environments.
Develop CRL algorithms that can handle dynamical data and multimodal data.
papers.abstract: Causal representation learning (CRL) has garnered increasing interests from the causal inference and artificial intelligence community, due to its capability of disentangling potentially complex data-generating mechanism into causally interpretable latent features, by leveraging the heterogeneity of modern datasets. In this paper, we further contribute to the CRL literature, by focusing on the stylized linear structural causal model over the latent features and assuming a linear mixing function that maps latent features to the observed data or measurements. Existing linear CRL methods often rely on stringent assumptions, such as accessibility to single-node interventional data or restrictive distributional constraints on latent features and exogenous measurement noise. However, these prerequisites can be challenging to satisfy in certain scenarios. In this work, we propose a novel linear CRL algorithm that, unlike most existing linear CRL methods, operates under weaker assumptions about environment heterogeneity and data-generating distributions while still recovering latent causal features up to an equivalence class. We further validate our new algorithm via synthetic experiments and an interpretability analysis of large language models (LLMs), demonstrating both its superiority over competing methods in finite samples and its potential in integrating causality into AI.
