papers.title: DILA: Dictionary Label Attention for Mechanistic Interpretability in High-dimensional Multi-label Medical Coding Prediction
papers.research_question: How to provide comprehensive, global explanations for high-dimensional multi-label predictions, specifically in medical coding, by disentangling dense embeddings into interpretable sparse concepts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DILA, a mechanistic interpretability module that uses dictionary learning to create sparse, interpretable embeddings and a sparse matrix mapping these features to labels, providing global explanations for multi-label predictions while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.conclusion: DILA provides a scalable and effective approach for mechanistic interpretability in high-dimensional multi-label prediction, successfully balancing interpretability, performance, and computational efficiency for tasks like medical coding.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse dictionary features from DILA are at least 50% more human-interpretable than dense embeddings.
An automated pipeline using medical LLMs can identify and summarize thousands of learned medical concepts from the sparse features.
DILA maintains competitive performance with state-of-the-art black-box models on the MIMIC-III clean medical coding dataset.
Ablating weights in the global sparse projection matrix (Aficd) precisely affects only the target ICD code prediction, unlike token-level perturbations which affect multiple codes.
Mechanistic interpretability via DILA is computationally efficient compared to model-agnostic methods like KernelSHAP for high-dimensional tasks.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary features are not always perfectly interpretable, and the LLM-based auto-interpretability pipeline can be improved.
DILA's performance is slightly lower than some black-box baselines.
future_direction: Improving the auto-interpretability pipeline with better LLM prompting and feature identification.
Extending the method to other domains and tasks beyond medical coding.
papers.abstract: Predicting high-dimensional or extreme multilabels, such as in medical coding, requires both accuracy and interpretability. Existing works often rely on local interpretability methods, failing to provide comprehensive explanations of the overall mechanism behind each label prediction within a multilabel set. We propose a mechanistic interpretability module called DIctionary Label Attention (\method) that disentangles uninterpretable dense embeddings into a sparse embedding space, where each nonzero element (a dictionary feature) represents a globally learned medical concept. Through human evaluations, we show that our sparse embeddings are more human understandable than its dense counterparts by at least 50 percent. Our automated dictionary feature identification pipeline, leveraging large language models (LLMs), uncovers thousands of learned medical concepts by examining and summarizing the highest activating tokens for each dictionary feature. We represent the relationships between dictionary features and medical codes through a sparse interpretable matrix, enhancing the mechanistic and global understanding of the model's predictions while maintaining competitive performance and scalability without extensive human annotation.

papers.title: Causal Abstractions of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What drives the success of the BERT-based model on the challenging MQNLI task? More broadly, can we derive interpretable causal explanations of neural network behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a methodology for causal abstraction analysis of neural networks, which aligns neural representations with variables in interpretable causal models and uses interchange interventions to verify causal properties. Demonstrates in a case study on MQNLI that BERT partially realizes the causal structure of the natural logic model, while LSTM does not.
papers.conclusion: The methodology of causal abstraction analysis is feasible and provides interpretable causal explanations of neural network behavior, demonstrating that high-level causal explanation can be achieved for complex neural models.
papers.key_findings:
BERT achieves high accuracy (88.5%) on the challenging MQNLI dataset, while a BiLSTM baseline fails (46.3%).
Causal abstraction analysis shows that BERT partially realizes the causal structure of the natural logic model used to generate MQNLI, with strong evidence for specific nodes like NPObj.
The BiLSTM model shows almost no evidence of realizing the causal structure of the natural logic model.
The methodology provides causal explanations of model behavior that go beyond correlational methods like probing.
Integrated gradients attribution results align with the causal abstraction findings for BERT, supporting the hypothesis that specific representations are causally important.
papers.abstract: Structural analysis methods (e.g., probing and feature attribution) are increasingly important tools for neural network analysis. We propose a new structural analysis method grounded in a formal theory of causal abstraction that provides rich characterizations of model-internal representations and their roles in input/output behavior. In this method, neural representations are aligned with variables in interpretable causal models, and then interchange interventions are used to experimentally verify that the neural representations have the causal properties of their aligned variables. We apply this method in a case study to analyze neural models trained on Multiply Quantified Natural Language Inference (MQNLI) corpus, a highly complex NLI dataset that was constructed with a tree-structured natural logic causal model. We discover that a BERT-based model with state-of-the-art performance successfully realizes parts of the natural logic model's causal structure, whereas a simpler baseline model fails to show any such structure, demonstrating that BERT representations encode the compositional structure of MQNLI.

papers.title: A Novel Framework for Inherently Interpretable Deep Neural Networks Using Attention-Based Feature Attribution in High-Dimensional Tabular Data
papers.research_question: How can deep learning models for tabular data be designed to be both accurate and inherently interpretable, providing intrinsic explanations for predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an attention-augmented neural network architecture for tabular data that inherently provides feature importance scores through its attention weights, achieving competitive accuracy while offering built-in interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The attention-based neural network delivers competitive accuracy and intrinsic interpretability for high-dimensional tabular data, bridging the gap between deep learning performance and the explainability required in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed AttentionNet model achieves predictive accuracy (0.97) comparable to or better than strong baselines like Random Forest (0.96).
The model's attention weights show strong agreement (Spearman correlation ~0.88) with SHAP values, indicating they serve as faithful feature attributions.
The attention mechanism successfully identifies key predictive features, as validated on synthetic data and a biomedical dataset.
The framework bridges performance and explainability by design, enabling reliable deployment of deep models in high-stakes domains like healthcare.
papers.limitation:
Attention-based models may misidentify features if trained on biased data, and attention distributions can appear degenerate (e.g., spreading weight over many features) without proper regularization.
The model's explanations inherit any biases present in the network, similar to other interpretability methods.
future_direction: Exploring extensions such as hierarchical attention (multi-layer).
Integration with causal inference to further validate feature importances.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models for tabular data often lack interpretability, posing challenges in domains like healthcare and finance where trust is critical. We propose an attention-augmented neural network architecture that inherently highlights the most informative features, thus providing intrinsic explanations for its predictions. Drawing inspiration from TabNet and Transformer-based models, our model applies multi-head feature-wise attention to automatically weight each feature’s contribution. We incorporate an attention-weight regularization scheme (e.g. sparsemax) to encourage focused attributions. For further interpretability, we compare these learned attention weights with SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) post-hoc values. We evaluate our approach on a high-dimensional healthcare dataset (e.g. clinical outcome prediction) and synthetic benchmarks. Experimental results show our model achieves competitive accuracy (Table 1) while providing clear feature importance insights. Feature attribution charts (Fig. 1) demonstrate that the attention mechanism successfully identifies key predictors, aligning well with SHAP analysis. This work bridges performance and explainability by design, enabling reliable deployment of deep models on complex tabular data.

papers.title: Systematic Evaluation of Single-Cell Foundation Model Interpretability Reveals Attention Captures Co-Expression Rather Than Unique Regulatory Signal
papers.research_question: Does attention in single-cell foundation models capture causal regulatory relationships or just co-expression? Do attention-derived edge scores provide incremental value beyond gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models encode structured biological information (e.g., protein-protein interactions in early layers, transcriptional regulation in late layers) but do not capture causal regulatory signal; they provide no incremental value over gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes.
papers.conclusion: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models capture co-expression rather than causal regulatory signal, and the proposed evaluation framework provides a reusable quality-control standard for mechanistic interpretability in this domain.
papers.key_findings:
Attention patterns show layer-specific biological specialization but do not outperform trivial gene-level baselines for perturbation prediction.
Pairwise edge scores (attention or correlation) provide no incremental predictive value beyond gene-level features.
Causal ablation of 'regulatory' attention heads does not degrade perturbation prediction, indicating distributed redundancy.
The relationship between attention and correlation is context-dependent across cell types and perturbation modalities.
Cell-State Stratified Interpretability (CSSI) improves attention-derived GRN recovery by controlling for heterogeneity.
papers.limitation:
Causal ablation only performed on Geneformer V2-316M, not on scGPT due to architectural differences.
Perturbation data limited to four cell types and two modalities; additional tissues, species, and architectures remain untested.
No decisive positive control demonstrates recovery of known causal regulatory structure in a realistic perturbation setting.
future_direction: Test additional tissues, species, and architectures (e.g., scFoundation).
Focus interpretability efforts on residual-stream geometry, MLP-stored knowledge, or representations from the full forward pass.
papers.abstract: We present a systematic evaluation framework - thirty-seven analyses, 153 statistical tests, four cell types, two perturbation modalities - for assessing mechanistic interpretability in single-cell foundation models. Applying this framework to scGPT and Geneformer, we find that attention patterns encode structured biological information with layer-specific organisation - protein-protein interactions in early layers, transcriptional regulation in late layers - but this structure provides no incremental value for perturbation prediction: trivial gene-level baselines outperform both attention and correlation edges (AUROC 0.81-0.88 versus 0.70), pairwise edge scores add zero predictive contribution, and causal ablation of regulatory heads produces no degradation. These findings generalise from K562 to RPE1 cells; the attention-correlation relationship is context-dependent, but gene-level dominance is universal. Cell-State Stratified Interpretability (CSSI) addresses an attention-specific scaling failure, improving GRN recovery up to 1.85x. The framework establishes reusable quality-control standards for the field.

papers.title: Causal AI for Data Scientists: A Framework to Automate Discovery of Causal Relationships in Noisy Datasets
papers.research_question: How can we develop a robust framework for causal discovery in noisy datasets with latent confounding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework that integrates mechanistic interpretability with causal inference to discover causal relationships in noisy datasets, validated on synthetic and real-world data.
papers.conclusion: The framework demonstrates superior performance in identifying robust, interpretable causal structures in noisy, high-dimensional systems, offering a valuable tool for advancing causal inference in machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
The framework outperforms existing methods (NOTEARS, DAG-GNN) in accuracy and Structural Hamming Distance (SHD).
It identifies monosemantic and polysemantic variables through Causal Effect Strength (CES), Intervention Specificity (IS), and Polysemanticity Score (PS).
It achieves high modularity in latent representations, with the latent layer showing the strongest separation.
It successfully recovers known causal relationships in clinical (e.g., medication to blood pressure) and climate (e.g., pressure to temperature) data.
Mediation analysis reveals direct and indirect causal pathways, quantifying the role of latent mediators.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> In the pursuit of advancing causal discovery methodologies, this research introduces a robust framework designed to navigate environments laden with noise and latent confounding. By integrating mechanistic interpretability with causal inference, the framework facilitates the structural disentanglement of complex causal influences, enabling a more transparent understanding of underlying mechanisms.The approach is validated using both synthetic datasets (Noisy-CausalSim, Sim-NCE+) and real-world datasets (MIMIC-IV clinical data and NOAA climate records), demonstrating versatility across diverse contexts. Key metrics—Causal Effect Strength (CES), Intervention Specificity (IS), and Polysemanticity Score (PS)—are employed to quantify the magnitude, focus, and dispersion of causal effects. Findings reveal that variables with high CES and low IS values act as monosemantic agents, exerting targeted influence, while higher PS scores indicate polysemantic variables affecting multiple targets.The framework's encoder-decoder architecture aligns latent representations with causal graphs, enhancing interpretability. Mediation analysis uncovers indirect causal pathways, highlighting the role of latent variables in effect transmission. Compared to traditional methods like NOTEARS and DAG-GNN, the proposed approach achieves superior performance, evidenced by higher CES and IS scores and lower Structural Hamming Distance (SHD).This work advances causal inference by providing tools for uncovering modular and interpretable causal structures, even amidst noise and latent confounding. The combination of mechanistic interpretability methods like activation patching and attention saliency allows for a more profound comprehension of the mechanisms of machine learning models. By closing the black-box prediction and causal processes underlying, this method not only increases the transparency but also the trustworthiness of causal AI systems. In addition, its applicability to a wide range of datasets demonstrates its flexibility and potential generalizability to a variety of fields.

papers.title: 3D ReX: Causal Explanations in 3D Neuroimaging Classification
papers.core_contribution: Introduces 3D-R EX, a causality-based post-hoc explainability tool for 3D models, generating responsibility maps to highlight regions crucial for model decisions in medical imaging.
papers.conclusion: 3D-R EX offers a causality-based approach for explaining 3D models in medical imaging, with potential to improve trust and provide biological insights.
papers.key_findings:
3D-R EX successfully generates causal responsibility maps for 3D MRI data.
Using 0-value occlusion produces explanations aligned with lesion locations, while healthy MRI occlusion highlights different regions.
The method reduces computational complexity by splitting on two axes instead of three.
Explanations can be visualized in 2D slices and 3D renderings for comprehensive insight.
The tool is model-agnostic and does not require access to internal model weights.
papers.limitation:
Computational complexity due to large search space in 3D data
Lack of comprehensive evaluation on a large-scale dataset
future_direction: Extend 3D-R EX to different medical imaging modalities.
Investigate explanations with different occlusion values on larger models.
Integrate with multi-modal data including genomic and patient history.
papers.abstract: Explainability remains a significant problem for AI models in medical imaging, making it challenging for clinicians to trust AI-driven predictions. We introduce 3D ReX, the first causality-based post-hoc explainability tool for 3D models. 3D ReX uses the theory of actual causality to generate responsibility maps which highlight the regions most crucial to the model's decision. We test 3D ReX on a stroke detection model, providing insight into the spatial distribution of features relevant to stroke.

papers.title: A Framework for Interpretability in Machine Learning for Medical Imaging
papers.research_question: Why does the need for interpretability in machine learning for medical imaging (MLMI) arise? What are the underlying elements of interpretability in MLMI? How can we formalize these into a framework for interpretability in MLMI?
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes interpretability needs in medical imaging by identifying five core elements (localization, visual recognizability, physical attribution, model transparency, and actionability) and proposes a framework to guide practitioners in designing and evaluating interpretable MLMI methods.
papers.conclusion: The paper formalizes interpretability in medical imaging through a framework based on five core elements, aiming to guide method design, improve real-world usage, and inspire future research.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability in MLMI can be decomposed into five core elements: localization, visual recognizability, physical attribution, model transparency, and actionability.
A framework is proposed that connects real-world medical imaging tasks and objectives to these interpretability elements and existing methods.
The framework provides a step-by-step guide for practitioners to approach interpretability in MLMI, from defining the problem to selecting appropriate methods.
Interpretability methods should be chosen based on the specific real-world objectives (e.g., troubleshooting, fairness, trust) and the intended users (e.g., clinicians, researchers).
Pixel-level tasks (e.g., segmentation, registration) have inherent interpretability due to their localizable and visually recognizable outputs.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability might induce or contribute to human biases such as automation bias (too much trust) or algorithmic aversion (too much distrust).
Low-dimensional projections of high-dimensional internal representations (e.g., 2D heatmaps) can give users a false sense of understanding.
Interpretability is not always necessary and can potentially hinder model performance or introduce new biases.
future_direction: Developing interpretability methods that address multiple elements simultaneously.
Creating benchmarks and evaluation metrics specifically for interpretability methods in MLMI.
Studying the impact of interpretability on clinical decision-making and outcomes.
Exploring the role of interpretability in the regulatory approval of MLMI systems.
papers.abstract: Interpretability for machine learning models in medical imaging (MLMI) is an important direction of research. However, there is a general sense of murkiness in what interpretability means. Why does the need for interpretability in MLMI arise? What goals does one actually seek to address when interpretability is needed? To answer these questions, we identify a need to formalize the goals and elements of interpretability in MLMI. By reasoning about real-world tasks and goals common in both medical image analysis and its intersection with machine learning, we identify five core elements of interpretability: localization, visual recognizability, physical attribution, model transparency, and actionability. From this, we arrive at a framework for interpretability in MLMI, which serves as a step-by-step guide to approaching interpretability in this context. Overall, this paper formalizes interpretability needs in the context of medical imaging, and our applied perspective clarifies concrete MLMI-specific goals and considerations in order to guide method design and improve real-world usage. Our goal is to provide practical and didactic information for model designers and practitioners, inspire developers of models in the medical imaging field to reason more deeply about what interpretability is achieving, and suggest future directions of interpretability research.

papers.title: Inducing Causal Structure for Interpretable Neural Networks Applied to Glucose Prediction for T1DM Patients
papers.research_question: Can Interchange Intervention Training (IIT) be effectively applied to real-world healthcare problems, specifically for blood glucose prediction in Type 1 Diabetes patients, to improve predictive performance and align models with expert causal knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Interchange Intervention Training (IIT) can be successfully applied to a real-world healthcare problem (glucose prediction for T1DM), improving predictive performance and aligning the neural network with a causal model derived from expert knowledge.
papers.conclusion: IIT shows promise for enhancing predictive models in healthcare by integrating causal expert knowledge, leading to improved performance and interpretability, though its effectiveness depends on the fidelity of the causal model and the neural network architecture.
papers.key_findings:
IIT-trained MLP tree models outperform standard training in terms of RMSE, MAE, MSE, and EGA across different prediction horizons when using an amended version of the simglucose causal model.
The counterfactual loss (L_INT) decreases during training, indicating the model is learning the causal structure, and its breakdown can identify which causal mechanisms are more or less effectively captured.
The model shows higher L_INT for modules aligned with complex, time-dependent physiological mechanisms (e.g., glucose mass in plasma and tissues), indicating abstraction difficulty.
When using the regular (non-amended) simglucose causal model, IIT does not consistently outperform standard training across all model architectures and prediction horizons.
The IIT-trained MLP tree model achieves results comparable to state-of-the-art glucose prediction models, despite using a simpler architecture and a more challenging test set, highlighting a trade-off between performance and causal interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The causal model used is the S2008 version of the simglucose simulator, which is outdated and does not faithfully reflect all real clinical scenarios.
The study is limited to simple MLP architectures and a simplified (amended) causal model that removes cyclical relationships, potentially affecting the accuracy of the captured glucose-insulin dynamics.
future_direction: Update the causal model to a more recent version (e.g., S2017) if it becomes publicly available.
Investigate more complex MLP architectures that do not collapse the time dimension, modeling each time-indexed variable distinctly.
Explore other neural network architectures and alignment configurations.
papers.abstract: Causal abstraction techniques such as Interchange Intervention Training (IIT) have been proposed to infuse neural network with expert knowledge encoded in causal models, but their application to real-world problems remains limited. This article explores the application of IIT in predicting blood glucose levels in Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) patients. The study utilizes an acyclic version of the simglucose simulator approved by the FDA to train a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) model, employing IIT to impose causal relationships. Results show that the model trained with IIT effectively abstracted the causal structure and outperformed the standard one in terms of predictive performance across different prediction horizons (PHs) post-meal. Furthermore, the breakdown of the counterfactual loss can be leveraged to explain which part of the causal mechanism are more or less effectively captured by the model. These preliminary results suggest the potential of IIT in enhancing predictive models in healthcare by effectively complying with expert knowledge.

papers.title: Causal Interpretation of Self-Attention in Pre-Trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How can self-attention in pre-trained Transformers be interpreted as estimating a structural equation model, and how can this be used for zero-shot causal discovery and explanation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a causal interpretation of self-attention in Transformers, showing that self-attention estimates a structural equation model. This enables zero-shot causal discovery and causal explanation for model predictions using pre-trained Transformers.
papers.conclusion: The paper establishes a relation between self-attention and structural causal models, enabling zero-shot causal discovery (ABCD) and causal explanation (CLEANN) using pre-trained Transformers, with potential applications in causal reasoning and model interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Self-attention can be interpreted as estimating a linear structural equation model for a given input sequence.
The attention matrix can be used to compute partial correlations for conditional independence tests, enabling causal discovery without additional training (zero-shot).
The ABCD method can learn causal graphs (equivalence classes) for individual input sequences, even in the presence of latent confounders.
The CLEANN method provides minimal causal explanations for model predictions by identifying sets of input symbols that are causally responsible for the output.
Empirical evaluation on sentiment classification and recommendation tasks shows CLEANN produces smaller explanation sets and more aligned replacement recommendations compared to attention-based baselines.
papers.limitation: ABCD is susceptible to errors from Transformer prediction inaccuracies and errors from the constraint-based causal discovery algorithm.
future_direction: Causal reasoning in applications with large-scale pre-trained models or unlabeled data.
Architectural modifications to the Transformer to alleviate causal inference.
papers.abstract: We propose a causal interpretation of self-attention in the Transformer neural network architecture. We interpret self-attention as a mechanism that estimates a structural equation model for a given input sequence of symbols (tokens). The structural equation model can be interpreted, in turn, as a causal structure over the input symbols under the specific context of the input sequence. Importantly, this interpretation remains valid in the presence of latent confounders. Following this interpretation, we estimate conditional independence relations between input symbols by calculating partial correlations between their corresponding representations in the deepest attention layer. This enables learning the causal structure over an input sequence using existing constraint-based algorithms. In this sense, existing pre-trained Transformers can be utilized for zero-shot causal-discovery. We demonstrate this method by providing causal explanations for the outcomes of Transformers in two tasks: sentiment classification (NLP) and recommendation.

papers.title: CausaLM: Causal Model Explanation Through Counterfactual Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we estimate the true causal effect of a high-level concept (e.g., adjectives, topics, gender, race) on the predictions of a text classifier, distinguishing between correlation and causation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CausaLM, a framework that uses adversarial fine-tuning of language representation models (like BERT) to learn counterfactual representations, enabling estimation of the causal effect of a concept on a classifier's predictions without generating counterfactual text.
papers.conclusion: Causal model explanation is crucial for understanding and mitigating biases in NLP models, and CausaLM provides an effective framework for estimating causal effects of concepts on classifier predictions using counterfactual language representations.
papers.key_findings:
CausaLM can effectively estimate the causal effect of concepts (adjectives, topics, gender, race) on model predictions, outperforming correlation-based baselines.
The method can create language representations that are unaffected by a specific concept, which can be used to mitigate unwanted bias ingrained in the data.
The framework provides a way to answer causal questions about model behavior without requiring manually created counterfactual examples, relying only on observational data.
papers.limitation:
The method requires a causal graph and the choice of control concepts, which depends on the model of the world and may not capture all confounders.
Evaluation is conducted on specific, constructed concepts and datasets; real-world applications may involve more complex and numerous concepts.
future_direction: Extending the framework to more complex causal graphs and a wider range of concepts.
Applying the method to other modalities beyond text.
Developing richer, more complex datasets for evaluating causal estimators in more realistic settings.
papers.abstract: Abstract Understanding predictions made by deep neural networks is notoriously difficult, but also crucial to their dissemination. As all machine learning–based methods, they are as good as their training data, and can also capture unwanted biases. While there are tools that can help understand whether such biases exist, they do not distinguish between correlation and causation, and might be ill-suited for text-based models and for reasoning about high level language concepts. A key problem of estimating the causal effect of a concept of interest on a given model is that this estimation requires the generation of counterfactual examples, which is challenging with existing generation technology. To bridge that gap, we propose CausaLM, a framework for producing causal model explanations using counterfactual language representation models. Our approach is based on fine-tuning of deep contextualized embedding models with auxiliary adversarial tasks derived from the causal graph of the problem. Concretely, we show that by carefully choosing auxiliary adversarial pre-training tasks, language representation models such as BERT can effectively learn a counterfactual representation for a given concept of interest, and be used to estimate its true causal effect on model performance. A byproduct of our method is a language representation model that is unaffected by the tested concept, which can be useful in mitigating unwanted bias ingrained in the data.

papers.title: Causal Abstraction Inference under Lossy Representations
papers.research_question: How can causal abstraction inference be performed when the abstract invariance condition (AIC) is violated, i.e., when using lossy abstraction functions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces projected abstractions, a new formalism that generalizes existing causal abstraction definitions to accommodate lossy representations (AIC violations), and provides methods for constructing high-level models and performing causal inference from low-level data.
papers.conclusion: Projected abstractions provide a consistent formalism for causal abstraction inference even under AIC violations, enabling tractable causal inference and high-quality causal sampling in the presence of extreme dimensionality reduction.
papers.key_findings:
Projected abstractions generalize existing causal abstraction definitions to settings where the Abstract Invariance Condition (AIC) does not hold.
An algorithm is provided to construct a high-level projected abstraction from a low-level model, ensuring consistency for all causal queries.
A new graphical criterion (projected C-DAG) is proven for identifying and estimating high-level causal queries from limited low-level data.
The effectiveness of projected abstraction models is demonstrated experimentally in high-dimensional image settings.
papers.limitation: The projected abstraction framework introduces additional dependencies between high-level variables (via the projected C-DAG), which may result in non-identifiability of certain causal queries or present additional computational challenges.
future_direction: Leveraging the projected generalizations to aid in mechanistic interpretability tasks.
Analyzing error bounds of the approach given imperfect optimization.
Exploring how to best optimize models for higher-dimensional problems.
papers.abstract: The study of causal abstractions bridges two integral components of human intelligence: the ability to determine cause and effect, and the ability to interpret complex patterns into abstract concepts. Formally, causal abstraction frameworks define connections between complicated low-level causal models and simple high-level ones. One major limitation of most existing definitions is that they are not well-defined when considering lossy abstraction functions in which multiple low-level interventions can have different effects while mapping to the same high-level intervention (an assumption called the abstract invariance condition). In this paper, we introduce a new type of abstractions called projected abstractions that generalize existing definitions to accommodate lossy representations. We show how to construct a projected abstraction from the low-level model and how it translates equivalent observational, interventional, and counterfactual causal queries from low to high-level. Given that the true model is rarely available in practice we prove a new graphical criteria for identifying and estimating high-level causal queries from limited low-level data. Finally, we experimentally show the effectiveness of projected abstraction models in high-dimensional image settings.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for Transformer-based Time Series Classification
papers.research_question: What novel insights can Mechanistic Interpretability methods, specifically, activation patching, attention saliency, and sparse autoencoders, yield when adapted to Time Series Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts activation patching, attention saliency, and sparse autoencoders to Time Series Transformers, enabling causal probing at the layer, head, and timestep levels, and constructs directed causal graphs to map information flow.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Mechanistic Interpretability techniques can be meaningfully adapted to Time Series Transformers, revealing causal circuits and latent features that enhance understanding of model internals for time series classification.
papers.key_findings:
Patching early layers (Layer 0) yields the largest increase in true-class probability, indicating strong causal signal at the model's entry point.
Individual attention heads (e.g., Head 6 in Layer 0) have significant causal influence, with patching raising true-class confidence substantially.
Specific timesteps are critical for correct classification, and their effects are non-additive due to nonlinear interactions within the model.
Attention saliency provides observational insights into which timesteps heads attend to, but does not imply causation.
Sparse autoencoders can uncover class-specific temporal motifs, suggesting disentangled latent features in the model's internal representations.
papers.limitation:
MI methods remain labor-intensive, requiring substantial domain expertise for pair selection, granularity choices, and interpretation.
The patching experiments focus solely on attention heads, leaving other components like MLP blocks, residual streams, and embeddings unexplored.
Time series features lack clear semantics compared to NLP tokens, making interpretation of causal motifs inherently more challenging.
Interventions can interfere or synergize non-additively due to the transformer's complex interplay of components, complicating isolation of independent causal factors.
future_direction: Expanding patching to include MLP activations, residual streams, and embeddings for a more comprehensive view.
Scaling analysis to multiple clean–corrupt pairs across classes and datasets to test generality of discovered circuits.
Integrating optimization-driven search to automatically identify minimal, non-redundant patch sets for causal graph construction.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based models have become state-of-the-art tools in various machine learning tasks, including time series classification, yet their complexity makes understanding their internal decision-making challenging. Existing explainability methods often focus on input-output attributions, leaving the internal mechanisms largely opaque. This paper addresses this gap by adapting various Mechanistic Interpretability techniques; activation patching, attention saliency, and sparse autoencoders, from NLP to transformer architectures designed explicitly for time series classification. We systematically probe the internal causal roles of individual attention heads and timesteps, revealing causal structures within these models. Through experimentation on a benchmark time series dataset, we construct causal graphs illustrating how information propagates internally, highlighting key attention heads and temporal positions driving correct classifications. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of sparse autoencoders for uncovering interpretable latent features. Our findings provide both methodological contributions to transformer interpretability and novel insights into the functional mechanics underlying transformer performance in time series classification tasks.

papers.title: Insights into a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model with sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders be applied to interpret the internal representations of a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model (MAIRA-2) and steer its generations?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology MLLM MAIRA-2, identifying a subset of interpretable clinical concepts within its representations and demonstrating the feasibility and challenges of steering model generations using these features.
papers.conclusion: The study provides initial insights into the internal concepts of MAIRA-2 using SAEs, marking a step toward mechanistic interpretability, while highlighting practical and methodological challenges in automated interpretability and steering.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset (1.8%) of SAE features are highly interpretable (F1 > 0.75), corresponding to clinically relevant concepts like medical devices, pathologies, and textual features.
Nearly half (46%) of SAE features are not interpretable by the automated pipeline (F1 < 0.5).
Steering model generations using SAE features is possible but produces more off-target changes than on-target changes, with success highly dependent on the specific feature.
There is a strong correlation between the on-target effects of positive and negative steering coefficients.
The trained SAEs and their automated interpretations are publicly released to foster further research.
papers.limitation:
Many SAE features (46%) are not interpretable by the automated pipeline.
Steering often produces more off-target changes than on-target changes.
The study reveals practical and methodological challenges across the SAE training, automated concept discovery, and steering pipeline.
papers.abstract: Interpretability can improve the safety, transparency and trust of AI models, which is especially important in healthcare applications where decisions often carry significant consequences. Mechanistic interpretability, particularly through the use of sparse autoencoders (SAEs), offers a promising approach for uncovering human-interpretable features within large transformer-based models. In this study, we apply Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology-specialised multimodal large language model, MAIRA-2, to interpret its internal representations. Using large-scale automated interpretability of the SAE features, we identify a range of clinically relevant concepts - including medical devices (e.g., line and tube placements, pacemaker presence), pathologies such as pleural effusion and cardiomegaly, longitudinal changes and textual features. We further examine the influence of these features on model behaviour through steering, demonstrating directional control over generations with mixed success. Our results reveal practical and methodological challenges, yet they offer initial insights into the internal concepts learned by MAIRA-2 - marking a step toward deeper mechanistic understanding and interpretability of a radiology-adapted multimodal large language model, and paving the way for improved model transparency. We release the trained SAEs and interpretations: https://huggingface.co/microsoft/maira-2-sae.

papers.title: Analysing Representations of Memory Impairment in a Clinical Notes Classification Model
papers.research_question: How can we interpret a recurrent neural network model for clinical document classification by analyzing sentence importance and clustering sentence embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a perturbative method for calculating sentence importance and uses cluster analysis to interpret an LSTM model for clinical document classification, revealing how the model uses sentence embeddings to make predictions.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of using pre-trained sentence embeddings and LSTMs for clinical document classification and shows how interpretability methods can reveal the model's decision-making process and class imbalances.
papers.key_findings:
The LSTM model using pre-trained sentence embeddings (InferSent) achieved the best performance in classifying clinical documents into dementia, MCI, and non-impaired categories.
A perturbative sentence importance measure identified sentences that are most informative or misleading for the model's predictions, providing insights into the model's decision process.
Cluster analysis of sentence embeddings revealed clusters that are significantly correlated with importance scores for specific diagnosis classes, helping to interpret the model's representations.
The model performed poorly on the dementia class, and no sentence clusters were significantly correlated with this class, indicating a limitation in the model's ability to capture features for dementia.
The average sentence importance tends to increase with sentence position in the document, possibly due to recency bias or the semi-structured nature of the clinical notes.
papers.limitation:
The dataset is small, which may limit the model's ability to capture long-distance dependencies and lead to recency bias.
The model performs poorly on the dementia class, with no sentence clusters significantly correlated with this class.
future_direction: Gather more clinical documents to continue analysis and improve model performance.
Apply state-of-the-art contextualized embeddings such as ELMO and BERT to the task.
Examine how models trained on one clinician's writing style apply to others, analyzing inter- and intra-clinician performance.
papers.abstract: Despite recent advances in the application of deep neural networks to various kinds of medical data, extracting information from unstructured textual sources remains a challenging task. The challenges of training and interpreting document classification models are amplified when dealing with small and highly technical datasets, as are common in the clinical domain. Using a dataset of de-identified clinical letters gathered at a memory clinic, we construct several recurrent neural network models for letter classification, and evaluate them on their ability to build meaningful representations of the documents and predict patients' diagnoses. Additionally, we probe sentence embedding models in order to build a humaninterpretable representation of the neural network's features, using a simple and intuitive technique based on perturbative approaches to sentence importance. In addition to showing which sentences in a document are most informative about the patient's condition, this method reveals the types of sentences that lead the model to make incorrect diagnoses. Furthermore, we identify clusters of sentences in the embedding space that correlate strongly with importance scores for each clinical diagnosis class.

papers.title: Towards Interpretable Deep Generative Models via Causal Representation Learning
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces causal representation learning (CRL) from a statistical perspective, highlighting its connections to classical latent variable models and causal graphical models, and discusses identifiability results and open problems.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that causal representation learning is a promising approach for building interpretable deep generative models, but many open problems remain, including scalability, handling of confounders, and integration with foundation models.
future_direction: Scalability of CRL methods to large-scale models and data.
Handling of confounders and unobserved confounding.
Integration of CRL with foundation models like large language models.
papers.abstract: Recent developments in generative artificial intelligence (AI) rely on machine learning techniques such as deep learning and generative modeling to achieve state-of-the-art performance across wide-ranging domains. These methods' surprising performance is due in part to their ability to learn implicit "representations" of complex, multi-modal data. Unfortunately, deep neural networks are notoriously black boxes that obscure these representations, making them difficult to interpret or analyze. To resolve these difficulties, one approach is to build new interpretable neural network models from the ground up. This is the goal of the emerging field of causal representation learning (CRL) that uses causality as a vector for building flexible, interpretable, and transferable generative AI. CRL can be seen as a synthesis of three intrinsically statistical ideas: (i) latent variable models such as factor analysis; (ii) causal graphical models with latent variables; and (iii) nonparametric statistics and deep learning. This paper introduces CRL from a statistical perspective, focusing on connections to classical models as well as statistical and causal identifiability results. We also highlights key application areas, implementation strategies, and open statistical questions.

papers.title: Enhancing the Interpretability of Deep Models in Heathcare Through Attention: Application to Glucose Forecasting for Diabetic People
papers.research_question: How can the RETAIN model be adapted for regression tasks in healthcare, specifically for glucose forecasting, and does it provide a good balance between accuracy and interpretability compared to other models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts the RETAIN architecture for regression tasks in healthcare (glucose forecasting) and proposes a new interpretability metric (absolute normalized contribution) to statistically analyze variable importance, showing RETAIN offers a good compromise between accuracy and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The RETAIN model is promising for glucose forecasting and healthcare tasks due to its interpretability, and the absolute normalized contribution metric enhances the analysis of variable importance.
papers.key_findings:
The RETAIN model is more accurate than decision-tree-based models (DT, RF, GBM) and slightly less accurate than deep models (LSTM, FCN) but with comparable or better clinical acceptability.
Interpretability analysis reveals that input variables older than one hour are not used by the RETAIN model for 30-minute ahead glucose predictions.
Upon events like carbohydrate intake or insulin infusion, the model strongly considers the patient's state just before the event, and the event's contribution diminishes after about 30 minutes.
The proposed absolute normalized contribution metric enables statistical analysis of variable importance across predictions.
The RETAIN model, due to its interpretability, is promising for biomedical applications like glucose forecasting.
papers.limitation: The RETAIN model may not be able to efficiently use long histories (beyond one hour) due to its quasi-linear structure, which might limit its accuracy compared to more complex models like LSTM and FCN.
future_direction: Incorporating additional data sources such as physical activity or sleep data to improve predictions.
Developing more complex hidden representations (e.g., using multi-layer perceptrons) while maintaining interpretability.
papers.abstract: The adoption of deep learning in healthcare is hindered by their "black box" nature. In this paper, we explore the RETAIN architecture for the task of glusose forecasting for diabetic people. By using a two-level attention mechanism, the recurrent-neural-network-based RETAIN model is interpretable. We evaluate the RETAIN model on the type-2 IDIAB and the type-1 OhioT1DM datasets by comparing its statistical and clinical performances against two deep models and three models based on decision trees. We show that the RETAIN model offers a very good compromise between accuracy and interpretability, being almost as accurate as the LSTM and FCN models while remaining interpretable. We show the usefulness of its interpretable nature by analyzing the contribution of each variable to the final prediction. It revealed that signal values older than one hour are not used by the RETAIN model for the 30-minutes ahead of time prediction of glucose. Also, we show how the RETAIN model changes its behavior upon the arrival of an event such as carbohydrate intakes or insulin infusions. In particular, it showed that the patient's state before the event is particularily important for the prediction. Overall the RETAIN model, thanks to its interpretability, seems to be a very promissing model for regression or classification tasks in healthcare.

papers.title: SHAMSUL: Systematic Holistic Analysis to investigate Medical Significance Utilizing Local interpretability methods in deep learning for chest radiography pathology prediction
papers.research_question: How do four local interpretability methods (LIME, SHAP, Grad-CAM, LRP) perform in quantitative and qualitative evaluation for medical significance in chest radiography pathology prediction?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces SHAMSUL, a systematic holistic analysis approach to evaluate four interpretability methods (LIME, SHAP, Grad-CAM, LRP) for medical significance in chest radiography. It finds that Grad-CAM performs best quantitatively, while LIME heatmap segmentation shows the highest medical significance qualitatively.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM performs best quantitatively, LIME performs best qualitatively, and there is a need for continued research and multimodal approaches for better interpretability in medical diagnostics.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM demonstrates the most favorable performance in quantitative evaluation (mean IoU scores).
LIME heatmap score segmentation visualization exhibits the highest level of medical significance in qualitative analysis.
SHAP segmentations are broad and lack precision, limiting their interpretive value.
LRP segmentations cover the entire image, are noisy, and lack class discriminability, offering limited medical significance.
The study highlights the challenges and limitations of current interpretability methods in medical image analysis.
papers.limitation: The interpretability methods have inherent limitations, and the evaluation is challenging due to the lack of ground truth and the subjective nature of qualitative analysis.
future_direction: Adopting a multimodality-based approach, integrating multiple information sources and diverse modalities.
Exploring different model architectures and quantitative assessment methods for more comprehensive comparison.
Developing a robust framework that incorporates impactful qualitative analysis augmented by the active guidance of medical experts.
papers.abstract: The interpretability of deep neural networks has become a subject of great interest within the medical and healthcare domain. This attention stems from concerns regarding transparency, legal and ethical considerations, and the medical significance of predictions generated by these deep neural networks in clinical decision support systems. To address this matter, our study delves into the application of four well-established interpretability methods: Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), and Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP). Leveraging the approach of transfer learning with a multi-label-multi-class chest radiography dataset, we aim to interpret predictions pertaining to specific pathology classes. Our analysis encompasses both single-label and multi-label predictions, providing a comprehensive and unbiased assessment through quantitative and qualitative investigations, which are compared against human expert annotation. Notably, Grad-CAM demonstrates the most favorable performance in quantitative evaluation, while the LIME heatmap score segmentation visualization exhibits the highest level of medical significance. Our research underscores both the outcomes and the challenges faced in the holistic approach adopted for assessing these interpretability methods and suggests that a multimodal-based approach, incorporating diverse sources of information beyond chest radiography images, could offer additional insights for enhancing interpretability in the medical domain.

papers.title: Diagnosing Transformers: Illuminating Feature Spaces for Clinical Decision-Making
papers.research_question: How does pre-training data affect fine-tuned transformer features for clinical note classification, and how can we interpret fine-tuned feature spaces to build trust in medical applications?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SUFO, a framework for interpreting fine-tuned transformer feature spaces, and finds that mixed-domain models are more robust to class imbalance, in-domain pre-training speeds up feature disambiguation, and fine-tuning leads to sparsified feature spaces that facilitate outlier analysis.
papers.conclusion: SUFO provides a systematic pipeline for interpreting fine-tuned transformer feature spaces, enhancing trust and safety in medical applications, and reveals the robustness of mixed-domain models, faster feature disambiguation with in-domain pre-training, and improved outlier detection.
papers.key_findings:
PubMedBERT (domain-specific) contains valuable information but can overfit to minority classes in imbalanced datasets, while mixed-domain models (BioBERT, Clinical BioBERT) are more resistant to overfitting.
In-domain pre-training accelerates feature disambiguation during fine-tuning.
Feature spaces undergo significant sparsification during fine-tuning, allowing for outlier analysis.
Clinical BioBERT, which includes clinical notes in pre-training, requires the fewest changes during fine-tuning and disambiguates features fastest.
Different pre-trained models exhibit qualitative differences in outlier modes, with Clinical BioBERT and PubMedBERT better at identifying missing medical information.
papers.limitation: Results are limited in scale and to clinical classification tasks; generalization to broader clinical tasks and models requires further work.
future_direction: Optimally combining general-domain and domain-specific corpora for effective pre-training
Generalizing findings to a broader set of clinical tasks and models
papers.abstract: Pre-trained transformers are often fine-tuned to aid clinical decision-making using limited clinical notes. Model interpretability is crucial, especially in high-stakes domains like medicine, to establish trust and ensure safety, which requires human engagement. We introduce SUFO, a systematic framework that enhances interpretability of fine-tuned transformer feature spaces. SUFO utilizes a range of analytic and visualization techniques, including Supervised probing, Unsupervised similarity analysis, Feature dynamics, and Outlier analysis to address key questions about model trust and interpretability. We conduct a case study investigating the impact of pre-training data where we focus on real-world pathology classification tasks, and validate our findings on MedNLI. We evaluate five 110M-sized pre-trained transformer models, categorized into general-domain (BERT, TNLR), mixed-domain (BioBERT, Clinical BioBERT), and domain-specific (PubMedBERT) groups. Our SUFO analyses reveal that: (1) while PubMedBERT, the domain-specific model, contains valuable information for fine-tuning, it can overfit to minority classes when class imbalances exist. In contrast, mixed-domain models exhibit greater resistance to overfitting, suggesting potential improvements in domain-specific model robustness; (2) in-domain pre-training accelerates feature disambiguation during fine-tuning; and (3) feature spaces undergo significant sparsification during this process, enabling clinicians to identify common outlier modes among fine-tuned models as demonstrated in this paper. These findings showcase the utility of SUFO in enhancing trust and safety when using transformers in medicine, and we believe SUFO can aid practitioners in evaluating fine-tuned language models for other applications in medicine and in more critical domains.

papers.title: Semantic match: Debugging feature attribution methods in XAI for healthcare
papers.research_question: When can feature attribution methods be reliably used in XAI for healthcare? The paper argues the problem of semantic mismatch is specific to unstructured data (like images) and that for structured data (like tabular EHR), low-level features have clear semantics, enabling reliable feature attribution.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that feature attribution methods can be reliable for structured data (e.g., EHR) where low-level features have clear semantics, and introduces the concept of semantic match and a conceptual procedure to test it for high-level features.
papers.conclusion: Feature attribution methods can be useful for structured data in healthcare, but for unstructured data they require careful validation of semantic match. Explanations should be built in the clinician's language.
papers.key_findings:
The core problem with feature attribution methods is a lack of semantic match between explanations and human understanding.
For structured data like Electronic Health Records (EHRs), low-level features have inherent, clear semantics, so feature attribution can be meaningful and useful.
For unstructured data like images, semantic match is not guaranteed and can lead to misleading explanations.
A conceptual procedure is sketched to test whether semantic match is achieved for high-level features.
Even with semantic match, explanations can fail if they are not faithful to the model's behavior.
papers.limitation:
Even in the presence of semantic match, explanations can still fail to deliver if they are not faithful to the model.
Not all data types neatly fall into structured or unstructured categories (e.g., text, time series), requiring cautious application of explanatory methods.
Semantic match is user-dependent; users with relevant background may correctly interpret an explanation, but others may not.
future_direction: Operationalizing the procedure to test semantic match.
Generating explanations that comply with human categories by design, possibly using hybrid models.
Combining visual explanation with image segmentation to fix the semantics of entities used in the explanation.
Using ontologies to regulate the relationship between entities in explanations.
papers.abstract: The recent spike in certified Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools for healthcare has renewed the debate around adoption of this technology. One thread of such debate concerns Explainable AI (XAI) and its promise to render AI devices more transparent and trustworthy. A few voices active in the medical AI space have expressed concerns on the reliability of Explainable AI techniques and especially feature attribution methods, questioning their use and inclusion in guidelines and standards. Despite valid concerns, we argue that existing criticism on the viability of post-hoc local explainability methods throws away the baby with the bathwater by generalizing a problem that is specific to image data. We begin by characterizing the problem as a lack of semantic match between explanations and human understanding. To understand when feature importance can be used reliably, we introduce a distinction between feature importance of low- and high-level features. We argue that for data types where low-level features come endowed with a clear semantics, such as tabular data like Electronic Health Records (EHRs), semantic match can be obtained, and thus feature attribution methods can still be employed in a meaningful and useful way. Finally, we sketch a procedure to test whether semantic match has been achieved.

papers.title: Addressing divergent representations from causal interventions on neural networks
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether causal interventions on neural networks create out-of-distribution (divergent) representations and whether this affects the faithfulness of the resulting explanations to the target model in its natural state.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that causal interventions often produce representations that diverge from the model's natural distribution, analyzes when such divergence is harmless or pernicious, and introduces a modified CL loss to mitigate pernicious divergence.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that divergent representations are a common issue in causal interventions, but by understanding and mitigating them (e.g., with the CL loss), we can move towards more reliable interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
Causal interventions (e.g., activation patching, DAS) often produce representations that diverge from the model's natural distribution.
Divergence can be harmless if it occurs in the behavioral null-space of the network layers.
Divergence can be pernicious if it activates hidden computational pathways or causes dormant behavioral changes.
The Counterfactual Latent (CL) loss can be used to reduce representational divergence in interventions while preserving behavioral accuracy.
A modified CL loss that targets causal subspaces can improve out-of-distribution intervention performance in synthetic tasks.
papers.limitation:
The work does not provide a principled, reliable method for classifying harmful divergence.
The modified CL loss is confined to a narrow set of simplistic settings and is not specific to pernicious divergence.
future_direction: Exploring ways to classify and mitigate pernicious divergence through self-supervised means
papers.abstract: A common approach to mechanistic interpretability is to causally manipulate model representations via targeted interventions in order to understand what those representations encode. Here we ask whether such interventions create out-of-distribution (divergent) representations, and whether this raises concerns about how faithful their resulting explanations are to the target model in its natural state. First, we demonstrate theoretically and empirically that common causal intervention techniques often do shift internal representations away from the natural distribution of the target model. Then, we provide a theoretical analysis of two cases of such divergences: "harmless" divergences that occur in the behavioral null-space of the layer(s) of interest, and "pernicious" divergences that activate hidden network pathways and cause dormant behavioral changes. Finally, in an effort to mitigate the pernicious cases, we apply and modify the Counterfactual Latent (CL) loss from Grant (2025) allowing representations from causal interventions to remain closer to the natural distribution, reducing the likelihood of harmful divergences while preserving the interpretive power of the interventions. Together, these results highlight a path towards more reliable interpretability methods.

papers.title: An Investigation of Interpretability Techniques for Deep Learning in Predictive Process Analytics
papers.research_question: Do patients with specific types of cancer have a targeted set of medical activities associated with them? What explainability mechanisms are appropriate for understanding predictions in this context?
papers.core_contribution: This paper applies interpretability techniques (autoencoders and LIME) to deep learning and random forest models on medical event logs, providing insights into cancer prediction and model decisions.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques like autoencoders and LIME can provide meaningful insights into model predictions for medical event logs, aiding in understanding and trust.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM neural networks achieved the best accuracy (0.552) for cancer prediction from medical event logs.
Autoencoders applied to hidden layers of LSTM networks revealed non-linear clusters corresponding to cancer types, helping identify misclassifications.
LIME provided local explanations for random forest predictions, highlighting features like age and specific activities as important for individual predictions.
Both autoencoders and LIME offered complementary interpretability insights: autoencoders via non-linear cluster representations and LIME via local feature impact.
papers.limitation:
The dataset is small (1142 patients) and models show overfitting.
Non-linear projections in autoencoders can distort distances, leading to misclassifications.
papers.abstract: This paper explores interpretability techniques for two of the most successful learning algorithms in medical decision-making literature: deep neural networks and random forests. We applied these algorithms in a real-world medical dataset containing information about patients with cancer, where we learn models that try to predict the type of cancer of the patient, given their set of medical activity records. We explored different algorithms based on neural network architectures using long short term deep neural networks, and random forests. Since there is a growing need to provide decision-makers understandings about the logic of predictions of black boxes, we also explored different techniques that provide interpretations for these classifiers. In one of the techniques, we intercepted some hidden layers of these neural networks and used autoencoders in order to learn what is the representation of the input in the hidden layers. In another, we investigated an interpretable model locally around the random forest's prediction. Results show learning an interpretable model locally around the model's prediction leads to a higher understanding of why the algorithm is making some decision. Use of local and linear model helps identify the features used in prediction of a specific instance or data point. We see certain distinct features used for predictions that provide useful insights about the type of cancer, along with features that do not generalize well. In addition, the structured deep learning approach using autoencoders provided meaningful prediction insights, which resulted in the identification of nonlinear clusters correspondent to the patients' different types of cancer.

papers.title: Priors in Time: Missing Inductive Biases for Language Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the temporal prior assumptions of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and how do they conflict with the actual temporal structure in language model activations? How can we design an interpretability method that incorporates appropriate temporal inductive biases?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Temporal Feature Analysis, a new interpretability protocol that decomposes language model activations into predictable (contextual) and novel (residual) components, capturing temporal structure that standard Sparse Autoencoders miss due to inappropriate inductive biases.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability tools must incorporate inductive biases that match the data's structure, and Temporal Feature Analysis offers a promising direction for capturing temporal dynamics in language model representations.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs impose an i.i.d. prior over time, assuming concepts are independent across time, which conflicts with the non-stationary temporal structure (e.g., increasing intrinsic dimensionality, context correlations) observed in language model activations.
Temporal Feature Analysis successfully decomposes activations into predictable (slow-moving, contextual) and novel (fast-moving, stimulus-driven) components, aligning with the generative structure of language.
The predictive component of Temporal Feature Analysis captures smooth temporal trajectories, event boundaries, and speaker roles in dialogue, while the novel component retains monosemantic features interpretable via standard autointerp pipelines.
In experiments on garden path sentences, stories, and in-context dialogue, Temporal Feature Analysis correctly parses linguistic structure and identifies event boundaries, whereas standard SAEs show significant pitfalls.
The method demonstrates that incorporating data-informed temporal inductive biases is crucial for robust interpretability tools.
papers.limitation: The method assumes that the residual novel component is i.i.d. over time, which may not hold in general.
future_direction: Explore other inductive biases (e.g., hierarchical, compositional) for interpretability.
Apply Temporal Feature Analysis to other modalities (e.g., video, audio).
Conduct more extensive causal intervention studies to validate the interpretability of the novel codes.
papers.abstract: Recovering meaningful concepts from language model activations is a central aim of interpretability. While existing feature extraction methods aim to identify concepts that are independent directions, it is unclear if this assumption can capture the rich temporal structure of language. Specifically, via a Bayesian lens, we demonstrate that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) impose priors that assume independence of concepts across time, implying stationarity. Meanwhile, language model representations exhibit rich temporal dynamics, including systematic growth in conceptual dimensionality, context-dependent correlations, and pronounced non-stationarity, in direct conflict with the priors of SAEs. Taking inspiration from computational neuroscience, we introduce a new interpretability objective -- Temporal Feature Analysis -- which possesses a temporal inductive bias to decompose representations at a given time into two parts: a predictable component, which can be inferred from the context, and a residual component, which captures novel information unexplained by the context. Temporal Feature Analyzers correctly parse garden path sentences, identify event boundaries, and more broadly delineate abstract, slow-moving information from novel, fast-moving information, while existing SAEs show significant pitfalls in all the above tasks. Overall, our results underscore the need for inductive biases that match the data in designing robust interpretability tools.

papers.title: Do learned representations respect causal relationships?
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether learned attribute-specific representations respect the same causal relations as the underlying attributes, and to what extent.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces NCINet, a learning-based method for observational causal discovery from high-dimensional representations, and shows that learned representations can respect the causal relations between attributes, with consistency correlated to predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that learned representations can respect causal relationships under controlled scenarios, and introduces NCINet, which outperforms existing methods for causal discovery from high-dimensional representations.
papers.key_findings:
NCINet significantly outperforms existing observational causal discovery approaches on synthetic and real data.
Under controlled scenarios, learned representations can satisfy the same causal relations as the underlying attribute labels.
The causal consistency between representations and labels is positively correlated with the predictive capability of the representations.
Causal consistency degrades with overfitting of the attribute predictors.
The adversarial loss component in NCINet improves its generalization ability.
papers.abstract: Data often has many semantic attributes that are causally associated with each other. But do attribute-specific learned representations of data also respect the same causal relations? We answer this question in three steps. First, we introduce NCINet, an approach for observational causal discovery from high-dimensional data. It is trained purely on synthetically generated representations and can be applied to real representations, and is specifically designed to mitigate the domain gap between the two. Second, we apply NCINet to identify the causal relations between image representations of different pairs of attributes with known and unknown causal relations between the labels. For this purpose, we consider image representations learned for predicting attributes on the 3D Shapes, CelebA, and the CASIA-WebFace datasets, which we annotate with multiple multi-class attributes. Third, we analyze the effect on the underlying causal relation between learned representations induced by various design choices in representation learning. Our experiments indicate that (1) NCINet significantly outperforms existing observational causal discovery approaches for estimating the causal relation between pairs of random samples, both in the presence and absence of an unobserved confounder, (2) under controlled scenarios, learned representations can indeed satisfy the underlying causal relations between their respective labels, and (3) the causal relations are positively correlated with the predictive capability of the representations.

papers.title: Causal Interpretability for Machine Learning -- Problems, Methods and Evaluation
papers.research_question: How can we provide causal explanations for machine learning models, focusing on methods that answer 'why' and 'what if' questions about model decisions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of causal interpretable models, categorizing existing methods, discussing evaluation metrics, and offering guidelines for assessing causal interpretability in machine learning.
papers.conclusion: The survey summarizes the state-of-the-art in causal interpretability, emphasizing its importance for understanding and trusting machine learning models, and outlines the challenges in evaluation.
papers.key_findings:
Causal interpretability aims to answer counterfactual questions about model decisions, going beyond traditional correlation-based explanations.
Existing causal interpretability methods are categorized into model-based interpretations, counterfactual explanation generators, causal fairness, and using interpretability to verify causal relationships.
Evaluating interpretability is challenging due to the lack of consensus; the paper reviews and categorizes existing evaluation metrics for both traditional and causal methods.
Causal interpretability is essential for ensuring model reliability, fairness, and trustworthiness in critical applications.
The survey highlights the need for more work on quantitative evaluation of causal interpretability, especially for fairness algorithms.
papers.abstract: Machine learning models have had discernible achievements in a myriad of applications. However, most of these models are black-boxes, and it is obscure how the decisions are made by them. This makes the models unreliable and untrustworthy. To provide insights into the decision making processes of these models, a variety of traditional interpretable models have been proposed. Moreover, to generate more human-friendly explanations, recent work on interpretability tries to answer questions related to causality such as "Why does this model makes such decisions?" or "Was it a specific feature that caused the decision made by the model?". In this work, models that aim to answer causal questions are referred to as causal interpretable models. The existing surveys have covered concepts and methodologies of traditional interpretability. In this work, we present a comprehensive survey on causal interpretable models from the aspects of the problems and methods. In addition, this survey provides in-depth insights into the existing evaluation metrics for measuring interpretability, which can help practitioners understand for what scenarios each evaluation metric is suitable.

papers.title: Towards a Science of Causal Interpretability in Deep Learning for Software Engineering
papers.research_question: How can we achieve causal interpretability for Neural Code Models (NCMs) in software engineering to understand and explain their predictions, moving beyond associational interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces docode, a causal interpretability method for Neural Code Models that uses Structural Causal Models and causal inference to explain model predictions and mitigate confounding bias.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation provides a formal framework and guidelines for causal interpretability in DL4SE, contributing to more reliable and trustworthy AI in software engineering.
papers.key_findings:
The presence or absence of buggy code did not appear to causally influence the prediction performance of the studied NCMs, suggesting confounding bias.
The presence of Type II clones in training data impacted the effectiveness of NCMs in terms of cross-entropy.
