The iReasonData dataset, while effective, requires more data to cover additional causal interactions that humans easily infer.
future_direction: Using a better object detector and language representation model to improve context availability and event coding.
Expanding the dataset to cover more causal interactions.
papers.abstract: Causality knowledge is vital to building robust AI systems. Deep learning models often perform poorly on tasks that require causal reasoning, which is often derived using some form of commonsense knowledge not immediately available in the input but implicitly inferred by humans. Prior work has unraveled spurious observational biases that models fall prey to in the absence of causality. While language representation models preserve contextual knowledge within learned embeddings, they do not factor in causal relationships during training. By blending causal relationships with the input features to an existing model that performs visual cognition tasks (such as scene understanding, video captioning, video question-answering, etc.), better performance can be achieved owing to the insight causal relationships bring about. Recently, several models have been proposed that have tackled the task of mining causal data from either the visual or textual modality. However, there does not exist widespread research that mines causal relationships by juxtaposing the visual and language modalities. While images offer a rich and easy-to-process resource for us to mine causality knowledge from, videos are denser and consist of naturally time-ordered events. Also, textual information offers details that could be implicit in videos. We propose iReason, a framework that infers visual-semantic commonsense knowledge using both videos and natural language captions. Furthermore, iReason's architecture integrates a causal rationalization module to aid the process of interpretability, error analysis and bias detection. We demonstrate the effectiveness of iReason using a two-pronged comparative analysis with language representation learning models (BERT, GPT-2) as well as current state-of-the-art multimodal causality models.

papers.title: Linking Model Intervention to Causal Interpretation in Model Explanation
papers.research_question: Under what conditions does the model intervention effect (a common feature attribution method) have a causal interpretation, i.e., indicate whether a feature is a direct cause of the outcome?
papers.core_contribution: This work establishes theoretical conditions under which the Average Model Intervention Effect (AMIE), a common feature attribution measure based on intervention intuition, can be given a causal interpretation, linking it to direct causes in the underlying data-generating mechanism.
papers.conclusion: The model intervention effect can be linked to causal interpretation under specific conditions, and this linkage provides a means to assess the trustworthiness of a machine learning model by comparing its perceived direct causes with domain knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Without unobserved variables and when the feature set contains no descendants of the outcome Y, a non-zero AMIE for a feature Xi is equivalent to Xi being a direct cause of Y.
When there are unobserved direct causes of Y (excluding standalone ones), a non-zero AMIE indicates that the feature is either a direct cause, an activator, or a proxy of an unobserved direct cause, but false positives may occur.
False positives in the presence of unobserved variables can arise from specific graphical structures (e.g., inducing paths) and some can be detected via statistical independence tests.
Experimental validation on synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets shows high consistency between features with non-zero AMIE and true direct causes when the conditions hold.
Using AMIE for causal interpretation when there are standalone unobserved direct causes leads to low model accuracy and unreliable interpretations.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical conditions require that there are no standalone unobserved direct causes of the outcome.
The assumptions of faithfulness and computational compatibility between the data, causal mechanism, and learned model may not hold in practice.
The feature set X must not include any descendant variables of the outcome Y.
papers.abstract: Intervention intuition is often used in model explanation where the intervention effect of a feature on the outcome is quantified by the difference of a model prediction when the feature value is changed from the current value to the baseline value. Such a model intervention effect of a feature is inherently association. In this paper, we will study the conditions when an intuitive model intervention effect has a causal interpretation, i.e., when it indicates whether a feature is a direct cause of the outcome. This work links the model intervention effect to the causal interpretation of a model. Such an interpretation capability is important since it indicates whether a machine learning model is trustworthy to domain experts. The conditions also reveal the limitations of using a model intervention effect for causal interpretation in an environment with unobserved features. Experiments on semi-synthetic datasets have been conducted to validate theorems and show the potential for using the model intervention effect for model interpretation.

papers.title: The Quest for the Right Mediator: Surveying Mechanistic Interpretability Through the Lens of Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How can the field of mechanistic interpretability be unified and understood through the lens of causal mediation analysis, and what are the right causal units (mediators) for analyzing neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: This survey proposes a perspective on interpretability research grounded in causal mediation analysis, taxonomizing the field according to the types of causal mediators (units of analysis) used and the methods for searching over them, to provide a more cohesive narrative and help researchers select appropriate methods.
papers.conclusion: The survey argues that framing mechanistic interpretability through causal mediation analysis provides a unifying perspective, highlights the importance of mediator choice, and offers actionable recommendations for future work, including discovering new mediators and developing standardized evaluations.
papers.key_findings:
The choice of mediator (e.g., neurons, attention heads, non-basis-aligned directions) and search method depends on the research goal: explaining behavior, verifying a hypothesis, or localization/editing.
Unsupervised optimization-based methods over fine-grained mediators like non-basis-aligned directions are a strong starting point for explaining model behavior in the absence of prior hypotheses.
For verifying a mechanistic hypothesis, multidimensional non-basis-aligned subspaces with counterfactual-based optimization are appropriate.
For localization and editing, basis-aligned components like neurons or attention heads with gradient-based search are often sufficient and more efficient.
The field lacks standardized evaluations; future work should develop benchmarks tailored to different goals and mediator types.
future_direction: Discovery of new mediators that better satisfy criteria like sparsity, generality, selectivity, and faithfulness.
Development of standardized evaluations and benchmarks tailored to different research goals and mediator types.
Formalizing theoretical foundations for interpretability and causal abstraction in neural networks.
papers.abstract: Interpretability provides a toolset for understanding how and why neural networks behave in certain ways. However, there is little unity in the field: most studies employ ad-hoc evaluations and do not share theoretical foundations, making it difficult to measure progress and compare the pros and cons of different techniques. Furthermore, while mechanistic understanding is frequently discussed, the basic causal units underlying these mechanisms are often not explicitly defined. In this article, we propose a perspective on interpretability research grounded in causal mediation analysis. Specifically, we describe the history and current state of interpretability taxonomized according to the types of causal units (mediators) employed, as well as methods used to search over mediators. We discuss the pros and cons of each mediator, providing insights as to when particular kinds of mediators and search methods are most appropriate. We argue that this framing yields a more cohesive narrative of the field and helps researchers select appropriate methods based on their research objective. Our analysis yields actionable recommendations for future work, including the discovery of new mediators and the development of standardized evaluations tailored to these goals.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: Decoding Decision Reasoning: A Counterfactual-Powered Model for Knowledge Discovery
papers.research_question: How to discern the rationale behind AI model's predictions in medical imaging for early disease detection and prognosis?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PrognosisEx, an explainable prognostic model that decodes decision reasoning by identifying class-specific features and generating counterfactual explanations for medical image classification.
papers.conclusion: This work presents an innovative, explainable prognostic model that provides insight into its decision process and identifies features used for decisions, improving the safety of AI in healthcare and demonstrating promise for biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
PrognosisEx achieves comparable prognostic performance to state-of-the-art deep learning models while providing explainability.
The model identifies class-specific features that drive predictions, such as ground-glass opacities and vascularisation for mortality risk.
Counterfactual examples generated by manipulating features reveal semantic meanings, like increased GGOs and reduced lung area indicating higher mortality.
Identified features align with existing prognostic knowledge, validating the model's decision-making.
PrognosisEx offers a cost-effective tool for biomarker discovery in diseases with limited prognostic understanding.
future_direction: Broader validation with different imaging modalities and medical scenarios using public datasets.
papers.abstract: In medical imaging, particularly in early disease detection and prognosis tasks, discerning the rationale behind an AI model's predictions is crucial for evaluating the reliability of its decisions. Conventional explanation methods face challenges in identifying discernible decisive features in medical image classifications, where discriminative features are subtle or not immediately apparent. To bridge this gap, we propose an explainable model that is equipped with both decision reasoning and feature identification capabilities. Our approach not only detects influential image patterns but also uncovers the decisive features that drive the model's final predictions. By implementing our method, we can efficiently identify and visualise class-specific features leveraged by the data-driven model, providing insights into the decision-making processes of deep learning models. We validated our model in the demanding realm of medical prognosis task, demonstrating its efficacy and potential in enhancing the reliability of AI in healthcare and in discovering new knowledge in diseases where prognostic understanding is limited.

papers.title: Causal disentanglement of multimodal data
papers.research_question: How can we perform causal representation learning in exploratory settings without interventional data or prior causal assumptions, by leveraging multimodal data and physics constraints?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces causalPIMA, an unsupervised causal representation learning algorithm that leverages multimodal data and physics constraints to discover interpretable causal structures without interventional data or prior causal assumptions.
papers.conclusion: These results show that meaningful causal disentanglement is possible, even in purely exploratory settings without interventional data.
papers.key_findings:
On the synthetic circles dataset, causalPIMA learns a directed acyclic graph (DAG) that correctly identifies causal relationships between circle radius, hue, and shift.
On the 3D printed lattices dataset, causalPIMA learns that lattice type (microstructure) causally influences the mechanical response (stress-strain curve profile).
The algorithm successfully handles multimodal data and can incorporate physics-based decoders (e.g., piecewise linear models for stress-strain curves).
causalPIMA achieves interpretable causal disentanglement in a fully unsupervised setting, without requiring interventional data or structural causal model assumptions.
future_direction: methods for optionally introducing interventions and structural causal models
papers.abstract: Causal representation learning algorithms discover lower-dimensional representations of data that admit a decipherable interpretation of cause and effect; as achieving such interpretable representations is challenging, many causal learning algorithms utilize elements indicating prior information, such as (linear) structural causal models, interventional data, or weak supervision. Unfortunately, in exploratory causal representation learning, such elements and prior information may not be available or warranted. Alternatively, scientific datasets often have multiple modalities or physics-based constraints, and the use of such scientific, multimodal data has been shown to improve disentanglement in fully unsupervised settings. Consequently, we introduce a causal representation learning algorithm (causalPIMA) that can use multimodal data and known physics to discover important features with causal relationships. Our innovative algorithm utilizes a new differentiable parametrization to learn a directed acyclic graph (DAG) together with a latent space of a variational autoencoder in an end-to-end differentiable framework via a single, tractable evidence lower bound loss function. We place a Gaussian mixture prior on the latent space and identify each of the mixtures with an outcome of the DAG nodes; this novel identification enables feature discovery with causal relationships. Tested against a synthetic and a scientific dataset, our results demonstrate the capability of learning an interpretable causal structure while simultaneously discovering key features in a fully unsupervised setting.

papers.title: SkinCon: A skin disease dataset densely annotated by domain experts for fine-grained model debugging and analysis
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SkinCon, a skin disease dataset densely annotated by dermatologists with 48 clinical concepts applicable across multiple diseases, and demonstrates its utility for explaining model mistakes and building interpretable concept bottleneck models.
papers.conclusion: SkinCon addresses the need for densely annotated medical datasets to enable interpretability and fine-grained error analysis in healthcare AI, providing a foundation for developing and validating concept-based methods in dermatology.
papers.key_findings:
The SkinCon dataset provides the first medical dataset with dense concept annotations that are broadly applicable across multiple disease processes, not just a single diagnosis.
Using SkinCon concepts, Conceptual Counterfactual Explanations (CCE) can generate human-understandable explanations for model misclassifications in skin disease diagnosis.
Post-hoc Concept Bottleneck Models (PCBMs) built with SkinCon concepts can match or exceed the performance of the original black-box model while providing interpretability.
The concept importance weights from the PCBM align with some clinical knowledge (e.g., Ulcer, Telangiectasia, Black predict malignancy) but also reveal potential biases (e.g., Scar predicts benign, though cancers can appear near scars).
The dataset enables fine-grained error analysis and slice discovery for dermatology AI models, addressing the need for interpretability in high-risk settings.
papers.limitation:
The dataset does not cover all dermatological diseases and is imbalanced in its concept representation due to real-world disease prevalence.
The dataset lacks patient demographic information (sex, gender, race, age), limiting fine-grained error analysis across protected classes.
The Fitzpatrick skin tone scale used may not have enough granularity to capture the full range of human skin diversity.
future_direction: Expand the size and scope of the dataset by densely labeling additional skin disease images.
papers.abstract: For the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) in high-risk settings, such as healthcare, methods that provide interpretability/explainability or allow fine-grained error analysis are critical. Many recent methods for interpretability/explainability and fine-grained error analysis use concepts, which are meta-labels that are semantically meaningful to humans. However, there are only a few datasets that include concept-level meta-labels and most of these meta-labels are relevant for natural images that do not require domain expertise. Densely annotated datasets in medicine focused on meta-labels that are relevant to a single disease such as melanoma. In dermatology, skin disease is described using an established clinical lexicon that allows clinicians to describe physical exam findings to one another. To provide a medical dataset densely annotated by domain experts with annotations useful across multiple disease processes, we developed SkinCon: a skin disease dataset densely annotated by dermatologists. SkinCon includes 3230 images from the Fitzpatrick 17k dataset densely annotated with 48 clinical concepts, 22 of which have at least 50 images representing the concept. The concepts used were chosen by two dermatologists considering the clinical descriptor terms used to describe skin lesions. Examples include "plaque", "scale", and "erosion". The same concepts were also used to label 656 skin disease images from the Diverse Dermatology Images dataset, providing an additional external dataset with diverse skin tone representations. We review the potential applications for the SkinCon dataset, such as probing models, concept-based explanations, and concept bottlenecks. Furthermore, we use SkinCon to demonstrate two of these use cases: debugging mistakes of an existing dermatology AI model with concepts and developing interpretable models with post-hoc concept bottleneck models.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: How Transformers Learn Causal Structure with Gradient Descent
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn causal structure with gradient descent?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that gradient descent on a two-layer transformer learns causal structure by encoding the latent causal graph in the first attention layer, with the gradient of the attention matrix encoding mutual information between tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformers learn causal structure by encoding the causal graph in the first attention layer through gradient descent, with the gradient encoding mutual information.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient descent on a two-layer transformer learns to encode the latent causal graph in the first attention layer.
The gradient of the attention matrix encodes mutual information between tokens, and the largest entries correspond to edges in the causal graph.
For in-context Markov chains, transformers learn an induction head.
Empirically, transformers trained on the task recover a wide variety of causal structures.
For multiple parents, transformers can distribute the causal graph across multiple attention heads.
papers.abstract: The incredible success of transformers on sequence modeling tasks can be largely attributed to the self-attention mechanism, which allows information to be transferred between different parts of a sequence. Self-attention allows transformers to encode causal structure which makes them particularly suitable for sequence modeling. However, the process by which transformers learn such causal structure via gradient-based training algorithms remains poorly understood. To better understand this process, we introduce an in-context learning task that requires learning latent causal structure. We prove that gradient descent on a simplified two-layer transformer learns to solve this task by encoding the latent causal graph in the first attention layer. The key insight of our proof is that the gradient of the attention matrix encodes the mutual information between tokens. As a consequence of the data processing inequality, the largest entries of this gradient correspond to edges in the latent causal graph. As a special case, when the sequences are generated from in-context Markov chains, we prove that transformers learn an induction head (Olsson et al., 2022). We confirm our theoretical findings by showing that transformers trained on our in-context learning task are able to recover a wide variety of causal structures.

papers.title: X-VMamba: Explainable Vision Mamba
papers.research_question: How can we understand what State Space Models (SSMs) have learned and how they process information, given the lack of transparent attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a controllability-based interpretability framework for State Space Models (SSMs) that quantifies how input patches influence internal state dynamics, with two formulations (Jacobian-based and Gramian-based) that operate in a single forward pass with linear complexity.
papers.conclusion: Controllability analysis establishes a principled, mathematically rigorous interpretability paradigm for SSMs, providing unprecedented visibility into their internal dynamics and hierarchical processing across domains.
papers.key_findings:
SSMs naturally implement hierarchical feature refinement, with early layers capturing diffuse low-level textures and deeper layers focusing on semantically meaningful, clinically relevant patterns.
Influence scores become progressively more focused in deeper layers, with fewer patches having high influence, indicating a hierarchical filtering mechanism.
The choice of image scanning strategy (e.g., forward, backward, transposed) substantially modulates the distribution of influence scores across patches.
The proposed controllability framework provides domain-specific signatures aligned with diagnostic criteria, such as lesion boundaries in dermatology and high-density areas in mammography.
papers.limitation:
The Gramian formulation assumes local linearity of the SSM dynamics and does not account for non-linearities between layers (e.g., activation functions, normalization).
The current analysis computes controllability independently at each layer and does not provide an end-to-end attribution map from raw inputs to final outputs.
For sequential data, the method provides static, per-time-step influence scores and does not capture temporal causal influence (how inputs at time t affect outputs at future times t+τ).
future_direction: Extending the controllability framework to account for non-linear transformations between SSM layers.
Developing methods for end-to-end attribution by propagating influence scores through the entire network depth.
Enabling temporal causal analysis for sequential data to capture how inputs influence future outputs over finite horizons.
papers.abstract: State Space Models (SSMs), particularly the Mamba architecture, have recently emerged as powerful alternatives to Transformers for sequence modeling, offering linear computational complexity while achieving competitive performance. Yet, despite their effectiveness, understanding how these Vision SSMs process spatial information remains challenging due to the lack of transparent, attention-like mechanisms. To address this gap, we introduce a controllability-based interpretability framework that quantifies how different parts of the input sequence (tokens or patches) influence the internal state dynamics of SSMs. We propose two complementary formulations: a Jacobian-based method applicable to any SSM architecture that measures influence through the full chain of state propagation, and a Gramian-based approach for diagonal SSMs that achieves superior speed through closed-form analytical solutions. Both methods operate in a single forward pass with linear complexity, requiring no architectural modifications or hyperparameter tuning. We validate our framework through experiments on three diverse medical imaging modalities, demonstrating that SSMs naturally implement hierarchical feature refinement from diffuse low-level textures in early layers to focused, clinically meaningful patterns in deeper layers. Our analysis reveals domain-specific controllability signatures aligned with diagnostic criteria, progressive spatial selectivity across the network hierarchy, and the substantial influence of scanning strategies on attention patterns. Beyond medical imaging, we articulate applications spanning computer vision, natural language processing, and cross-domain tasks. Our framework establishes controllability analysis as a unified, foundational interpretability paradigm for SSMs across all domains. Code and analysis tools will be made available upon publication

papers.title: Finding Alignments Between Interpretable Causal Variables and Distributed Neural Representations
papers.research_question: Can an interpretable symbolic algorithm be used to faithfully explain a complex neural network model? Specifically, how can we find alignments between interpretable causal variables and distributed neural representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces distributed alignment search (DAS), a method that uses gradient descent to find distributed alignments between high-level causal models and neural representations, overcoming limitations of brute-force search and localist alignments.
papers.conclusion: DAS removes previous obstacles to uncovering conceptual structure in trained neural nets and can discover internal structure that prior approaches miss.
papers.key_findings:
DAS finds perfect alignments (100% IIA) for both hierarchical equality and MoNLI tasks, showing the neural networks implement the high-level algorithms.
DAS outperforms brute-force search and localist alignment baselines in finding faithful alignments.
In the hierarchical equality task, the representation of equality is abstract and not decomposable into input identities, while in MoNLI, the entailment representation can be decomposed into word identities.
DAS can manipulate random network behavior only when the hidden representation is oversized, indicating it cannot construct entirely new behaviors from random structure.
The method reveals that distributed representations (non-standard bases) are crucial for finding interpretable alignments.
papers.limitation:
Scalability to large foundation models is limited because the rotation matrix size grows polynomially with hidden representation size.
The orthogonal matrix assumes linear transformation, which may not be optimal if the aligned variable is represented in a non-linear sub-manifold.
The optimization process stability depends on initialization, requiring multiple runs with different seeds.
Requires counterfactual data (base and source inputs) based on a causal graph.
future_direction: Investigate non-linear transformations (e.g., normalizing flows) for alignment.
Explore better initialization schemes for the rotation matrix.
Scale to large models by using low-rank approximations of the rotation matrix.
papers.abstract: Causal abstraction is a promising theoretical framework for explainable artificial intelligence that defines when an interpretable high-level causal model is a faithful simplification of a low-level deep learning system. However, existing causal abstraction methods have two major limitations: they require a brute-force search over alignments between the high-level model and the low-level one, and they presuppose that variables in the high-level model will align with disjoint sets of neurons in the low-level one. In this paper, we present distributed alignment search (DAS), which overcomes these limitations. In DAS, we find the alignment between high-level and low-level models using gradient descent rather than conducting a brute-force search, and we allow individual neurons to play multiple distinct roles by analyzing representations in non-standard bases-distributed representations. Our experiments show that DAS can discover internal structure that prior approaches miss. Overall, DAS removes previous obstacles to conducting causal abstraction analyses and allows us to find conceptual structure in trained neural nets.

papers.title: Interpretability at Scale: Identifying Causal Mechanisms in Alpaca
papers.research_question: How can we scale causal interpretability methods to large language models to faithfully understand their internal mechanisms, and what causal mechanisms does Alpaca use for a numerical reasoning task?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Boundless DAS, a method that scales causal interpretability to large language models by replacing brute-force search with learned parameters, and uses it to show that Alpaca implements a simple causal model with interpretable boolean variables for a numerical reasoning task.
papers.conclusion: Boundless DAS is a step towards understanding the internal causal mechanisms of large language models, and Alpaca uses interpretable algorithmic structure for the task.
papers.key_findings:
Boundless DAS can efficiently search for interpretable causal structure in large language models.
Alpaca solves the Price Tagging task by implementing a causal model with two interpretable boolean variables (left and right boundary checks).
The alignment of neural representations with these variables is robust to changes in inputs and instructions.
Only a small fraction (5-10%) of the representation space is needed to align each causal variable.
The found alignments are not due to random structure, as shown by comparisons with random models.
papers.limitation:
Failure to find causal structure with Boundless DAS is not a proof that such structure is missing, because the method is not completely exhaustive and the space of causal models tested is limited.
For models where task accuracy is below 100%, IIA is constrained by task performance.
future_direction: Tighten the connection by modeling errors in the language model in more detail.
Involve humans in the loop for testing different hypotheses of the high-level causal model.
Apply Boundless DAS to larger LLMs with stronger reasoning abilities.
papers.abstract: Obtaining human-interpretable explanations of large, general-purpose language models is an urgent goal for AI safety. However, it is just as important that our interpretability methods are faithful to the causal dynamics underlying model behavior and able to robustly generalize to unseen inputs. Distributed Alignment Search (DAS) is a powerful gradient descent method grounded in a theory of causal abstraction that has uncovered perfect alignments between interpretable symbolic algorithms and small deep learning models fine-tuned for specific tasks. In the present paper, we scale DAS significantly by replacing the remaining brute-force search steps with learned parameters -- an approach we call Boundless DAS. This enables us to efficiently search for interpretable causal structure in large language models while they follow instructions. We apply Boundless DAS to the Alpaca model (7B parameters), which, off the shelf, solves a simple numerical reasoning problem. With Boundless DAS, we discover that Alpaca does this by implementing a causal model with two interpretable boolean variables. Furthermore, we find that the alignment of neural representations with these variables is robust to changes in inputs and instructions. These findings mark a first step toward faithfully understanding the inner-workings of our ever-growing and most widely deployed language models. Our tool is extensible to larger LLMs and is released publicly at `https://github.com/stanfordnlp/pyvene`.

papers.title: Outcome-Explorer: A Causality Guided Interactive Visual Interface for Interpretable Algorithmic Decision Making
papers.research_question: How can algorithmic decision-making systems be made interpretable for both expert and non-expert users using a causality-based approach without requiring auxiliary models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Outcome-Explorer, a causality-guided interactive visual interface that uses inherently interpretable causal models (Directed Acyclic Graphs) to support the explanation needs of both expert and non-expert users without requiring auxiliary approximation models.
papers.conclusion: Outcome-Explorer advances research towards interpretable interfaces by leveraging the explanatory power of causal models and provides a visual design that can be extended to other graphical models, as validated by user studies.
papers.key_findings:
Non-expert users reduced interactions with non-impacting variables by 47% and the magnitude of changes to these variables by 36% when using Outcome-Explorer compared to SHAP, indicating better model understanding.
All three expert users found Outcome-Explorer comprehensive for building and interpreting predictive causal models.
Non-expert users rated Outcome-Explorer as easier to use and expressed a higher intention to use it compared to SHAP.
The causal DAG visualization and interaction design allowed users to understand variable relationships and their effects on the outcome.
The two-module design (Model Creation and Model Interpretation) successfully supported the distinct needs of expert and non-expert users.
papers.limitation:
Scalability is limited to a small number of variables (around 7±2), which may not handle real-world scenarios with hundreds of variables.
The study participants were from a younger generation (19-35), and the interface may require adjustments for older users.
Causal models require sufficient variable coverage to avoid islands of variables or correlations, and may be affected by confounders.
future_direction: Experiment with evolutionary and confirmatory factor analysis to introduce latent variables for model completeness.
Develop visual interfaces for expert users to detect and eliminate confounding effects.
Enhance the Model Creation Module with advanced feature engineering (clustering, dimension reduction, pooling) and level-of-detail visualization to handle more variables.
Study how much complexity non-expert users can handle and which methods work best for them.
Study the reception of the system by older members of society and potentially add tooltips and pop-up suggestions.
papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of algorithmic decision-making systems has brought about the necessity to interpret the reasoning behind these decisions. The majority of these systems are complex black box models, and auxiliary models are often used to approximate and then explain their behavior. However, recent research suggests that such explanations are not overly accessible to lay users with no specific expertise in machine learning and this can lead to an incorrect interpretation of the underlying model. In this article, we show that a predictive and interactive model based on causality is inherently interpretable, does not require any auxiliary model, and allows both expert and non-expert users to understand the model comprehensively. To demonstrate our method we developed Outcome Explorer, a causality guided interactive interface, and evaluated it by conducting think-aloud sessions with three expert users and a user study with 18 non-expert users. All three expert users found our tool to be comprehensive in supporting their explanation needs while the non-expert users were able to understand the inner workings of a model easily.

papers.title: Intermediate Entity-based Sparse Interpretable Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can we maintain the interpretable semantics afforded by Interpretable Entity Representations (IERs) while improving predictive performance on downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ItsIRL, an extension of IERs that adds a decoder to improve downstream task performance while preserving interpretability, and enables counterfactual entity type manipulation for debugging.
papers.conclusion: ItsIRL improves predictive performance over prior IERs while maintaining interpretability, and the intermediate entity type layer enables useful debugging via counterfactual manipulation and prototype analysis.
papers.key_findings:
ItsIRL outperforms prior IER methods on two biomedical benchmark tasks (Cancer Genetics and BIOSSES).
ItsIRL maintains an interpretable entity type layer that can be used for counterfactual manipulation to debug and correct model errors.
Counterfactual entity type manipulation using coarse class-specific type sets can improve test accuracy, sometimes surpassing dense non-interpretable models.
Class prototypes constructed from entity type representations reveal global semantic properties learned by the model for each class.
Pre-training the decoder network is important for task performance, as ablations show degraded results without it.
papers.abstract: Interpretable entity representations (IERs) are sparse embeddings that are “human-readable” in that dimensions correspond to fine-grained entity types and values are predicted probabilities that a given entity is of the corresponding type. These methods perform well in zero-shot and low supervision settings. Compared to standard dense neural embeddings, such interpretable representations may permit analysis and debugging. However, while fine-tuning sparse, interpretable representations improves accuracy on downstream tasks, it destroys the semantics of the dimensions which were enforced in pre-training. Can we maintain the interpretable semantics afforded by IERs while improving predictive performance on downstream tasks? Toward this end, we propose Intermediate enTity-based Sparse Interpretable Representation Learning (ItsIRL). ItsIRL realizes improved performance over prior IERs on biomedical tasks, while maintaining “interpretability” generally and their ability to support model debugging specifically. The latter is enabled in part by the ability to perform “counterfactual” fine-grained entity type manipulation, which we explore in this work. Finally, we propose a method to construct entity type based class prototypes for revealing global semantic properties of classes learned by our model. Code for pre-training and experiments will be made publicly available.

papers.title: Explainable Transformer Prototypes for Medical Diagnoses
papers.research_question: How can we improve explainability in transformer-based models for medical image diagnosis by focusing on region-to-region attention rather than pixel-to-pixel?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an interpretable self-attention mechanism using prototype learning for medical image diagnosis, providing region-to-region attention for better visual explanations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method offers a promising direction for explainability in medical diagnostics, with both quantitative and qualitative results supporting its effectiveness.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed interpretable self-attention mechanism achieves a mean AUC of 0.798 on the NIH Chest X-Ray dataset without pre-training, competitive with state-of-the-art methods.
The region-to-region attention more accurately identifies lesion locations in chest X-rays compared to ad-hoc explanation methods like Grad-CAM.
The method provides visual explanations at multiple resolution levels by replacing all self-attention layers in CvT.
The use of parametric prototype vectors for keys and values allows learning canonical representations for important patterns.
papers.limitation: The performance gap compared to some state-of-the-art methods might be closed by pre-training on large datasets.
future_direction: Explore the robustness of the proposed algorithm in medical and non-medical domains.
papers.abstract: Deployments of artificial intelligence in medical diagnostics mandate not just accuracy and efficacy but also trust, emphasizing the need for explainability in machine decisions. The recent trend in automated medical image diagnostics leans towards the deployment of Transformer-based architectures, credited to their impressive capabilities. Since the self-attention feature of transformers contributes towards identifying crucial regions during the classification process, they enhance the trustability of the methods. However, the complex intricacies of these attention mechanisms may fall short of effectively pinpointing the regions of interest directly influencing AI decisions. Our research endeavors to innovate a unique attention block that underscores the correlation between 'regions' rather than 'pixels'. To address this challenge, we introduce an innovative system grounded in prototype learning, featuring an advanced self-attention mechanism that goes beyond conventional ad-hoc visual explanation techniques by offering comprehensible visual insights. A combined quantitative and qualitative methodological approach was used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on the large-scale NIH chest X-ray dataset. Experimental results showed that our proposed method offers a promising direction for explainability, which can lead to the development of more trustable systems, which can facilitate easier and rapid adoption of such technology into routine clinics. The code is available at www.github.com/NUBagcilab/r2r_proto.

papers.title: Neural Network Attributions: A Causal Perspective
papers.research_question: What is the causal effect of a particular input neuron on a particular output neuron of a neural network? The paper proposes a causal attribution method to answer this.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a causal attribution method for neural networks that computes the Average Causal Effect of input neurons on output neurons, satisfying key axioms and providing a global perspective.
papers.conclusion: The proposed causal attribution method provides meaningful attributions that align with domain knowledge and outperforms gradient-based methods like Integrated Gradients in identifying true causal factors.
papers.key_findings:
On the Iris dataset, the method reveals causal trends consistent with decision tree boundaries and data scatter plots.
On simulated sequence data, the method correctly identifies that the third feature is not causal, unlike Integrated Gradients which is biased by correlations.
On airplane anomaly detection, the method identifies causal factors (e.g., lateral acceleration) that agree with flight data recorder reports.
On a VAE with disentangled latents, the method correctly identifies latent dimensions that control rotation and scaling of digits.
The method satisfies axioms (ii)-(v) for attribution methods and avoids implicit biases present in gradient-based methods.
papers.limitation:
Assumes input neurons are not causally related, which is violated in RNNs with output-to-input connections.
Computing interventional expectations exactly can be costly for high-dimensional data, requiring approximations.
papers.abstract: We propose a new attribution method for neural networks developed using first principles of causality (to the best of our knowledge, the first such). The neural network architecture is viewed as a Structural Causal Model, and a methodology to compute the causal effect of each feature on the output is presented. With reasonable assumptions on the causal structure of the input data, we propose algorithms to efficiently compute the causal effects, as well as scale the approach to data with large dimensionality. We also show how this method can be used for recurrent neural networks. We report experimental results on both simulated and real datasets showcasing the promise and usefulness of the proposed algorithm.

papers.title: Language-Based Causal Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can the state variables and causal structure of a dynamical system be learned from unstructured state graphs without prior domain knowledge? How can we learn general causal representations, policies, and subgoal structures using domain-independent languages?
papers.core_contribution: State variables and causal structure can be learned from unstructured state graphs by seeking the most compact representation in a first-order causal language (like STRIPS), and this approach can be extended to learning general policies and subgoal structures.
papers.conclusion: First-order causal languages (like STRIPS) are necessary for learning compact causal representations in dynamic worlds with objects, and the preference for compact representations in such languages uncovers objects, relations, and causes. Richer languages and learning methods are needed for continuous, exogenous, and non-deterministic changes.
papers.key_findings:
The internal structure of states (state variables) can be recovered from black-box state graphs by learning the most compact lifted STRIPS representation that generates the observed graph.
The learned domain representations generalize to instances with different numbers of objects (e.g., grid size, number of packages).
General policies can be learned by searching for the simplest policy over a pool of features derived from domain predicates.
Subgoal structures (sketches) can be learned that decompose problems into subproblems of bounded width, enabling efficient solving.
The use of first-order languages and a preference for compact representations provides a strong inductive bias that uncovers objects, relations, and causes.
papers.limitation:
The method is limited to deterministic, discrete dynamics and cannot handle continuous, exogenous, or non-deterministic changes.
The target language must be expressive enough to capture the dynamics, and the method is inherently incapable of learning dynamics that cannot be expressed compactly in the chosen language.
future_direction: Learning reusable and meaningful language-based dynamic models from raw pixels (e.g., Atari games) is an open challenge.
Richer languages and more powerful learning methods (possibly based on deep learning) are needed for continuous, exogenous, and non-deterministic change.
papers.abstract: Consider the finite state graph that results from a simple, discrete, dynamical system in which an agent moves in a rectangular grid picking up and dropping packages. Can the state variables of the problem, namely, the agent location and the package locations, be recovered from the structure of the state graph alone without having access to information about the objects, the structure of the states, or any background knowledge? We show that this is possible provided that the dynamics is learned over a suitable domain-independent first-order causal language that makes room for objects and relations that are not assumed to be known. The preference for the most compact representation in the language that is compatible with the data provides a strong and meaningful learning bias that makes this possible. The language of structured causal models (SCMs) is the standard language for representing (static) causal models but in dynamic worlds populated by objects, first-order causal languages such as those used in "classical AI planning" are required. While "classical AI" requires handcrafted representations, similar representations can be learned from unstructured data over the same languages. Indeed, it is the languages and the preference for compact representations in those languages that provide structure to the world, uncovering objects, relations, and causes.

papers.title: Causal-oriented representation learning for time-series forecasting based on the spatiotemporal information transformation
papers.research_question: How can causal analysis and multistep forecasting be jointly performed from a unified perspective to understand system dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Causal-oriented Representation Learning Predictor (CReP), a neural network framework that jointly conducts causal analysis and multistep forecasting from a unified perspective.
papers.conclusion: CReP effectively achieves multi-step-ahead forecasting and infers causal networks for target variables, offering a comprehensive understanding of system dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
CReP demonstrates satisfactory forecasting performance with low RMSE and high PCC on simulation models like Lorenz 96.
The framework successfully infers cause and effect networks for target variables, aligning with known causal structures.
CReP applies to real-world datasets, such as cardiovascular inpatients and COVID-19 spread, providing practical insights.
Ablation studies show that all loss components (reconstruction, future-consistency, orthogonal) are necessary for optimal performance.
The method is self-supervised and handles nonlinearity and non-separability better than Granger causality-based approaches.
papers.abstract: In real-world high-dimensional systems, both causal dependencies and temporal information of key variables are essential for dissecting the underlying mechanisms governing system dynamics. However, effective approaches to synthesize these two interconnected aspects for deeper insights remain lacking. Here we show a neural network framework, the Causal-oriented Representation Learning Predictor (CReP), which jointly conducts causal analysis and multistep forecasting from a unified perspective. CReP implicitly learns latent causal representations from observed data while simultaneously making multistep predictions, and explicitly interprets the representations to uncover the causes and effects of target variable. The core idea of CReP is to decompose the original space into three orthogonal latent factors, each capturing distinct causal representations: cause-related, effect-related, and non-causal representations of the target variable. The reconstruction-based dynamic causation, generalized through spatiotemporal information (STI) transformation mechanism, provides a theoretical foundation for simultaneously modeling causal interactions via latent representations and predicting future states using the effect representation. Evaluations on three simulation models and two real-world datasets demonstrate CReP’s robust forecasting accuracy and reliable causal insights. As a self-supervised-learning approach, CReP shows significant potential for practical applications and provides a unified framework to reveal intrinsic mechanisms in dynamical systems by integrating causal relationships and temporal information. In complex high-dimensional systems like power grids or COVID-19 transmission, both causal dependencies and temporal information of key variables are essential for dissecting the underlying mechanisms governing system dynamics. This paper presents Causal-oriented Representation Learning Predictor, a neural network framework designed to jointly conduct causal analysis and multistep forecasting.

papers.title: Representation Learning: A Causal Perspective
papers.research_question: How can causal inference concepts formalize non-spuriousness and disentanglement in representation learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a causal framework to formally define non-spuriousness and disentanglement in representation learning.
papers.conclusion: A causal perspective provides a formal framework to define and enforce non-spuriousness and disentanglement in representation learning.
papers.key_findings:
Non-spurious representations capture sufficient causes of labels, formalized using probabilities of sufficiency and necessity.
Efficient representations avoid redundant features, ensuring minimal sufficient causes.
Disentanglement requires independent features without causal connections in unsupervised learning.
papers.limitation: Not all causal quantities are observable from the data, making implementation challenging.
papers.abstract: Representation learning constructs low-dimensional representations to summarize essential features of high-dimensional data. This learning problem is often approached by describing various desiderata associated with learned representations; e.g., that they be non-spurious, efficient, or disentangled. It can be challenging, however, to turn these intuitive desiderata into formal criteria that can be measured and enhanced based on observed data. In this paper, we take a causal perspective on representation learning, formalizing desiderata like non-spuriousness and demonstrating their practical utility.

papers.title: Missed Causes and Ambiguous Effects: Counterfactuals Pose Challenges for Interpreting Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What problems arise from using counterfactual theories of causality in neural network interpretability, specifically regarding overdetermination and the non-transitivity of counterfactual dependencies?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two key challenges in using counterfactual interventions for interpretability: overdetermination (redundant causes are missed) and the non-transitivity of counterfactual dependencies, which bias findings and complicate causal graph extraction.
papers.conclusion: Counterfactual theories of causality are sufficient for interpreting neural networks, but researchers must account for their pitfalls—non-transitivity and overdetermination—by using diverse data, multiple intervention types, and careful interpretation of causal graphs.
papers.key_findings:
Counterfactual dependencies in neural networks are generally not transitive, complicating the interpretation of causal chains.
Overdetermination (multiple sufficient causes) leads counterfactual methods to systematically miss certain causes, lowering recall.
Local causal dependencies (nodes that affect intermediate components but not the output directly) should be included in circuits to understand how abstractions are composed.
Using diverse datasets and both positive and negative counterfactuals can help mitigate these issues.
Counterfactual theories are still the most actionable for interpretability, but must be applied with awareness of their limitations.
future_direction: Use more diverse datasets and held-out evaluation sets to improve generalization of interpretability methods.
Employ both positive and negative counterfactuals (ablating and injecting activations) to capture redundant causes.
Create toy models with built-in overdetermination and preemption to develop and test methods that handle these challenges.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research takes counterfactual theories of causality for granted. Most causal methods rely on counterfactual interventions to inputs or the activations of particular model components, followed by observations of the change in models' output logits or behaviors. While this yields more faithful evidence than correlational methods, counterfactuals nonetheless have key problems that bias our findings in specific and predictable ways. Specifically, (i) counterfactual theories do not effectively capture multiple independently sufficient causes of the same effect, which leads us to miss certain causes entirely; and (ii) counterfactual dependencies in neural networks are generally not transitive, which complicates methods for extracting and interpreting causal graphs from neural networks. We discuss the implications of these challenges for interpretability researchers and propose concrete suggestions for future work.

papers.title: Emergence of Biological Structural Discovery in General-Purpose Language Models
papers.research_question: Can general-purpose language models infer biological structural logic through abstract reasoning without domain-specific training, or is it dependent on massive biological data?
papers.core_contribution: General-purpose language models possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery through cross-modal transfer from linguistic syntax, enabling zero-shot performance on tasks like protein homology detection without domain-specific training.
papers.conclusion: The deep isomorphism between human language and biological sequences suggests that syntax is a universal property of organized information, and general-purpose LLMs can serve as powerful probes for decoding biological structure without domain-specific training.
papers.key_findings:
A GPT-2 model fine-tuned on English paraphrasing achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, demonstrating cross-modal syntactic transfer.
Scaling to large models like Qwen-3 reveals a phase transition to near-perfect accuracy on standard tasks and maintains 75% precision on remote homology datasets.
Chain-of-Thought analysis shows that models perform 'mental folding', leveraging implicit structural knowledge for reasoning beyond sequence alignment.
The capability extends to DNA homology and Central Dogma mapping, with performance varying based on model scale and pre-training exposure.
The BioPAWS benchmark is introduced to standardize evaluation of cross-modal biological understanding in LLMs.
papers.limitation: Generative tasks such as de novo design of functional enzymes may lead to biologically plausible but physically unstable structures due to hallucinations.
future_direction: Hybrid architecture using general LLMs as high-level architects and domain-specific models as engineers to enforce physical constraints.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) are evolving into engines for scientific discovery, yet the assumption that biological understanding requires domain-specific pre-training remains unchallenged. Here, we report that general-purpose LLMs possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery. First, we demonstrate that a small-scale GPT-2, fine-tuned solely on English paraphrasing, achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, where network-based interpretability confirms a deep structural isomorphism between human language and the language of life. Scaling to massive models (e.g., Qwen-3) reveals a phase transition, achieving near-perfect accuracy (~100%) on standard tasks while maintaining 75% precision on specially constructed remote homology datasets. Chain-of-Thought interpretability reveals that these models transcend simple sequence alignment, leveraging implicit structural knowledge to perform reasoning akin to "mental folding." We formalize this cross-modal universality through the BioPAWS benchmark. Our work establishes a minimalist paradigm for AI for Science, proving that abstract logical structures distilled from human language constitute a powerful cognitive prior for decoding the complex syntax of biology.

papers.title: Causality-Induced Positional Encoding for Transformer-Based Representation Learning of Non-Sequential Features
papers.research_question: How can transformer architectures be extended to data with non-sequential yet causally-related features by generating positional encodings that capture underlying causal structure without predefined feature order?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CAPE, a method to generate causality-aware positional encodings for transformers on non-sequential yet causally-related features, eliminating the need for predefined order and incorporating causal structure via hyperbolic embedding of learned causal graphs.
papers.conclusion: CAPE successfully extends transformer-based representation learning to non-sequential data by incorporating causal structure into positional encodings, with theoretical guarantees and empirical improvements across multiple omics domains.
papers.key_findings:
CAPE effectively identifies underlying causal structure and preserves it in hyperbolic embeddings, encoding causal strength as pairwise distance and causal specificity as distance to origin.
CAPE-generated rotary positional encodings exhibit causal distance-induced attention attenuation and causal generality-induced attention attenuation, as theoretically proven.
CAPE enhances transformer performance on real-world multi-omics tasks including gene perturbation prediction, cell type annotation, cell clustering, and age prediction.
The attention scores computed with CAPE are robust to positional disturbances caused by measurement errors, as shown theoretically and empirically.
Ablation studies show the importance of hyperparameters like DAG pruning threshold, k-hop neighborhood size, and causal generality regularization weight.
papers.limitation:
Effectiveness relies on the quality of the inferred causal graph, which may be inaccurate in extremely noisy or undersampled settings.
Assumes feature-wise causal structure is static across samples, which may not capture sample-specific heterogeneity in highly dynamic systems.
future_direction: Incorporating uncertainty-aware causal discovery.
Adapting CAPE to sample-dependent causal structures.
papers.abstract: Positional encoding is essential for supplementing transformer with positional information of tokens. Existing positional encoding methods demand predefined token/feature order, rendering them unsuitable for real-world data with non-sequential yet causally-related features. To address this limitation, we propose CAPE, a novel method that identifies underlying causal structure over non-sequential features as a weighted directed acyclic graph (DAG) using generalized structural equation modeling. The DAG is then embedded in hyperbolic space where its geometric structure is well-preserved using a hyperboloid model-based approach that effectively captures two important causal graph properties (causal strength & causal specificity). This step yields causality-aware positional encodings for the features, which are converted into their rotary form for integrating with transformer's self-attention mechanism. Theoretical analysis reveals that CAPE-generated rotary positional encodings possess three valuable properties for enhanced self-attention, including causal distance-induced attenuation, causal generality-induced attenuation, and robustness to positional disturbances. We evaluate CAPE over both synthetic and real-word datasets, empirically demonstrating its theoretical properties and effectiveness in enhancing transformer for data with non-sequential features. Our code is available at https://github.com/Catchxu/CAPE.

papers.title: CoT Vectors: Transferring and Probing the Reasoning Mechanisms of LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we transfer the essence of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning into LLMs in a compact, reusable, and efficient way? Also, how can CoT Vectors be used to probe the underlying mechanisms of reasoning in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge, and proposes Learnable CoT Vectors optimized via a teacher-student framework for more stable and robust guidance.
papers.conclusion: CoT Vectors extend the task vector paradigm to multi-step reasoning, and Learnable CoT Vectors provide stronger and more stable gains, while also serving as a valuable probe into the mechanisms and organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Extracted CoT Vectors show a U-shaped performance curve across layers, revealing a three-stage reasoning process (perception, reasoning, expression) in LLMs.
Learnable CoT Vectors outperform extracted vectors and are more stable across layers.
CoT Vectors achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA while requiring orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters.
The effectiveness of CoT Vectors varies with latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences.
CoT Vectors can be used as a probe to analyze the functional organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Performance variability in intermediate layers highlights structural limitations, suggesting that task-level vectors may not fully capture intra-task diversity.
CoT Vectors can sometimes interfere with correct reasoning paths and lead to incorrect answers, as shown in case studies.
future_direction: Explore finer-grained or adaptive vectorization strategies to improve robustness and generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has emerged as a powerful approach to enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing implementations, such as in-context learning and fine-tuning, remain costly and inefficient. To improve CoT reasoning at a lower cost, and inspired by the task vector paradigm, we introduce CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge. Through experiments with Extracted CoT Vectors, we observe pronounced layer-wise instability, manifesting as a U-shaped performance curve that reflects a systematic three-stage reasoning process in LLMs. To address this limitation, we propose Learnable CoT Vectors, optimized under a teacher-student framework to provide more stable and robust guidance. Extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks and models demonstrate that CoT Vectors not only outperform existing baselines but also achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, while requiring fewer trainable parameters. Moreover, by treating CoT Vectors as a probe, we uncover how their effectiveness varies due to latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences, offering new insights into the functional organization of multi-step reasoning in LLMs. The source code will be released.

papers.title: How Well do Feature Visualizations Support Causal Understanding of CNN\n Activations?
papers.research_question: Do synthetic feature visualizations (activation maximization) provide humans with better causal understanding of CNN unit activations compared to other visualization methods like natural dataset samples?
papers.core_contribution: Synthetic feature visualizations do not provide a substantial advantage over simple alternative visualizations (e.g., natural dataset samples) in helping humans gain causal understanding of CNN activations, as measured by a psychophysical task where participants predict the effect of image occlusions on unit activations.
papers.conclusion: Feature visualizations do not offer a meaningful advantage over simpler alternatives for causal understanding of CNN activations, and the proposed psychophysical task serves as a quantitative benchmark for future interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
Synthetic feature visualizations yield 68±4% accuracy, only slightly above the 60±3% baseline with no visualizations and not significantly higher than other visualizations (66±3% to 67±3%).
Simple heuristics (e.g., choosing the image with an unoccluded center or lower variance) can achieve similar performance (up to 63%) without any reference visualizations.
There is no evidence that the widely-used feature visualization method by Olah et al. provides better causal understanding than natural dataset examples or other alternatives.
Human performance and strategy agreement (measured by Cohen's kappa) are only moderate, indicating room for subjective decisions.
The proposed psychophysical task provides an objective benchmark for evaluating unit-level interpretability methods.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a single network architecture (InceptionV1) and a single task (image classification).
The two-alternative forced choice task is a simplified version of counterfactual reasoning and may not capture all aspects of causality.
future_direction: Adapt the psychophysical task to account for other notions of causality and interpretability.
Extend the evaluation to other network architectures and tasks.
Use the task as a challenging test case to steer further development of feature visualizations.
papers.abstract:
A precise understanding of why units in an artificial network respond to
certain stimuli would constitute a big step towards explainable artificial
intelligence. One widely used approach towards this goal is to visualize unit
responses via activation maximization. These synthetic feature visualizations
are purported to provide humans with precise information about the image
features that cause a unit to be activated - an advantage over other
alternatives like strongly activating natural dataset samples. If humans indeed
gain causal insight from visualizations, this should enable them to predict the
effect of an intervention, such as how occluding a certain patch of the image
(say, a dog's head) changes a unit's activation. Here, we test this hypothesis
by asking humans to decide which of two square occlusions causes a larger
change to a unit's activation. Both a large-scale crowdsourced experiment and
measurements with experts show that on average the extremely activating feature
visualizations by Olah et al. (2017) indeed help humans on this task ($68 \pm
4$% accuracy; baseline performance without any visualizations is $60 \pm 3$%).
However, they do not provide any substantial advantage over other
visualizations (such as e.g. dataset samples), which yield similar performance
($66\pm3$% to $67 \pm3$% accuracy). Taken together, we propose an objective
psychophysical task to quantify the benefit of unit-level interpretability
methods for humans, and find no evidence that a widely-used feature
visualization method provides humans with better "causal understanding" of unit
activations than simple alternative visualizations.

papers.title: Measuring Causal Effects of Data Statistics on Language Model's `Factual' Predictions
papers.research_question: To what extent are predictions of neural language models influenced by simple statistics in the training data, rather than by deeper understanding of the text?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a causal framework to estimate the effect of training data statistics (like co-occurrence counts) on model predictions from observational data alone, and uses it to show that pretrained language models causally rely on shallow heuristics for factual knowledge extraction.
papers.conclusion: Causal-based approaches are crucial for understanding and interpreting neural networks, and the presented framework demonstrates that co-occurrence statistics from training data causally affect model predictions, indicating a lack of robust generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The Exact-Match heuristic (memorizing utterances) has a causal effect on model predictions.
The Subject-Object Co-occurrence heuristic (predicting the object that co-occurs most with a subject) has a strong causal effect on model predictions.
The Pattern-Object Co-occurrence heuristic (predicting the object that co-occurs most with a pattern) has a negligible causal effect on model predictions.
The causal effects indicate that models rely on shallow heuristics, suggesting sub-optimal generalization capabilities.
The effects are consistent across 32 different pretrained models from the BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT families.
papers.limitation: The analysis relies on the untestable assumption that all variables affecting both treatment and outcome are observed (ignorability assumption); unobserved confounding could bias the estimation.
future_direction: Explore what other heuristics these models employ.
Refine and discuss the exact structure of the causal graph.
Apply the causal framework to other analysis setups, tasks, and model architectures.
papers.abstract: Large amounts of training data are one of the major reasons for the high performance of state-of-the-art NLP models. But what exactly in the training data causes a model to make a certain prediction? We seek to answer this question by providing a language for describing how training data influences predictions, through a causal framework. Importantly, our framework bypasses the need to retrain expensive models and allows us to estimate causal effects based on observational data alone.
