Addressing the problem of extracting factual knowledge from pretrained language models (PLMs), we focus on simple data statistics such as co-occurrence counts and show that these statistics do influence the predictions of PLMs, suggesting that such models rely on shallow heuristics. Our causal framework and our results demonstrate the importance of studying datasets and the benefits of causality for understanding NLP models.

papers.title: Causal-SAM-LLM: Large Language Models as Causal Reasoners for Robust Medical Segmentation
papers.research_question: Can we harness the abstract reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models to enforce causal invariance in vision models during training and facilitate interactive, user-guided error correction during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework that uses LLMs as causal reasoners to guide a vision model for robust medical image segmentation, via linguistic adversarial disentanglement and test-time causal intervention.
papers.conclusion: Our results demonstrate a path beyond pure pattern recognition toward a new class of hybrid AI systems that integrate powerful perceptual backbones with explicit reasoning engines.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method sets a new state-of-the-art in out-of-distribution robustness, improving average Dice by up to 6.2 points and reducing Hausdorff Distance by 15.8 mm over the strongest baseline.
The method uses less than 9% of the full model's trainable parameters.
The linguistic adversarial disentanglement (LAD) is more effective than a GRL-based approach for style disentanglement.
The test-time intervention via natural language prompts allows for interactive error correction, improving Dice by 5.2 points on a hard subset.
The method achieves a small generalization gap (only 3.9 points drop in Dice from in-domain to OOD) compared to baselines.
papers.abstract: The clinical utility of deep learning models for medical image segmentation is severely constrained by their inability to generalize to unseen domains. This failure is often rooted in the models learning spurious correlations between anatomical content and domain-specific imaging styles. To overcome this fundamental challenge, we introduce Causal-SAM-LLM, a novel framework that elevates Large Language Models (LLMs) to the role of causal reasoners. Our framework, built upon a frozen Segment Anything Model (SAM) encoder, incorporates two synergistic innovations. First, Linguistic Adversarial Disentanglement (LAD) employs a Vision-Language Model to generate rich, textual descriptions of confounding image styles. By training the segmentation model's features to be contrastively dissimilar to these style descriptions, it learns a representation robustly purged of non-causal information. Second, Test-Time Causal Intervention (TCI) provides an interactive mechanism where an LLM interprets a clinician's natural language command to modulate the segmentation decoder's features in real-time, enabling targeted error correction. We conduct an extensive empirical evaluation on a composite benchmark from four public datasets (BTCV, CHAOS, AMOS, BraTS), assessing generalization under cross-scanner, cross-modality, and cross-anatomy settings. Causal-SAM-LLM establishes a new state of the art in out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness, improving the average Dice score by up to 6.2 points and reducing the Hausdorff Distance by 15.8 mm over the strongest baseline, all while using less than 9% of the full model's trainable parameters. Our work charts a new course for building robust, efficient, and interactively controllable medical AI systems.

papers.title: CXR-LanIC: Language-Grounded Interpretable Classifier for Chest X-Ray Diagnosis
papers.research_question: How to make chest X-ray diagnosis models interpretable for clinical adoption by providing transparent, verifiable explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CXR-LanIC, a framework for interpretable chest X-ray diagnosis through task-aligned pattern discovery using transcoder-based sparse autoencoders on a BiomedCLIP classifier.
papers.conclusion: CXR-LanIC addresses the black-box problem in medical AI by providing interpretable patterns, achieving competitive accuracy, and supporting safer clinical deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Discovers approximately 5,000 monosemantic visual patterns spanning clinical categories through transcoder ensembles.
Achieves competitive diagnostic accuracy on five key findings while providing interpretable explanations.
Demonstrates that task-aligned pattern discovery from classifier embeddings yields clinically relevant features.
papers.limitation: Patterns currently lack natural language descriptions, requiring future LMM-based annotation.
future_direction: Complete LMM-based annotation of patterns to generate natural language explanations.
Validate explanation quality through LMM verification and radiologist evaluation.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have achieved remarkable accuracy in chest X-ray diagnosis, yet their widespread clinical adoption remains limited by the black-box nature of their predictions. Clinicians require transparent, verifiable explanations to trust automated diagnoses and identify potential failure modes. We introduce CXR-LanIC (Language-Grounded Interpretable Classifier for Chest X-rays), a novel framework that addresses this interpretability challenge through task-aligned pattern discovery. Our approach trains transcoder-based sparse autoencoders on a BiomedCLIP diagnostic classifier to decompose medical image representations into interpretable visual patterns. By training an ensemble of 100 transcoders on multimodal embeddings from the MIMIC-CXR dataset, we discover approximately 5,000 monosemantic patterns spanning cardiac, pulmonary, pleural, structural, device, and artifact categories. Each pattern exhibits consistent activation behavior across images sharing specific radiological features, enabling transparent attribution where predictions decompose into 20-50 interpretable patterns with verifiable activation galleries. CXR-LanIC achieves competitive diagnostic accuracy on five key findings while providing the foundation for natural language explanations through planned large multimodal model annotation. Our key innovation lies in extracting interpretable features from a classifier trained on specific diagnostic objectives rather than general-purpose embeddings, ensuring discovered patterns are directly relevant to clinical decision-making, demonstrating that medical AI systems can be both accurate and interpretable, supporting safer clinical deployment through transparent, clinically grounded explanations.

papers.title: How Well do Feature Visualizations Support Causal Understanding of CNN Activations?
papers.research_question: Do synthetic feature visualizations provide humans with better causal understanding of unit activations in CNNs compared to alternative visualizations like natural dataset samples?
papers.core_contribution: Synthetic feature visualizations by Olah et al. provide only a small improvement over no visualizations and no significant advantage over natural dataset samples in a psychophysical task measuring causal understanding of CNN unit activations.
papers.conclusion: Feature visualizations do not provide better causal understanding than simple alternatives like natural dataset samples, and the proposed psychophysical task serves as a benchmark for evaluating interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
Synthetic feature visualizations yield 68% accuracy in a human psychophysical task, but natural references yield 66-67% accuracy, showing no substantial advantage.
Without any visualizations, human accuracy is 60%.
Simple baselines (e.g., center or variance heuristics) can reach similar performance (up to 63% accuracy).
There is systematic but fairly low agreement (Cohen's kappa up to 0.40) between participants and between participants and baselines.
The results suggest that all tested visualization methods are similarly helpful for humans in predicting the effect of interventions on unit activations.
papers.limitation:
The experiment only tests one specific notion of causality (predicting the effect of an occlusion intervention).
The task is simplified to a two-alternative forced choice, which may not capture all aspects of causal understanding.
The results are based on a specific network (InceptionV1) and a limited set of units and images, which may not generalize.
future_direction: Adapt the psychophysical task to account for other notions of causality and interpretability.
Use the task as a challenging test case to steer further development of feature visualizations.
papers.abstract: A precise understanding of why units in an artificial network respond to certain stimuli would constitute a big step towards explainable artificial intelligence. One widely used approach towards this goal is to visualize unit responses via activation maximization. These synthetic feature visualizations are purported to provide humans with precise information about the image features that cause a unit to be activated - an advantage over other alternatives like strongly activating natural dataset samples. If humans indeed gain causal insight from visualizations, this should enable them to predict the effect of an intervention, such as how occluding a certain patch of the image (say, a dog's head) changes a unit's activation. Here, we test this hypothesis by asking humans to decide which of two square occlusions causes a larger change to a unit's activation. Both a large-scale crowdsourced experiment and measurements with experts show that on average the extremely activating feature visualizations by Olah et al. (2017) indeed help humans on this task ($68 \pm 4$% accuracy; baseline performance without any visualizations is $60 \pm 3$%). However, they do not provide any substantial advantage over other visualizations (such as e.g. dataset samples), which yield similar performance ($66\pm3$% to $67 \pm3$% accuracy). Taken together, we propose an objective psychophysical task to quantify the benefit of unit-level interpretability methods for humans, and find no evidence that a widely-used feature visualization method provides humans with better "causal understanding" of unit activations than simple alternative visualizations.

papers.title: Feature visualization for convolutional neural network models trained on neuroimaging data
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates, for the first time, the application of feature visualization to CNNs trained on neuroimaging data, showing that it can reveal learned concepts such as lesion shapes and hierarchical features similar to natural image CNNs, with implications for model interpretability and validation.
papers.conclusion: Feature visualization is a promising method for interpreting CNNs in neuroimaging, capable of revealing learned patterns and aiding in model validation, though interpretability for abstract features like sex classification remains limited.
papers.key_findings:
Lower-level patterns in neuroimaging CNNs are similar to those found in natural image studies, supporting the idea of transfer learning across domains.
Feature visualization reveals the shapes of artificial lesions in higher layers, with square lesions showing sharp edges and Gaussian lesions showing smoother patterns.
Abstract patterns for the sex classification task remain difficult to interpret, indicating challenges for complex real-world tasks.
Different regularization strategies (e.g., jitter, rotation, total variation denoising) affect the quality and interpretability of generated images.
Generated images can serve as a validation tool, with uniform distributions potentially indicating model overparameterization.
papers.limitation:
Abstract features in the sex classification task are hard to interpret.
Generated images with almost uniform distributions are a potential sign of overparameterization of the model.
future_direction: Training on larger data sets of clinical tasks.
Assessment of further regularization methods.
Involving scenarios where neuropathological indicators can be clearly described, such as the hummingbird sign in progressive supranuclear palsy.
papers.abstract: A major prerequisite for the application of machine learning models in clinical decision making is trust and interpretability. Current explainability studies in the neuroimaging community have mostly focused on explaining individual decisions of trained models, e.g. obtained by a convolutional neural network (CNN). Using attribution methods such as layer-wise relevance propagation or SHAP heatmaps can be created that highlight which regions of an input are more relevant for the decision than others. While this allows the detection of potential data set biases and can be used as a guide for a human expert, it does not allow an understanding of the underlying principles the model has learned. In this study, we instead show, to the best of our knowledge, for the first time results using feature visualization of neuroimaging CNNs. Particularly, we have trained CNNs for different tasks including sex classification and artificial lesion classification based on structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. We have then iteratively generated images that maximally activate specific neurons, in order to visualize the patterns they respond to. To improve the visualizations we compared several regularization strategies. The resulting images reveal the learned concepts of the artificial lesions, including their shapes, but remain hard to interpret for abstract features in the sex classification task.

papers.title: Rethinking LLM-as-a-Judge: Representation-as-a-Judge with Small Language Models via Semantic Capacity Asymmetry
papers.research_question: Can small language models serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations, even when their generation is poor?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis and introduces INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that extracts evaluation signals from small model representations, enabling efficient and accurate reference-free evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Small LMs retain strong evaluative signals in their internal representations, and the Representation-as-a-Judge paradigm via INSPECTOR offers a scalable and interpretable solution for evaluation and data curation.
papers.key_findings:
Small LMs encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states despite weak generation.
Probing internal representations with INSPECTOR outperforms prompt-based evaluation with small LMs and closely approximates large LLM judges.
The Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis is supported: evaluation requires less semantic capacity than generation.
Probing classifiers can serve as reliable data filters for supervised fine-tuning, leading to performance gains.
Larger LLMs do not necessarily provide stronger evaluation signals than smaller ones.
papers.limitation:
Multiclass prediction performance of probing classifiers is modest (50-60%) compared to binary classification.
Out-of-distribution generalization for multiclass probing is limited, with F1 scores dropping significantly.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as reference-free evaluators via prompting, but this "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm is costly, opaque, and sensitive to prompt design. In this work, we investigate whether smaller models can serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations instead of surface generation. We uncover a consistent empirical pattern: small LMs, despite with weak generative ability, encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states. This motivates us to propose the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis: evaluation requires significantly less semantic capacity than generation and can be grounded in intermediate representations, suggesting that evaluation does not necessarily need to rely on large-scale generative models but can instead leverage latent features from smaller ones. Our findings motivate a paradigm shift from LLM-as-a-Judge to Representation-as-a-Judge, a decoding-free evaluation strategy that probes internal model structure rather than relying on prompted output. We instantiate this paradigm through INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that predicts aspect-level evaluation scores from small model representations. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, GPQA) show that INSPECTOR substantially outperforms prompting-based small LMs and closely approximates full LLM judges, while offering a more efficient, reliable, and interpretable alternative for scalable evaluation.

papers.title: A Survey of the Interpretability Aspect of Deep Learning Models
papers.research_question: This paper surveys the interpretability of deep learning models, classifying previous work and identifying gaps for future improvement.
papers.core_contribution: This survey paper provides a classification of interpretability research in deep learning and identifies gaps for future work, aiming to establish a comprehensive framework for interpretable deep learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper surveys interpretability in deep learning, highlighting the need for a comprehensive framework and terminology to guide future research and application.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability is a multi-dimensional concept involving simulatability, decomposability, and computational accountability.
Post-hoc interpretations can be textual, visual, local, or by instance, as categorized in the literature.
There is a trade-off between model interpretability and predictive accuracy, with simpler models often being more interpretable but less accurate.
Bayesian Deep Learning (BDL) offers a potential unified framework for modeling, reasoning, and interpretability.
Challenges remain in ensuring fairness, accountability, and the distinction between explainability and interpretability in deployed models.
papers.limitation: There is a trade-off between interpretability and accuracy in models, which is a challenge for deploying complex models in critical applications.
future_direction: Developing a comprehensive paradigm and terminology for interpretable deep learning.
Addressing challenges in fairness and accountability in interpretable models.
Exploring Bayesian deep learning as a unified framework for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have attained near-human degree of quality in images, textual, audio, and video recording categorization and predictions tasks. The networks, on the other hand, are still typically thought of as black-box functional probabilistic models that transfer an input data to a trained classifier. Integrating these systems into mission-critical activities like clinical diagnosis, scheduling, and management is the next stage in this human-machine evolutionary change, and it necessitates a degree of confidence in the technology output. Statistical measures are often employed to estimate an output's volatility. The idea of trust, on the other hand, is dependent on a human's sight into a machine's inner workings. To put it another way, the neural networks must justify its outputs in a way that is intelligible to humans, leading to new insights into its internal workings. "Interpretable deep networks" is the name we give to such networks. The concept of interpretability is not one-dimensional. Indeed, the variability of an interpretation owing to varying degrees of human comprehension necessitates the existence of a plethora of characteristics that together define interpretability. Furthermore, the model's interpretations may be expressed in terms of low-level network variables or input properties. We describe several of the variables that are helpful for model interpretability in this study, as well as previous work on those dimensions. We do a gap analysis to determine what remains to be improved to increase models interpretability as step of the procedure.

papers.title: Learn-Explain-Reinforce: Counterfactual Reasoning and Its Guidance to Reinforce an Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis Model
papers.research_question: How can we unify diagnostic model learning, visual explanation generation, and model reinforcement guided by the explanation for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a unified LEAR framework that integrates diagnostic model training, counterfactual visual explanation generation, and explanation-guided model reinforcement to improve both interpretability and performance.
papers.conclusion: The LEAR framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in Alzheimer's disease diagnosis and provides high-quality visual explanations through counterfactual reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The LEAR framework generates multi-way counterfactual maps for visual explanation in hypothetical scenarios.
The explanation-guided attention (XGA) module reinforces the diagnostic model, improving classification accuracy.
Iterative training of the explanation and reinforcement units further enhances both diagnostic performance and explanation quality.
The method outperforms state-of-the-art models in Alzheimer's disease diagnosis on the ADNI dataset.
The framework is portable and effective across different backbone diagnostic models (ResNet18, VoxCNN, SonoNet16).
papers.abstract: Existing studies on disease diagnostic models focus either on diagnostic model learning for performance improvement or on the visual explanation of a trained diagnostic model. We propose a novel learn-explain-reinforce (LEAR) framework that unifies diagnostic model learning, visual explanation generation (explanation unit), and trained diagnostic model reinforcement (reinforcement unit) guided by the visual explanation. For the visual explanation, we generate a counterfactual map that transforms an input sample to be identified as an intended target label. For example, a counterfactual map can localize hypothetical abnormalities within a normal brain image that may cause it to be diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease (AD). We believe that the generated counterfactual maps represent data-driven and model-induced knowledge about a target task, i.e., AD diagnosis using structural MRI, which can be a vital source of information to reinforce the generalization of the trained diagnostic model. To this end, we devise an attention-based feature refinement module with the guidance of the counterfactual maps. The explanation and reinforcement units are reciprocal and can be operated iteratively. Our proposed approach was validated via qualitative and quantitative analysis on the ADNI dataset. Its comprehensibility and fidelity were demonstrated through ablation studies and comparisons with existing methods.

papers.title: The Dead Salmons of AI Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the failure modes and statistical fragilities of contemporary AI interpretability methods, and how can they be addressed through a statistical-causal reframing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues for a statistical-causal reframing of AI interpretability, where explanations are treated as parameters of a statistical model inferred from computational traces, to address false discoveries and statistical fragility.
papers.conclusion: Situating interpretability within the standard toolkit of statistical inference opens promising avenues for turning AI interpretability into a pragmatic and rigorous science.
papers.key_findings:
Many interpretability methods (feature attribution, probing, sparse autoencoders, circuit discovery) produce plausible-looking explanations even when applied to randomly initialized neural networks, demonstrating 'dead salmon' artifacts.
Interpretability methods suffer from broader statistical fragility, including poor generalization, high variance, and sensitivity to experimental design choices.
The root cause of these issues is the non-identifiability of many interpretability queries, meaning computational traces do not uniquely determine explanations.
Hypothesis testing against randomized null models (e.g., comparing a trained network to a randomly initialized one) can mitigate dead salmon artifacts, as shown in probing experiments.
A formal statistical-causal framework, where explanations are surrogate models answering distributions of causal queries, provides a principled foundation for evaluating and improving interpretability methods.
future_direction: Active selection of queries to reduce uncertainty
Meta-analysis of interpretability studies
Bayesian uncertainty quantification for explanations
papers.abstract: In a striking neuroscience study, the authors placed a dead salmon in an MRI scanner and showed it images of humans in social situations. Astonishingly, standard analyses of the time reported brain regions predictive of social emotions. The explanation, of course, was not supernatural cognition but a cautionary tale about misapplied statistical inference. In AI interpretability, reports of similar ''dead salmon'' artifacts abound: feature attribution, probing, sparse auto-encoding, and even causal analyses can produce plausible-looking explanations for randomly initialized neural networks. In this work, we examine this phenomenon and argue for a pragmatic statistical-causal reframing: explanations of computational systems should be treated as parameters of a (statistical) model, inferred from computational traces. This perspective goes beyond simply measuring statistical variability of explanations due to finite sampling of input data; interpretability methods become statistical estimators, and findings should be tested against explicit and meaningful alternative computational hypotheses, with uncertainty quantified with respect to the postulated statistical model. It also highlights important theoretical issues, such as the identifiability of common interpretability queries, which we argue is critical to understand the field's susceptibility to false discoveries, poor generalizability, and high variance. More broadly, situating interpretability within the standard toolkit of statistical inference opens promising avenues for future work aimed at turning AI interpretability into a pragmatic and rigorous science.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Interpretation of Multi-Step Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models perform multi-step reasoning tasks by using a reasoning mechanism or by memorizing answers from pretraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MechanisticProbe, a probing method that recovers reasoning trees from attention patterns, providing evidence that LMs perform multi-step reasoning mechanistically.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that reasoning trees can often be detected from LM attention patterns, supporting the claim that LMs may reason mechanistically.
papers.key_findings:
MechanisticProbe can recover reasoning trees from attention patterns of GPT-2 and LLaMA for most examples.
LMs identify useful statements in bottom layers and perform reasoning steps in higher layers.
Pruning attention heads that contribute to reasoning tree detection degrades performance, indicating a causal role.
Higher probing scores correlate with higher model accuracy and robustness to noise.
Finetuned models show clearer reasoning patterns in attention than few-shot models.
papers.limitation:
The study considered fairly simple reasoning tasks.
The analysis averages over attention heads, but heads may have different functions, especially in shallow models.
The analysis is limited to single-token prediction tasks and does not cover chain-of-thought reasoning.
future_direction: Explore more challenging reasoning tasks.
Analyze reasoning in chain-of-thought prompting settings.
papers.abstract: Yifan Hou, Jiaoda Li, Yu Fei, Alessandro Stolfo, Wangchunshu Zhou, Guangtao Zeng, Antoine Bosselut, Mrinmaya Sachan. Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2023.

papers.title: Can Role Vectors Affect LLM Behaviour?
papers.research_question: Can we identify role vectors in the activation space that improve performance on objective tasks? Do these directions effectively impersonate the role of interest? Does ablating these directions degrade performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces role vectors, a method to steer LLM behavior by manipulating internal activations, showing that this approach improves in-domain and cross-domain task performance more effectively than persona-based prompting.
papers.conclusion: Role vectors can effectively steer LLM behavior and improve performance on objective tasks, providing a more direct and effective control mechanism than persona-based prompting.
papers.key_findings:
Role vectors can be identified and used to improve performance on domain-specific tasks, with in-domain improvements and unexpected cross-domain gains.
Ablating the role vectors degrades performance, indicating their causal role in the model's behavior.
The effect of role vectors is more consistent and substantial than traditional persona-based prompting.
The results support the linear representation hypothesis, showing that high-level concepts are linearly represented in the activation space.
The method generalizes across multiple models and domains, as shown by cross-dataset validation on MedQA.
papers.abstract: The influence of personas on Large Language Models (LLMs) has been widely studied, yet their direct impact on performance remains uncertain. This work explores a novel approach to guiding LLM behaviour through role vectors, an alternative to persona-based prompting. We construct 29 role vectors derived from model activations and evaluate their impact on benchmark performance across multiple domains. Our analysis investigates whether these vectors can effectively steer models toward domain-specific expertise. We measure two key interventions: (i) activation addition, which reinforces role-specific directions, and (ii) directional ablation, which removes them. Results on well-established benchmarks indicate that role vectors do, in fact, influence model behaviour, improving in-domain task performance while also yielding unexpected cross-domain gains. This, in turn, suggests that manipulating internal model representations has a greater impact on outcomes than persona-based prompting.

papers.title: CANDLE: A Cross-Modal Agentic Knowledge Distillation Framework for Interpretable Sarcopenia Diagnosis
papers.research_question: How can we deeply integrate the structured decision logic of traditional machine learning (via SHAP) with the semantic reasoning of large language models to achieve interpretable and accurate clinical diagnosis?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces CANDLE, a framework that integrates SHAP-derived statistical evidence from traditional machine learning (XGBoost) with reinforcement-trained LLM reasoning to achieve interpretable and accurate clinical diagnosis, specifically for sarcopenia.
papers.conclusion: By coupling SHAP-derived statistical evidence with reinforcement-trained LLM reasoning, CANDLE mitigates the interpretability–performance trade-off, enhances predictive accuracy, and preserves high decision consistency, offering a scalable approach for interpretable clinical decision support.
papers.key_findings:
CANDLE achieved an accuracy of 79.3%, exceeding the baseline XGBoost by 6 percentage points while preserving its confusion pattern alignment.
The framework demonstrated high reproducibility with an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) of 0.956 for probability outputs and Cohen’s kappa of 0.842 for binary classifications.
The model maintained stable discrimination (AUC = 0.760 ± 0.010) and balanced sensitivity–specificity across repeated runs under fixed prompts.
Prompt-specific evaluations revealed that the model dynamically adapts its decision boundary rather than merely replicating XGBoost outputs.
The framework mitigates the interpretability–performance trade-off by coupling statistical evidence with semantic reasoning.
papers.limitation:
The framework was evaluated only on a single disease (sarcopenia) and a specific dataset (CHARLS), limiting generalizability.
The integration of statistical attributions with clinical knowledge could be improved to enhance interpretability and semantic richness.
future_direction: Evaluate the approach across a broader range of clinical scenarios and disease domains to assess generalizability.
Develop strategies for more seamless integration of statistical attributions with clinical knowledge.
Validate the approach with a wider variety of predictive models and interpretability methods.
papers.abstract: Background and Aims: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable generalization and transfer capabilities by learning from vast corpora of text and web data. Their semantic representations allow cross-task knowledge transfer and reasoning, offering promising opportunities for data-scarce and heterogeneous domains such as clinical medicine. Yet, in diagnostic tasks like sarcopenia, major challenges remain: interpretability, transparency, and deployment efficiency. Traditional machine learning (TML) models provide stable performance and feature-level attribution, ensuring traceable and auditable decision logic, but lack semantic breadth. Conversely, LLMs enable flexible inference but often function as opaque predictors. Existing integration strategies remain shallow, rarely embedding the structured reasoning of TML into LLM inference. Methods: Using sarcopenia diagnosis as a case study, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were extracted from a baseline XGBoost model and transformed into structured, LLM-compatible representations. An actor-critic reinforcement learning (RL) strategy guided the LLM to reason over these SHAP-based inputs, producing calibrated rationales and refined decision rules. The distilled reasoning was consolidated into a structured knowledge repository and deployed via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for case-based inference. Results: (Omitted here.) Conclusion: By coupling SHAP-derived statistical evidence with reinforcement-trained LLM reasoning, CANDLE mitigates the interpretability-performance trade-off, enhances predictive accuracy, and preserves high decision consistency. The framework offers a scalable approach to knowledge assetization of TML models, enabling interpretable, reproducible, and clinically aligned decision support in sarcopenia and potentially broader medical domains.

papers.title: Explainable multi-modal deep learning for transparent cancer diagnosis: integrating radiology, clinical features, and decision visualization
papers.research_question: How can radiological and clinical features be effectively integrated into a unified multi-modal deep learning framework for cancer diagnosis? Which explainable AI techniques can provide transparent, robust, and clinically coherent insights into multi-modal diagnostic decisions? Does the proposed explainable multi-modal framework enhance both diagnostic accuracy and interpretability when compared with uni-modal and non-explainable models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an explainable multi-modal deep learning framework that integrates radiological imaging and structured clinical data using attention-based fusion, providing transparent and clinically coherent explanations for cancer diagnosis without compromising predictive accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed explainable multi-modal deep learning framework achieves high diagnostic performance and provides clinically relevant explanations, demonstrating that explainable multi-modal learning can reconcile precision, resilience, and openness in oncological diagnosis.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed multi-modal model consistently outperforms uni-modal approaches and simple fusion baselines.
Attention-based fusion demonstrates superior performance compared to feature concatenation.
The integration of explainability does not compromise predictive accuracy.
The model provides clinically relevant explanations that align with radiologist annotations.
The model shows strong generalization across different cancer types and datasets.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation was based on retrospective, publicly available datasets, which might not account for the full extent of variations in real-world clinical scenarios.
The clinician assessment was qualitative and of a small scale, involving a limited number of experts.
Grad-CAM++ and SHAP are post-hoc methods and might not necessarily identify the true causal relationships in the model.
The present setup assumes that complete multi-modal data are available; missing or partially observed modalities are not addressed.
future_direction: Develop the framework for clinical trials and deployment in real-time scenarios.
Incorporate uncertainty estimation, causal explainability methods, and temporal clinical data.
Investigate approaches for resilient multi-modal learning when data is missing and broaden clinician-in-the-loop assessment.
papers.abstract: Introduction Although artificial intelligence–based cancer diagnostic models have demonstrated strong predictive performance, their lack of transparency and reliance on single-modality data continue to limit clinical trust and adoption. Effectively integrating multi-modal data with interpret-able decision-making remains a key challenge. Methods We propose an explainable multi-modal deep learning framework that integrates radiological imaging and structured clinical features using attention-based fusion. Image-level explanations are generated using Grad-CAM++, while SHAP is employed to quantify clinical feature contributions, enabling unified and cross-modal aligned interpretation rather than independent uni-modal explanations. The framework was evaluated on publicly available datasets, including CBIS-DDSM mammography, Duke Breast Cancer MRI, and TCGA cohorts (BRCA, LUAD, and GBM), comprising a total of 3,842 images from 2,917 patients. Results The proposed model consistently outperformed uni-modal approaches and simple fusion baselines, achieving an improved balance between sensitivity and specificity. Attention-based fusion demonstrated superior performance compared with feature concatenation, and the integration of explainability did not compromise predictive accuracy. Visual and clinical explanations highlighted diagnostically relevant tumor regions and established oncological risk factors. Stable performance across datasets indicates strong generalization capability. Discussion These results demonstrate that explainable multi-modal learning can effectively combine accuracy, interpret-ability, and robustness, supporting the development of reliable AI-based decision-support systems for cancer diagnosis.

papers.title: On the Internal Semantics of Time-Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How do time-series foundation models internally represent fundamental time-series concepts? Specifically, which layers encode which concepts, are concept parameters linearly recoverable, how do representations evolve in terms of disentanglement and abstraction across depth, and how do models process compositions of concepts?
papers.core_contribution: A systematic probe-based analysis of time-series foundation models reveals that early layers capture local, time-domain patterns while deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals, and that while atomic concepts are linearly recoverable, representing compositions of concepts remains a challenge.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a structured account of TSFM semantics, showing a layered hierarchy of concept learning and highlighting composition as a key limitation for representing interacting temporal phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers mainly capture local, time-domain patterns such as AR(1) coefficient, trend slope, and level shifts.
Deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals (e.g., variance shifts), with representations becoming more disentangled and abstract with depth.
Spectral and time-warping concepts are the least linearly recoverable from model embeddings.
TSFMs exhibit strong linear compositional properties for most concept pairs, but probe performance degrades for composite concepts, revealing interference.
Representations become more organized and linearly recoverable with increased context length in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
While atomic concepts are reliably localized, composition remains a challenge, underscoring a key limitation in current TSFMs’ ability to represent interacting temporal phenomena.
Spectral and time-warping factors are the least linearly accessible.
future_direction: Explore additional TSFMs, multivariate and irregular datasets.
Adopt controlled-capacity non-linear or causal probes.
Investigate architectures and objectives that better linearize phase and time-warping, and non-linear conditional steering.
papers.abstract: Time-series Foundation Models (TSFMs) have recently emerged as a universal paradigm for learning across diverse temporal domains. However, despite their empirical success, the internal mechanisms by which these models represent fundamental time-series concepts remain poorly understood. In this work, we undertake a systematic investigation of concept interpretability in TSFMs. Specifically, we examine: (i) which layers encode which concepts, (ii) whether concept parameters are linearly recoverable, (iii) how representations evolve in terms of concept disentanglement and abstraction across model depth, and (iv) how models process compositions of concepts. We systematically probe these questions using layer-wise analyses, linear recoverability tests, and representation similarity measures, providing a structured account of TSFM semantics. The resulting insights show that early layers mainly capture local, time-domain patterns (e.g., AR(1), level shifts, trends), while deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals, with spectral and warping factors remaining the hardest to recover linearly. In compositional settings, however, probe performance degrades, revealing interference between concepts. This highlights that while atomic concepts are reliably localized, composition remains a challenge, underscoring a key limitation in current TSFMs' ability to represent interacting temporal phenomena.

papers.title: Interpreting Transformers Through Attention Head Intervention
papers.research_question: How has attention head intervention emerged as a key method for causal interpretability of transformers, and what are its findings and limitations?
papers.core_contribution: Surveys the evolution of attention head intervention as a method for causal interpretability in transformers, highlighting key findings like specialization and redundancy, and demonstrating its utility for model control and safety.
papers.conclusion: Attention head intervention provides a rigorous methodology for causal interpretability in transformers, enabling validation of mechanistic hypotheses and practical applications like model control, though limitations like distribution shift and polysemanticity remain.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit both specialization for specific functions and massive redundancy, with 70-90% removable without catastrophic failure.
Plausible attention patterns (e.g., from visualization) do not guarantee causal importance; heads with interpretable patterns may be dispensable.
Heads interact through complex dynamics, including suppression where some heads inhibit others, revealed through ablation.
Mechanistic understanding from head intervention enables targeted control of model behavior, such as suppressing toxic outputs by manipulating specific heads.
Head ablation provides causal evidence for interpretability, satisfying faithfulness criteria by testing necessity through intervention.
papers.limitation:
Distribution shift creates artificial activation patterns during ablation, complicating causal interpretation.
Polysemanticity prevents clean isolation of individual functions within heads due to superposition.
Scalability constraints limit exhaustive analysis to smaller models, and importance rankings vary across metrics and tasks.
Ablation primarily tests necessity rather than sufficiency, and backup heads can activate, affecting interpretation.
Cross-modal attention mechanisms in multimodal models remain largely unexplored with current ablation methods.
future_direction: Developing intervention methods that avoid distribution shift and unrealistic model states.
Integrating ablation with methods to decompose polysemantic heads for fine-grained understanding.
Extending ablation methodology to cross-attention mechanisms in multimodal models.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are growing more capable on their own, but we do not understand their neural mechanisms. Understanding these mechanisms' decision-making processes, or mechanistic interpretability, enables (1) accountability and control in high-stakes domains, (2) the study of digital brains and the emergence of cognition, and (3) discovery of new knowledge when AI systems outperform humans. This paper traces how attention head intervention emerged as a key method for causal interpretability of transformers. The evolution from visualization to intervention represents a paradigm shift from observing correlations to causally validating mechanistic hypotheses through direct intervention. Head intervention studies revealed robust empirical findings while also highlighting limitations that complicate interpretation. Recent work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding now enables targeted control of model behaviour, successfully suppressing toxic outputs and manipulating semantic content through selective attention head intervention, validating the practical utility of interpretability research for AI safety.

papers.title: Are language models aware of the road not taken? Token-level uncertainty and hidden state dynamics
papers.research_question: Do language models represent the alternate paths they could take during generation? How do hidden activations correlate with token-level uncertainty and steering success?
papers.core_contribution: Hidden activations in language models correlate with token-level uncertainty and can be used to steer generation and predict future outcome distributions, indicating that models implicitly represent alternate reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: Hidden activations in language models reflect token-level uncertainty and can be used to estimate outcome distributions efficiently, offering a way to understand and control model decision-making.
papers.key_findings:
Steering success correlates with token-level uncertainty: models are most steerable when they are least certain about the final answer.
Hidden activations contain information about the model's future outcome distribution, as linear probes on the model's own activations predict outcome distribution better than probes on another model's embeddings.
The dynamics of steering success and outcome distribution are similar, with abrupt changes at the same token positions identified by change point detection.
The correlation between steering success and base outcome probability is moderate (R=0.57) and consistent across examples (average R=0.64).
Linear probes are most predictive in middle layers (layers 6-10) of the model.
papers.limitation:
The computational cost of Forking Paths Analysis is high, requiring millions of tokens to analyze a single base path completion.
Only a handful of examples from three datasets are analyzed due to computational constraints.
papers.abstract: When a language model generates text, the selection of individual tokens might lead it down very different reasoning paths, making uncertainty difficult to quantify. In this work, we consider whether reasoning language models represent the alternate paths that they could take during generation. To test this hypothesis, we use hidden activations to control and predict a language model's uncertainty during chain-of-thought reasoning. In our experiments, we find a clear correlation between how uncertain a model is at different tokens, and how easily the model can be steered by controlling its activations. This suggests that activation interventions are most effective when there are alternate paths available to the model -- in other words, when it has not yet committed to a particular final answer. We also find that hidden activations can predict a model's future outcome distribution, demonstrating that models implicitly represent the space of possible paths.

papers.title: Explaining Chest X-ray Pathology Models using Textual Concepts
papers.research_question: How can we explain black-box medical image classifiers using textual concepts without requiring manually annotated concept datasets?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CoCoX, a method that leverages a vision-language model's joint embedding space to generate conceptual counterfactual explanations for chest X-ray pathology classifiers without needing annotated concept data.
papers.conclusion: CoCoX provides clinically relevant conceptual explanations for chest X-ray pathology classifiers and can be extended to other medical imaging domains with domain-specific concept banks.
papers.key_findings:
CoCoX generates top concepts that align with clinically relevant features for pathologies like Cardiomegaly, Pleural Effusion, and Atelectasis.
The method achieves high recall for primary clinical findings but lower recall for secondary findings, which are more numerous and include non-visual attributes.
CoCoX generates explanations faster than the baseline method CheXplaining in Style.
The approach works across different classifier architectures (DenseNet121, ResNet34, VLM+Linear).
The concept bank can be easily augmented with new textual concepts without requiring annotated images.
papers.limitation: Concepts such as 'Older patients' in the secondary list for Cardiomegaly and Atelectasis are non-visual attributes and challenging to generate conceptual counterfactuals for.
future_direction: Extending the method to other medical imaging domains (e.g., MRI or CT scans) with tailored concept banks.
Exploring ways to improve concept bank creation.
Exploring standardized metrics like expert consensus scores and counterfactual faithfulness in future iterations.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have revolutionized medical imaging and diagnostics, yet their opaque nature poses challenges for clinical adoption and trust. Amongst approaches to improve model interpretability, concept-based explanations aim to provide concise and human-understandable explanations of any arbitrary classifier. However, such methods usually require a large amount of manually collected data with concept annotation, which is often scarce in the medical domain. In this paper, we propose Conceptual Counterfactual Explanations for Chest X-ray (CoCoX), which leverages the joint embedding space of an existing vision-language model (VLM) to explain black-box classifier outcomes without the need for annotated datasets. Specifically, we utilize textual concepts derived from chest radiography reports and a pre-trained chest radiography-based VLM to explain three common cardiothoracic pathologies. We demonstrate that the explanations generated by our method are semantically meaningful and faithful to underlying pathologies.

papers.title: Mammo-SAE: Interpreting Breast Cancer Concept Learning with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to interpret breast cancer concept learning in a vision-language foundation model, specifically to identify latent neurons associated with clinically relevant concepts and understand the model's decision-making process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Mammo-SAE, a sparse autoencoder framework for interpreting breast cancer concept learning in the Mammo-CLIP foundation model, demonstrating that it can identify clinically relevant latent neurons and that finetuning improves concept separation and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Mammo-SAE provides a valuable tool for understanding the causal mechanisms within foundation models for medical imaging and opens new avenues for inference-time interventions to improve interpretability and performance in breast cancer detection.
papers.key_findings:
Top-activated class-level latent neurons often align with ground-truth regions of interest, but some neurons respond to confounding background features.
Finetuning Mammo-CLIP leads to larger concept separation in the latent space, improving both interpretability and predictive performance.
SAE-reconstructed features retain most of the original information, with a drop in AUC-ROC of less than 2%.
A small subset of latent neurons (as few as 10) captures most of the task-relevant signal, as shown by intervention experiments.
The model sometimes relies on spurious or task-irrelevant background regions when making predictions, especially in the pretrained variant.
papers.limitation:
Focus exclusively on the final layer of the Mammo-CLIP model, leaving earlier layers unexplored.
Evaluation limited to only two breast cancer-related concepts (mass and suspicious calcification), not extending to other clinically relevant findings.
Analysis confined to Mammo-CLIP; applying the framework to other vision-language models in medical imaging remains for future work.
Visual probing restricted to the top-10 class-level latent neurons per class, which may overlook other relevant neurons.
future_direction: Applying the interpretability framework to other vision-language models in medical imaging, such as MedCLIP or GLoRIA.
Understanding and controlling for background-sensitive neurons to build more robust and interpretable breast cancer detection models.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Interpretability is critical in high-stakes domains such as medical imaging, where understanding model decisions is essential for clinical adoption. In this work, we introduce Sparse Autoencoder (SAE)-based interpretability to breast imaging by analyzing {Mammo-CLIP}, a vision--language foundation model pretrained on large-scale mammogram image--radiology report pairs. We train a patch-level \texttt{Mammo-SAE} on Mammo-CLIP visual features to identify and probe latent neurons associated with clinically relevant breast concepts such as \textit{mass} and \textit{suspicious calcification}. We show that top-activated class-level latent neurons often tend to align with ground-truth regions, and also uncover several confounding factors influencing the model’s decision-making process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that finetuning Mammo-CLIP leads to larger concept separation in the latent space, improving interpretability and predictive performance. Our findings suggest that sparse latent representations offer a powerful lens into the internal behavior of breast foundation models. The code will be released at https://krishnakanthnakka.github.io/MammoSAE/.

papers.title: Interpretability machine learning models: A critical analysis of techniques and applications
papers.research_question: What are the various techniques and applications of interpretable machine learning models, and what are their strengths and limitations?
papers.core_contribution: A critical review of interpretable machine learning techniques and their applications, highlighting strengths, limitations, and future directions.
papers.conclusion: Interpretable machine learning is essential for transparency and accountability, with future trends emphasizing proactive decision-making, integration with technologies like IoT, and a focus on ethics and fairness.
papers.key_findings:
Traditional linear models are interpretable but may not capture complex relationships in modern datasets.
Model-agnostic techniques like LIME and SHAP provide post-hoc interpretability but may face challenges in faithfully representing model decision boundaries.
Interpretable models are crucial in critical domains like healthcare and finance for gaining trust and ensuring accountability.
There is an interpretability-accuracy trade-off that needs to be considered when selecting models.
Future applications will focus on proactive decision-making, integration with emerging technologies, and ethical considerations.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability-accuracy trade-off in model selection.
Lack of standardized evaluation metrics for interpretability.
future_direction: Integration of domain knowledge into interpretable models
Incorporation of interpretability as an integral part of the model development process
Emphasis on transparency, fairness, and accountability in algorithmic decision-making
papers.abstract: In the rapidly evolving landscape of machine learning, the demand for interpretable models has become paramount to ensure transparency, accountability, and user trust. This review paper critically examines various techniques and applications associated with interpretable machine learning models. The burgeoning complexity of black-box models, such as deep neural networks, has underscored the need for understanding and explaining model decisions, especially in domains where critical decisions impact human lives, such as healthcare, finance, and criminal justice. The paper begins by exploring the motivations behind the surge in interest in interpretable machine learning, elucidating the challenges posed by inherently opaque models. Subsequently, it provides an in-depth analysis of popular interpretable model techniques, ranging from traditional linear models to modern approaches like LIME (Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations) and SHAP (SHapley Additive ex Planations). By dissecting the strengths and limitations of each technique, the paper aims to empower practitioners and researchers to make informed choices based on their specific use cases and requirements. Furthermore, the review delves into real-world applications where interpretable models play a pivotal role. Examples include healthcare diagnostics, where the interpretability of a model's decisions is crucial for gaining the trust of medical professionals and ensuring patient safety. Similarly, in the financial sector, interpretable models aid in risk assessment and regulatory compliance. The paper critically examines these applications, shedding light on instances where interpretable models offer tangible benefits over their opaque counterparts. The review also addresses the ongoing challenges in the field, such as the interpretability-accuracy trade-off and the need for standardized evaluation metrics. It emphasizes the importance of developing universally accepted benchmarks to objectively assess the interpretability of different models. Moreover, the paper discusses emerging trends and future directions in interpretable machine learning, including the integration of domain knowledge and the incorporation of interpretability as an integral part of the model development process.

papers.title: Interpretability Bottleneck Breakthrough Method for Deep Learning Algorithms
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental challenges in model interpretability, and how can they be addressed through innovative methods such as self-explaining neural architectures, adaptive interpretation frameworks, and collaborative systems?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes self-explaining neural architectures, adaptive interpretation frameworks, and collaborative systems to enhance model interpretability while preserving predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: This paper investigates the core issues of interpretability in deep learning and proposes several innovative methods, including self-explaining architectures, dynamic interpretation optimization, and human-AI collaborative interpretation, which significantly enhance interpretability while preserving model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Current interpretability methods face challenges in providing meaningful explanations due to unclear semantics of learned features and limitations of explanation techniques.
Self-explaining neural architectures that generate explanations alongside predictions can enhance transparency.
Adaptive interpretation frameworks that adjust to different contexts improve interpretability.
Collaborative systems that combine AI analysis with human expertise advance trustworthy AI.
Experimental results show the proposed methods enhance model transparency while preserving predictive performance.
papers.limitation: need for improved interpretation capabilities for time-series and multimodal data, as well as further optimization of computational efficiency
future_direction: incorporating causal reasoning techniques to generate more logically sound explanations
exploring interpretability enhancement methods under privacy-preserving frameworks
establishing interdisciplinary evaluation standards
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success across various domains, yet their opaque decision-making processes hinder their deployment in critical applications such as healthcare and finance. This paper examines fundamental challenges in model interpretability, including the unclear semantics of learned features, limitations of current explanation techniques, and the inherent tension between accuracy and explainability. We analyze prevailing interpretation methods, including attention mechanisms, feature attribution approaches, and surrogate models, identifying key shortcomings in their ability to provide meaningful explanations. To address these limitations, we introduce several innovative approaches: self-explaining neural architectures that generate explanations alongside predictions, adaptive interpretation frameworks that adjust to different contexts, and collaborative systems that combine AI analysis with human expertise. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed methods significantly enhance model transparency while preserving predictive performance. These contributions advance both theoretical understanding of deep learning interpretability and practical methodologies for developing more trustworthy AI systems. The findings provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners seeking to implement explainable AI solutions in real-world scenarios where decision accountability is paramount.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: Promoting cross-modal representations to improve multimodal foundation models for physiological signals
papers.research_question: Which pretraining strategies are most effective for multimodal foundation models with diverse physiological signals, and how can cross-modal representation learning be encouraged?
papers.core_contribution: Adding input modality drop to multimodal masked autoencoding (MultiMAE) pretraining improves cross-modal representation learning and downstream task performance for diverse physiological signals.
papers.conclusion: Multimodal foundation models are effective for physiological signals, and explicitly promoting cross-modal reconstruction through input modality drop improves representation quality and downstream task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Pretrained multimodal models develop representations that support a diverse set of downstream tasks in physiological data.
Adding input modality drop to MAE pretraining improves downstream task performance compared to standard MultiMAE.
Late fusion models pretrained with contrastive learning objectives are more variable in performance and underperform MAE with modality drop on aggregate.
MAE with input modality drop encourages cross-modal fusion in attention weights and leads to more distributed tuning of embedding units across modalities.
The learned representations are effective even with limited labeled data.
papers.limitation: Making comparisons with other datasets would be additionally informative, since multimodal fusion strategies are often dependent on the dataset and task at hand.
future_direction: Developing a large range of downstream tasks to better understand the strengths of different pretraining strategies.
Developing new formulations of contrastive learning that may improve task performance for multimodal biosignals.
papers.abstract: Many healthcare applications are inherently multimodal, involving several physiological signals. As sensors for these signals become more common, improving machine learning methods for multimodal healthcare data is crucial. Pretraining foundation models is a promising avenue for success. However, methods for developing foundation models in healthcare are still in early exploration and it is unclear which pretraining strategies are most effective given the diversity of physiological signals. This is partly due to challenges in multimodal health data: obtaining data across many patients is difficult and costly, there is a lot of inter-subject variability, and modalities are often heterogeneously informative across downstream tasks. Here, we explore these challenges in the PhysioNet 2018 dataset. We use a masked autoencoding objective to pretrain a multimodal model. We show that the model learns representations that can be linearly probed for a diverse set of downstream tasks. We hypothesize that cross-modal reconstruction objectives are important for successful multimodal training, as they encourage the model to integrate information across modalities. We demonstrate that modality dropout in the input space improves performance across downstream tasks. We also find that late-fusion models pretrained with contrastive learning objectives are less effective across multiple tasks. Finally, we analyze the model's representations, showing that attention weights become more cross-modal and temporally aligned with our pretraining strategy. The learned embeddings also become more distributed in terms of the modalities encoded by each unit. Overall, our work demonstrates the utility of multimodal foundation models with health data, even across diverse physiological data sources. We further argue that explicit methods for inducing cross-modality may enhance multimodal pretraining strategies.

papers.title: On Hierarchical Encoding and Reasoning in Deep Transformer-based Generative Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internalize hierarchical structures from data, what is the relationship between this internalization and behaviors like generalization versus memorization, and how can insights into hierarchical reasoning guide the development of more unified, robust, and interpretable multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis investigates how Transformer models learn and represent hierarchical structures, develops methods to probe these structures and mitigate harmful memorization, introduces the PSViT model for hierarchical video prediction, and demonstrates a unified next-frame prediction framework for multimodal tasks.
papers.conclusion: The capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional Transformer models (e.g., BERT) concentrate hierarchical linguistic information near the top layers, while autoregressive/permutation-masked models (e.g., GPT-2, XLNet, Reformer) distribute it more evenly.
Verbatim memorization during fine-tuning is often preceded by a spike in n-gram overlap, which can be used for early-stopping or regularization to reduce leakage by up to 90%.
The PSViT model, designed with hierarchical priors, outperforms latent-space baselines on physical simulation benchmarks, extending accurate prediction horizons by up to 50%.
Abstract physical parameters governing video dynamics are most linearly recoverable from the middle layers of PSViT, mirroring the mid-layer abstraction peak for linguistic hierarchy.
Diverse tasks across text, image, audio, and video can be reformulated into a unified next-frame prediction task, enabling a single PSViT-based model to achieve competitive performance without modality-specific encoders.
papers.limitation:
Probing tasks relied primarily on English datasets (SST, PTB), limiting linguistic diversity.
Memorization experiments used datasets of up to 5,000 samples and greedy decoding; different scales or decoding strategies may alter dynamics.
PSViT was evaluated at 128x128 resolution on deterministic simulations; generalizability to complex real-world video is untested.
The multimodal model was trained separately per task; joint multitask training might better foster shared representations.
future_direction: Extend ancestor probing to morphologically rich languages, different syntactic formalisms, and broader discourse structures.
Scale the n-gram-aware loss regularizer to operate efficiently on hundreds of billions of tokens.
Test PSViT on larger-scale, stochastic, real-world video and integrate differentiable renderers for more direct interpretability.
Explore joint multitask training on a diverse corpus of reformulated multimodal data and richer encodings within the visual canvas.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative Transformer-based foundation models have driven remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, yet their internal mechanisms for representing complex hierarchical structures remain largely unknown, posing significant challenges for interpretability, safety, and robust generalisation. This thesis aims to progress on these issues by systematically investigating how such models internalise hierarchical structures, the relationship between this learning and behaviours like generalisation versus memorisation, and how hierarchical principles can inform the development of safer, more accurate, generative models. To this end, we first introduce novel probing techniques to map the layer-wise emergence of linguistic hierarchies in language models and extend this analysis to the visual domain by developing PSViT: a pixel-space Transformer with hierarchical decompositions of video image patches, shown to learn and generalise hierarchical physical dynamics from raw video data. We investigate memorisation during fine-tuning, establishing an n-gram based early warning signal for verbatim leakage and proposing scalable defences that promote structural generalisation over verbatim memorisation. Building on these insights, we further demonstrate that a unified next-frame prediction framework enables a single model to process text, images, audio, and video without modality-specific encoders, thereby learning shared hierarchical patterns across these diverse inputs. Collectively, our findings underscore that the capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and that a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization. By fine-tuning an LLM on a domain-specific, highly structured dataset, we analyze attention patterns across layers, identifying inefficiencies caused by non-semantic tokens with outlier high attention scores. To address this, we propose an algorithm that emulates early layer attention patterns across downstream layers to re-balance skewed attention distributions and enhance knowledge abstraction. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics of LLMs but also significantly improves their reasoning capabilities, particularly in non-STEM domains. Our study lays the groundwork for further innovations in LLM design, aiming to create more powerful, versatile, and responsible models capable of tackling a broad range of real-world applications.

papers.title: LLaVA Steering: Visual Instruction Tuning with 500x Fewer Parameters through Modality Linear Representation-Steering
papers.research_question: How can the number of trainable parameters for visual instruction tuning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be significantly reduced by addressing the intrinsic imbalance between text and visual modalities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Modality Linear Representation-Steering (MoReS), a method that rebalances text and visual modalities in MLLMs by steering visual representations through linear transformations, achieving comparable performance to LoRA with 500x fewer trainable parameters.
papers.conclusion: MoReS provides an efficient and effective approach for visual instruction tuning in MLLMs by addressing modality imbalance, significantly reducing parameter count while maintaining performance, and offering a pathway for more accessible and customizable multimodal model development.
papers.key_findings:
MoReS requires 287 to 1,150 times fewer trainable parameters than LoRA while maintaining competitive performance on multiple visual benchmarks.
MoReS effectively rebalances the attention distribution between visual and textual representations, mitigating the intrinsic modality imbalance in MLLMs.
The method reduces hallucination in MLLMs, as shown by improved performance on POPE and HallucinationBench.
MoReS preserves the LLM's pre-trained world knowledge and performs well on text-only tasks, demonstrating its generalizability.
A dynamic steering ratio mechanism allows MoReS to adapt to tasks of varying complexity, with optimal ratios differing per dataset.
papers.abstract: Jinhe Bi, Yujun Wang, Haokun Chen, Xun Xiao, Artur Hecker, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Causal Abstraction: A Theoretical Foundation for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Under what conditions does a transparent algorithm constitute a faithful interpretation of the known, but opaque, low-level details of a black box model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper generalizes the theory of causal abstraction from mechanism replacement to arbitrary mechanism transformation, and uses this framework to provide a flexible, precise formalization for core mechanistic interpretability concepts (polysemantic neurons, linear representation hypothesis, modular features, graded faithfulness) and to unify a wide range of existing interpretability methods.
